We start this chapter with a question that the earlier chapters left open. In chapter 3 we showed that a body expands when heated and that stresses arise in it if the expansion is not free. There we took the temperature as known, for example 30 K of difference in a steel bar between two walls. Here we will compute it: from how the body is heated or cooled at its boundary we will find the temperature at every point and how it changes with time. Then we will compute the stresses from it.

The word conduction says what happens: heat is led through the material from point to point, as a stream of water is led through a pipe, while the material itself stays at rest. Heat is energy that passes from one part of a body to another because of a difference in temperature. In everyday experience, such as a spoon left in hot soup, we see only that the handle becomes warm. The chapter shows along which path and how fast.

A pipe and a housing show why this matters. In a thick-walled pipe carrying a hot fluid the inner wall is warmer than the outer one, and the stresses caused by this difference add to the stresses from internal pressure from chapter 11. In a steel bar between rigid walls the temperature alone decides how large a stress arises in it. Without knowing the temperature we cannot predict these stresses.

The chapter promises four things. First, we will say what the flow of heat is and what determines it, and from the conservation of energy derive the equation that the temperature satisfies, with all assumptions and with a proof that the solution is not doubled for given data at the boundary and at the start. Second, we will solve the equation for a wall, a bar and a rectangle, also with the Fourier series from chapters 9 and 13. Third, from the computed temperature we will determine the stresses in a bar, a beam and a pipe. Fourth, we will carry the same computation over to the finite elements of chapters 7 and 12, also for a process that changes with time.

14.1 Heat flow and Fourier's law

A spoon left in hot soup cannot be held by its handle after a few minutes, although the soup never reaches the handle. The end in the soup is hot, the end in the hand cool, and in time the hand warms too. Something has moved along the metal. By which path, how fast and how much? In chapters 3 and 5 we took the temperature of a body as known, for instance a cantilever whose upper edge is 20 K warmer than its lower edge. Here we shall compute it from how the body is heated at its boundary. The first step is the question about the spoon: what flows, and what decides how much.

From history

For fourteen years Fourier was prefect of Grenoble, and in that time he carried out elaborate investigations on the propagation of heat in solid bodies, published in 1822 in La Théorie analytique de la chaleur (CAJORI, PDF p. 286). Cajori calls this work the source of all modern methods of mathematical physics in which partial differential equations are integrated for fixed boundary values (CAJORI, PDF p. 286). That is why we return to him in this chapter: we too shall have a body, on its surface a temperature or a heat flow will be given, and in the interior we shall look for the temperature field. The law that connects the flow of heat with the temperature difference carries his name in the books (CM §6.7.2, PDF p. 281, SADD §12.1, PDF p. 378). The story of Fourier series and of the dispute over them was told in section 9.11.

Back to the spoon. To compute, we first have to name three things: the temperature, the heat, and the heat that flows through a surface.

Definition 14.1 Temperature field and heat (temperaturno polje in toplota)

The temperature (temperatura) of a point of a body is the number a thermometer shows when it comes into equilibrium with the piece of the body at that point. It is measured in kelvins (K). In degrees Celsius (°C) a temperature difference is the same as in kelvins, so differences may be measured in either unit (COOK §12.1, PDF p. 469). The temperature field (temperaturno polje) of a body is the function \(T\) that assigns to a point \(P\) of the body at time \(t\) the temperature \(T(P, t)\), a number. When time does not change we do not write it. Heat (toplota) is energy that, because of a temperature difference, passes from one part of a body to another or from one body to another (CM §6.7.1, PDF p. 280). The unit of heat is the joule (J), the unit of power, that is heat per second, is the watt, \(1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}\) (COOK §12.1, PDF p. 469).

Source: COOK §12.1 (PDF p. 469) for the units, CM §6.7.1 (PDF p. 280) for heat.

The Slovenian word for heat, toplota, comes from topel, warm. A field is a rule that assigns a value to every point (definition 1.23 for displacements), so the temperature field is the temperature at every point. As every quantity in a continuum, the temperature of a point means the temperature of a piece around the point that is large compared with the grains of the material and small compared with the body (definition 1.1). The beam of chapter 5 also has a temperature field, there written \(\theta\) as a change of temperature. Here we write \(T\), as in chapter 3. In chapter 13 \(T\) is the tension in a string, in this chapter it is always the temperature.

Heat is transferred in three ways: by conduction, by the motion of a fluid that carries it, and by radiation (CM §6.7.1, PDF pp. 280-281). Conduction (prevajanje) is the transfer of heat inside a material because of temperature differences between neighbouring points (CM §6.7.1, PDF p. 280). The name says what happens: heat is led through the material from point to point. The transfer by the motion of a fluid is called convection (konvekcija) and we shall meet it in this chapter only at the boundary of the body, where a solid touches a fluid. Radiation (sevanje) is the transfer by electromagnetic waves, which needs no material, and it follows a law in which the fourth power of the temperature appears (CM §6.7.1, PDF p. 281). Because of the fourth power the problem is no longer linear (COOK §12.1, PDF p. 469), so we only name radiation in this chapter and do not compute it. The chapter treats conduction in a solid body at rest.

14.1.1 A slab between two temperatures

First let us see what an experiment shows on the simplest body. We use only what the reader knows from mechanics: that energy is conserved and that for two equal parts side by side the effects add.

We take a slab of one material. One of its faces is held at the temperature \(T_1\), for instance by a flame, the other at a lower temperature \(T_2\), for instance by ice. The thickness of the slab is \(\ell\) and the area of each face is \(A\). The slab is wide, so that we neglect its side edges: at \(\ell = 40\) mm and an area of \(1\) m² the ratio is \(\ell/\sqrt{A} = 0{,}04\), an estimate of the order of magnitude, not a calculation. We wait until the temperatures in the slab stop changing. This is the steady state (ustaljeno stanje). In it the slab stores no energy: if more heat entered it than left it, its energy would grow by the conservation of energy (CM §5.4.2, PDF p. 236) and the temperature would not stay still. So in the steady state the same heat per second flows through every cross section of the slab. We call it \(\dot Q\), its unit is W.

Measurements show that for a given slab \(\dot Q\) is proportional to the difference \(T_1 - T_2\). Most materials satisfy this approximately, and the nonlinearity shows only for a large range of temperatures (BARBER §14.2, PDF p. 235). From this and from the conservation of energy it follows how \(\dot Q\) depends on \(A\) and on \(\ell\).

  1. Area. Two equal slabs of area \(A\), laid one above the other between the same faces, are a slab of area \(2A\). \(\dot Q\) flows through each, \(2\dot Q\) through both together, because heats per second add like energies. For the same temperature difference \(\dot Q\) is therefore proportional to \(A\). We write \(\dot Q = A\,c(\ell)\,(T_1 - T_2)\), where \(c(\ell)\) is a number that for a given material depends only on the thickness.
  2. Thickness. A slab of thickness \(2\ell\) is two equal slabs of thickness \(\ell\), one behind the other. Let the temperature of the joint be \(T_{\mathrm{m}}\) and the total thickness \(2\ell\). In the steady state the same \(\dot Q\) flows through both slabs, so \(A\,c(\ell)\,(T_1 - T_{\mathrm{m}}) = A\,c(\ell)\,(T_{\mathrm{m}} - T_2)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{m}} = (T_1 + T_2)/2\). Each slab therefore has half of the temperature difference. For the whole slab \(A\,c(2\ell)\,(T_1 - T_2) = A\,c(\ell)\,(T_1 - T_{\mathrm{m}}) = A\,c(\ell)\,(T_1 - T_2)/2\), so \(c(2\ell) = c(\ell)/2\).
  3. The same argument for \(n\) equal slabs, one behind the other, gives \(c(n\ell) = c(\ell)/n\). The product \(\ell\,c(\ell)\) is therefore the same for all thicknesses that are whole multiples of one thickness, and we denote it by \(k\). For other thicknesses we assume it from measurements.

The result for the slab of figure 14.1 is

\[\dot Q = k\,A\,\frac{T_1 - T_2}{\ell} , \qquad k = \frac{\dot Q\,\ell}{A\,(T_1 - T_2)} . \tag{14.1}\]

The number \(k\) is a property of the material and is called the thermal conductivity (toplotna prevodnost), because it tells how well the material conducts: the larger it is, the more heat flows for the same temperature difference. Its unit is W/(m K). For real substances it lies between \(0{,}01\) and \(300\) W/(m K) (COOK §12.1, PDF p. 469). For the cantilever of chapter 5 (\(\ell = 40\) mm, \(T_1 - T_2 = 20\) K) we get \(\dot Q/A = k \cdot 20/0{,}040 = 500\,k\) W/m², if \(k\) is in W/(m K). For a slab of the same faces and twice the thickness it is \(250\,k\) W/m², and each of two 40 mm slabs in series has \(20/2 = 10\) K and \(10/0{,}040 = 250\) K/m, so also \(250\,k\) W/m². The books of the project give no value of \(k\) for steel, so we leave the computations dependent on \(k\).

The slab has one direction, the flow is perpendicular to its faces. In a body of any shape heat flows in different directions and through surfaces of any position, so a single \(\dot Q\) is not enough.

14.1.2 Heat flux

Take again the cantilever of chapter 5, now in the steady state.

We draw the block of its longitudinal section, with the axes \(x\) along and \(y\) up. The upper edge is 20 K warmer than the lower one, and in chapter 5 we took the temperature in the section linear, \(T = T_{\mathrm{m}} + g\,y\) with \(g = 20/0{,}040 = 500\) K/m. The surfaces of equal temperature are here horizontal planes, in the section lines, drawn at \(0\), \(10\) and \(20\) K above the lower edge. A surface of equal temperature is called an isotherm (izoterma), from the Greek words for equal and heat. The temperature grows upwards, so the temperature gradient, the column of partial derivatives (definition 8.22, item 3), has the components \(\nabla T = (0,\ 500,\ 0)\) K/m. Heat flows toward the cooler side, that is downwards, and the arrows \(\vek q\) point down. We define the vector \(\vek q\) as follows.

Definition 14.2 Heat flux and heat flow (gostota toplotnega toka in toplotni tok)

Let \(T\) be the temperature field of a body, such as figure 14.2 shows. The heat flux (gostota toplotnega toka) is a field of vectors \(\vek q(P, t)\) with unit W/m² such that: through every surface \(S\) the book knows (a piece of the surface of a body between two graphs by definition 4.36, or a surface described by two parameters, definition 4.61), with a chosen unit normal \(\vek n\), heat flows at the rate

\[\Phi_{\mathrm{S}} = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{14.2}\]

that is the flux of the field \(\vek q\) through \(S\). The number \(\Phi_{\mathrm{S}}\) is the heat flow through the surface (toplotni tok skozi ploskev), unit W. It is positive when heat flows in the direction of the normal \(\vek n\). Through the surface of a body with the outward normal \(\Phi_{\mathrm{S}}\) is the heat that leaves the body per second, and \(-\Phi_{\mathrm{S}}\) enters it.

Source: CM §5.4.2 (PDF p. 237): \(\vek q\) is the heat flux vector, the heat entering through a surface with the outward normal \(\hat{\vek n}\) is \(-\vek q\cdot\hat{\vek n}\). COOK §12.1 (PDF p. 470): the flux is a vector quantity that transforms like a displacement. SADD §12.1 (PDF p. 378).

The name density is as in the density of mass: a quantity per unit, here heat per second and per unit area, which each arrow \(\vek q\) shows. The letters \(q\) and \(k\) already have other meanings in the book: \(q\) is the load per length in chapter 5, \(k\) is the shear factor there and the spring stiffness in chapter 9. Since they never meet in the same calculation, we tell them apart by context: in this chapter \(\vek q\) is always the heat flux and \(k\) the thermal conductivity. That a vector field describes heat is an assumption of the model, introduced in the same way by CM (§5.4.2, PDF p. 237). As the stress vector (theorem 2.24) tells what the surroundings transmit through a surface, \(\vek q\) tells how much heat flows through it.

We test the definition on the cantilever, where \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T = (0,\ -500\,k,\ 0)\) W/m². On three patches of area \(1\ \text{cm}^2 = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\) the vector \(\vek q\) is the same everywhere, so \(\Phi_{\mathrm{S}} = \vek q\cdot\vek n\,A\) exactly. The horizontal patch with the normal \(\vek n_1 = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) has \(\vek q\cdot\vek n_1 = -500\,k\) and \(\Phi = -0{,}05\,k\) W. The sign is minus because heat flows against the normal, downwards. The vertical patch with \(\vek n_2 = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) has \(\vek q\cdot\vek n_2 = 0\) and \(\Phi = 0\): heat flows parallel to it and does not cross it. The inclined patch with the normal \(\vek n_3 = (\sin 60^\circ,\ \cos 60^\circ,\ 0)\) has \(\vek q\cdot\vek n_3 = -250\,k\) and \(\Phi = -0{,}025\,k\) W. Through a horizontal section of the beam, 1 m long and 20 mm wide, so of area \(0{,}02\ \text{m}^2\), \(10\,k\) W flows downwards. For a piece of the cantilever 0,1 m long, bounded above and below by faces of area \(0{,}1 \cdot 0{,}02 = 0{,}002\ \text{m}^2\), we get \(\Phi = -1{,}0\,k\) W through the upper face (normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), heat enters) and \(+1{,}0\,k\) W through the lower face (normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), heat leaves). The side faces contribute nothing, the sum is zero: as much heat enters the piece as leaves it, which the steady state requires.

14.1.3 Fourier's law

How is \(\vek q\) connected with the temperature field? The slab of figure 14.1 and equation (14.1) is the answer in one case. Let the axis \(x\) be perpendicular to the faces, \(T(0) = T_1\) and \(T(\ell) = T_2\). The flux per unit area in the direction \(x\) is \(q_{\mathrm{x}} = \dot Q/A = k\,(T_1 - T_2)/\ell = -k\,(T_2 - T_1)/\ell\). The number \((T_2 - T_1)/\ell\) is the mean derivative of \(T\) with respect to \(x\) across the slab. That the derivative is the same everywhere follows from the law (14.1) applied to parts of the slab, as for the two slabs one behind the other. Since the slab is wide, every plane parallel to the faces has a single temperature, at the depth \(x\) the temperature \(T(x)\). Take two depths \(0 \le x_1 < x_2 \le \ell\). The part of the slab between them is a slab of thickness \(x_2 - x_1\) with faces at the temperatures \(T(x_1)\) and \(T(x_2)\). In the steady state the same \(\dot Q\) flows through it as through every cross section. By equation (14.1), \(\dot Q = k\,A\,\big(T(x_1) - T(x_2)\big)/(x_2 - x_1)\), so

\[\frac{T(x_2) - T(x_1)}{x_2 - x_1} = -\frac{\dot Q}{k\,A} \qquad \text{for any depths } x_1 < x_2 .\]

The difference quotient is the same number for every pair of depths, so \(T\) is a linear function of \(x\) and its derivative is everywhere \(\partial T/\partial x = -\dot Q/(k\,A) = (T_2 - T_1)/\ell\). So \(q_{\mathrm{x}} = \dot Q/A = -k\,\partial T/\partial x\).

For a body of any shape, for instance the cantilever in figure 14.2, we need three more answers: in which direction \(\vek q\) points, how large it is and which sign it has. The answer for the direction is an argument that is not from a source. Let the material be isotropic also for conduction: slabs cut from the neighbourhood of a point in any direction give the same \(k\) (as in definition 3.4, only that we measure conductivity). We also assume that \(\vek q(P)\) depends only on the material and on the gradient \(\nabla T(P)\) at the same point, not on the temperatures elsewhere. This is how CM (§6.7.2, PDF p. 281) writes the law, and SADD calls it the constitutive relation between \(\vek q\) and \(\nabla T\) (SADD §12.1, PDF p. 378). The slab agrees with this, since its \(q_{\mathrm{x}}\) depends only on \(\partial T/\partial x\). Take a point \(P\) with \(\nabla T(P) \ne \vek 0\). The only direction that is distinguished at \(P\) is the direction of \(\nabla T(P)\), because the material is the same in all directions. Turn the body together with its temperature field about the line through \(P\) in the direction of \(\nabla T(P)\). The material stays the same, because it is isotropic. The gradient at \(P\) stays the same, because it lies on the axis of the rotation. The temperatures at other points do move, but by the assumption they have no influence on \(\vek q(P)\). So the turned body has the same flux at \(P\) as the original one. This flux is also the original \(\vek q(P)\) turned together with the body, so \(\vek q(P)\) does not change under the rotation. A vector that stays the same under every rotation about a line lies on that line. So \(\vek q(P)\) is parallel to \(\nabla T(P)\). For \(\nabla T(P) = \vek 0\) the same argument holds for the rotation about every line through \(P\), so \(\vek q(P)\) lies on each of them and \(\vek q(P) = \vek 0\). The size: a slab with \(\nabla T = (T_2 - T_1)/\ell\ \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) gives \(|\vek q| = k\,|\nabla T|\), and since the material is the same in all directions, \(k\) is the same for every direction. The sign: heat flows from warm to cold (CM §6.7.2, PDF p. 281, SADD §12.1, PDF p. 378), \(\vek q\) points toward falling \(T\), that is toward \(-\nabla T\).

Definition 14.3 Fourier's law and thermal conductivity (Fourierjev zakon in toplotna prevodnost)

Let the body be of an isotropic material (by the argument above, also for conduction, figure 14.2) and let the temperature field \(T\) be continuously differentiable (definition 1.90). Fourier's law (Fourierjev zakon) says that the heat flux is

\[\vek q = -k\,\nabla T , \tag{14.3}\]

where the thermal conductivity (toplotna prevodnost) \(k > 0\) is a number with unit W/(m K), a property of the material. In this chapter \(k\) is constant over the body and independent of the temperature, which is an idealization: for a large range of temperatures the problem becomes nonlinear (BARBER §14.2, PDF p. 235, COOK §12.1, PDF p. 469).

Source: CM (6.7.1) (PDF p. 281), where \(k\) is a tensor of second order, SADD (12.1.1), (12.1.2) (PDF p. 378), BARBER (14.14) (PDF p. 235), COOK §12.1 (PDF p. 470).

The law is not a theorem. It is a model that measurements support, like Hooke's law in chapter 3. It contains three statements that we have explained: direction, size and sign. On the slab it agrees with equation (14.1). On the cantilever \(\vek q = -k\,(0,\ 500,\ 0) = (0,\ -500\,k,\ 0)\), as the gradient pointing up and the flux pointing down show. If \(k\) depended on the temperature the problem would be nonlinear, which the chapter does not treat (COOK §12.1, PDF p. 469). What actually carries heat in a metal or a crystal, at the level of atoms, is in no book of the project, so we do not justify the law by a mechanism and take it from measurements (BARBER §14.2, PDF p. 235).

14.1.4 Direction of the flux against the isotherms

What does the law say about the path of heat? For the cantilever the answer is in figure 14.2: the isotherm is horizontal, \(\vek q\) points vertically down, so perpendicular to it. We check this for a general field. First numbers. The rate of change of \(T\) in the direction of a unit vector \(\vek d\) that makes the angle \(\varphi\) with \(\nabla T\) is \(\nabla T\cdot\vek d\). For \(\nabla T = (0,\ 500,\ 0)\) K/m this is \(500\cos\varphi\) K/m: \(500\) at \(\varphi = 0^\circ\) (\(\vek d\) along the gradient, upwards), \(433\) at \(30^\circ\), \(250\) at \(60^\circ\), \(0\) at \(90^\circ\) (horizontal, along the isotherm) and \(-500\) at \(180^\circ\) (downwards, along \(\vek q\)). The temperature falls fastest along \(\vek q\), along the isotherm it does not change at all.

Lemma 14.4 Heat flows from warm to cold and perpendicular to the isotherms (tok teče od toplega k hladnemu in pravokotno na izoterme)

Let (figure 14.2) \(D\) be an open set of points of the body, \(T\) continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90), \(k > 0\), \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T\), and \(P\) a point of \(D\) with \(\nabla T(P) \ne \vek 0\). The isotherm (izoterma) through \(P\) is the set of points of \(D\) at which the temperature equals \(T(P)\).

  1. For a unit vector \(\vek d\) the rate of change of \(T\) in the direction \(\vek d\) is the number \(\nabla T(P)\cdot\vek d\) (figure 14.2: largest along the gradient). It is largest at \(\vek d = \nabla T/|\nabla T|\), smallest at \(\vek d = -\nabla T/|\nabla T| = \vek q/|\vek q|\), and these are the only vectors with this property.
  2. \(\vek q(P)\cdot\nabla T(P) = -k\,|\nabla T(P)|^2 < 0\), the flux and the gradient point to opposite sides.
  3. For every continuously differentiable curve \(\vek c\), defined on an open interval that contains \(0\), with \(\vek c(0) = P\) that lies in the isotherm through \(P\), \(\vek q(P)\cdot\vek c'(0) = 0\). The isotherm has such curves in two independent directions.
Proof

On the cantilever (figure 14.2) we see all three items. The first two items we prove with the derivative along a segment and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the third with the chain rule.

  1. Let \(\vek d\) be a unit vector, in figure 14.2 for instance the horizontal normal, and \(g(t) = T(P + t\,\vek d)\). By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment \(g\) is differentiable at \(t = 0\) and \(g'(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial T/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} = \nabla T(P)\cdot\vek d\). This is the rate of change of \(T\) in the direction \(\vek d\).
  2. By lemma 6.19 (in figure 14.2: no direction gives more than along the gradient) for the scalar product (definition 2.8), \(|\nabla T\cdot\vek d| \le |\nabla T|\,|\vek d| = |\nabla T|\), so the rate of change is at most \(|\nabla T|\) in absolute value. Equality holds only when \(\vek d\) is a multiple of \(\nabla T\), that is at \(\vek d = \pm\nabla T/|\nabla T|\).
  3. At \(\vek d = \nabla T/|\nabla T|\), in figure 14.2 upwards, \(\nabla T\cdot\vek d = |\nabla T|^2/|\nabla T| = |\nabla T|\), the upper bound, and at \(\vek d = -\nabla T/|\nabla T|\) it is \(-|\nabla T|\), the lower bound. Since \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T\) and \(k > 0\), \(\vek q/|\vek q| = -\nabla T/|\nabla T|\). This proves item 1.
  4. The gradient and the flux in figure 14.2: \(\vek q\cdot\nabla T = -k\,\nabla T\cdot\nabla T = -k\,|\nabla T|^2\) by definition 2.8. The sum of squares of the components is positive because \(\nabla T(P) \ne \vek 0\). This proves item 2.
  5. Let \(\vek c\) be a curve in the isotherm (in figure 14.2 this is the horizontal line) and \(h(s) = T(\vek c(s))\). Since \(T(\vek c(s)) = T(P)\) for every \(s\), \(h\) is constant and \(h'(0) = 0\).
  6. By the chain rule (lemma 4.43, with an interval in place of \(D\)), for the curve in figure 14.2, \(h'(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial T/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\,c_{\mathrm{i}}'(0) = \nabla T(P)\cdot\vek c'(0)\). So \(\nabla T(P)\cdot\vek c'(0) = 0\), and \(\vek q(P)\cdot\vek c'(0) = -k\cdot 0 = 0\).
  7. Curves in the isotherm (in figure 14.2 the horizontal line in the section and the one in the direction \(z\)): since \(\nabla T(P) \ne \vek 0\), one partial component is nonzero, after renaming the coordinates \(\partial T/\partial z(P) \ne 0\). By theorem 8.34 (\(N = 3\), \(m = 1\)) the isotherm near \(P\) is the graph of a continuously differentiable function \(z = \gamma(x, y)\), and the curves \(s \mapsto (x_0 + s,\ y_0,\ \gamma(x_0 + s, y_0))\) and \(s \mapsto (x_0,\ y_0 + s,\ \gamma(x_0, y_0 + s))\) lie in the isotherm and have independent tangents. This proves item 3.

Source: The lemma is not from a source. The direction against the gradient is stated by CM §6.7.2 (PDF p. 281) and SADD §12.1 (PDF p. 378).

The lemma has shown why the direction of the flux makes sense at all: heat does not flow in an arbitrary direction but where the temperature falls fastest, and an isotherm does not conduct heat, because along it the temperature does not change. On the cantilever this agrees with the figure, \(\vek q\) is perpendicular to the isotherm and points opposite to the gradient.

14.1.5 A layered material where this fails

The lemma holds for Fourier's law in the form (14.3), that is for an isotropic material. What happens when the material is not isotropic? An example is a layered material (figure 14.3), for instance wood with fibres or a plate of glued layers, which has another conductivity along the layers than across them. It has two perpendicular principal directions, \(r\) along the layers and \(s\) across them, so COOK calls it orthotropic (ortotropen). For it COOK (§12.1, equation (12.1-2), PDF p. 470) writes \(q_{\mathrm{r}} = -k_{\mathrm{r}}\,\partial T/\partial r\) and \(q_{\mathrm{s}} = -k_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial T/\partial s\) with two conductivities \(k_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{s}}\). We compute both conclusions of the lemma as before, but with \(k_{\mathrm{r}} = 3\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\) (the ratio is chosen for illustration, not from a source) and a gradient of size \(100\) K/m at \(45^\circ\) to the layers.

Example 14.5 Layered material, the flux is not perpendicular to the isotherms (plastni material, tok ni pravokoten na izoterme)

Goal: for the layered material of figure 14.3 with \(k_{\mathrm{r}} = 3\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\), compute \(\vek q\) at a point where the gradient is at \(45^\circ\) to the layers, and check items 2 and 3 of lemma 14.4.

  1. We draw the layers with the axes \(r\) and \(s\) and the point \(P\). The gradient has the components \(\partial T/\partial r = \partial T/\partial s = 100\cos 45^\circ = 70{,}71\) K/m, it points at \(45^\circ\). The isotherm is perpendicular to it, at \(135^\circ\), since by step 6 of the proof of lemma 14.4 \(\nabla T\cdot\vek c' = 0\) for the tangent of every curve in an isotherm, for every function \(T\).
  2. By COOK (components of the flux) \(q_{\mathrm{r}} = -k_{\mathrm{r}} \cdot 70{,}71 = -212{,}13\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\) W/m² and \(q_{\mathrm{s}} = -k_{\mathrm{s}} \cdot 70{,}71 = -70{,}71\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\) W/m².
  3. Direction of the flux: \(\arctan(70{,}71/212{,}13) = 18{,}43^\circ\) below the layers toward \(-r\), so at \(198{,}43^\circ\) from the axis \(r\). The direction of \(-\nabla T\), which the flux would have in an isotropic material, is \(225^\circ\). The angle between them is \(225^\circ - 198{,}43^\circ = 26{,}57^\circ\). The flux is turned toward the layers, because the layers conduct three times better.
  4. Item 2 of the lemma, the gradient and the flux: \(\vek q\cdot\nabla T = q_{\mathrm{r}}\,\partial T/\partial r + q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial T/\partial s = (-212{,}13 - 70{,}71)\cdot 70{,}71\,k_{\mathrm{s}} = -20\,000\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\) (W/m²)(K/m). The sum is negative because \(k_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{s}}\) are positive, so heat still flows toward the cooler side. The form \(-k\,|\nabla T|^2\) does not hold here: with \(k_{\mathrm{s}}\) it would give \(-10\,000\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\), with \(k_{\mathrm{r}}\) it would give \(-30\,000\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\), the true value lies between.
  5. Item 3: the unit tangent vector of the isotherm is \(\vek t = (-0{,}7071,\ 0{,}7071)\). Then \(\vek q\cdot\vek t = (-212{,}13)(-0{,}7071) + (-70{,}71)(0{,}7071) = 150 - 50 = 100\,k_{\mathrm{s}} \ne 0\). The flux is not perpendicular to the isotherm.
  6. Why (the layers are another direction): the argument about the direction, by which \(\vek q\) is parallel to \(\nabla T\), used that the material is the same in all directions. The layers give another direction in which the material differs, so a rotation about \(\nabla T\) does not leave the material unchanged. At \(k_{\mathrm{r}} = k_{\mathrm{s}}\) the angle is \(\varphi = 0\) and both conclusions hold again.

Source: COOK §12.1, equation (12.1-2) and figure 12.1-2 (PDF p. 470). The numbers are our computation.

The layered material of figure 14.3 shows which part of the lemma is firm and which is not. The sign of the flux stays: heat flows toward the cooler side here too. The direction of the flux as the direction of fastest fall, and the perpendicularity to the isotherms, however, need isotropy. We wrote Fourier's law for an isotropic material with the number \(k\) (definition 14.3). For a general material CM writes a tensor \(k_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of order two (CM §6.7.2, PDF p. 281), and SADD states that this tensor is symmetric (SADD §12.1, PDF p. 378). For the layered material this is the matrix with \(k_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{s}}\) on the diagonal in the axes \(r\), \(s\).

So we have the answer to the question about the spoon (figure 14.2). Heat flows through the metal, its density is \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T\), it points from warm to cold and perpendicular to the surfaces of equal temperature, and how fast is decided by \(k\). What remains is what happens to the temperature when heat enters a piece of the body differently from how it leaves: the piece warms or cools, and how much is told by a quantity called the specific heat. That is the topic of the next section.

14.2 The heat equation

Section 14.1 said how heat flows through matter when the temperature is known: the flux is proportional to the temperature gradient, \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T\) (definition 14.3). But we do not know the temperature, we are looking for it. We want to know how the temperature at every point of a body changes with time. Take a steel bar with one end held in hot water and the other in the air. If we push thermometers into the bar at several places, we see the places warm up one after another, those near the water first. What decides how fast a place in the middle warms? The answer must connect the flow of heat with the calculation of temperature: the more heat a piece of the bar receives than it gives away, the more its temperature rises. This equation is the goal of the section.

From history

To write how much heat there is in a piece of a body between two points \(a\) and \(b\) we need an integral over that piece with its limits in the notation (this is our reason for the story). The modern notation for a definite integral, with the limits written beside the integral sign, was introduced by Fourier in his book on the conduction of heat of 1822 (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 273). In the book he says that the sign denotes the integral that begins when the variable equals \(a\) and is complete when it equals \(b\) (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 274). The reason this notation fits the balance of a piece is ours: the piece is given in advance by \(a\) and \(b\), so every quantity of the piece must be written with the two limits. Fourier had used the notation earlier, in the Memoirs of the Paris Academy for 1819 and 1820, from which the beginning of the 1822 book is reprinted (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 274). Figure 14.4 shows such an integral as an area under a curve.

The piece of the body that we shall look at is thus the part of the bar between the limits \(a\) and \(b\) on the axis \(x\), which runs along the bar. The integral over it is the area under the curve of a quantity that this section has still to determine. We do the first calculation for the simplest body. Take a straight bar of constant cross-section, with cross-section area \(A\). We wrap the whole mantle of the bar in insulation, a material through which practically no heat flows, as in a thermos flask. Heat can then flow only along the bar, and the temperature is the same across every cross-section, \(T = T(x, t)\), where \(x\) is the position of the cross-section along the bar and \(t\) the time. Figure 14.5 shows the bar.

From the bar we take the piece between the cross-sections \(a\) and \(b\), \(a < b\). The piece is arbitrary, not necessarily short. We shall get the equation at a point from the balance holding for every piece, without ever making the piece shorter, as theorem 14.8 shows. The hatching along the mantle means that no heat enters or leaves there. Through the cross-section at \(a\) heat flows into the piece, through the cross-section at \(b\) out of it. The heat flux \(q(x, t)\) is by definition 14.2 the power of heat per unit area, in W/m\(^2\), and it is positive when heat flows in the direction of increasing \(x\). The power with which heat enters the piece is therefore \(A\,q(a, t)\), and the power with which it leaves is \(A\,q(b, t)\). Both powers have the unit W, because \(\text{W/m}^2\cdot\text{m}^2 = \text{W}\).

What happens to the difference between the power that enters and the power that leaves, \(A\,q(a, t) - A\,q(b, t)\)? It is like the state of an account: what comes in, goes out or stays, and that is why such an accounting is called a balance. We use a law the reader knows: energy is neither lost nor created, it changes only by as much as has entered the piece or left it (the first law of thermodynamics, CM §5.4.2, PDF p. 236, where it is written for a body as a whole: the rate of change of the total energy equals the power of the external forces plus the heat supplied per unit time). In a bar at rest there is no kinetic energy and the external forces do no work, so the difference of the fluxes is stored as internal energy of the piece. It is called internal because it is energy inside the matter, not the energy of the motion of the body as a whole. CM (PDF p. 236) says that internal energy is the sum of the energy of the microscopic motions of the molecules, the elastic strain energy and other forms of energy that we do not see as motion of the body. For us only this matters: when heat is supplied to a piece, its temperature rises. By how much is a property of the material that we measure: we supply heat to a piece of mass \(m\) and measure how much its temperature rises, if it is the same throughout the piece. For different materials the response is different, and we write it as a definition.

Definition 14.6 Specific heat (specifična toplota)
Motivation

A piece of material of mass \(m\) that has the same temperature \(T\) at every point gets a higher temperature when heat is supplied. The quotient of the supplied heat and the product \(m\,\Delta T\) is a number for the material, independent of the size of the piece.

Let \(e\) be the internal energy per unit mass of the material, in J/kg. The material has specific heat \(c\) (in J/(kg K)) if \(e\) depends only on the temperature \(T\) and \(\mathrm{d}e/\mathrm{d}T = c\). For constant \(c\) this is the same as \(e(T) = e(T_0) + c\,(T - T_0)\). A piece of mass \(m\) with uniform temperature whose temperature rises from \(T_0\) to \(T_1\) therefore receives the heat \(m\,c\,(T_1 - T_0)\). The word "specific" means "per unit mass": \(c\) is the heat that we must supply to one kilogram of the material to raise its temperature by one kelvin.

Source: CM §8.3.1 (PDF p. 402, read): \(e = e(T)\) and \(\mathrm{d}e/\mathrm{d}T = c_{\mathrm{v}}\), the specific heat at constant volume, which CM replaces by \(c_{\mathrm{p}}\) at constant pressure for solids. SADD §12.1 (PDF p. 379, read) uses \(c\) at constant volume. The sources differ and neither estimates the difference, so we take \(c\) as one measured number of the material. The unit J/(kg K) and the range \(10^2 < c < 10^4\) for all solids and fluids are given by COOK (PDF p. 469, read). The reason for the name "specific heat" is ours.

From now on \(\rho c\) means the product of density and specific heat. It has the unit \(\text{kg/m}^3\cdot\text{J/(kg K)} = \text{J/(m}^3\,\text{K)}\) and says how much heat a volume of \(1\ \text{m}^3\) of the material needs for its temperature to rise by one kelvin (BARBER §14.2, PDF p. 235). The heat that must be added to the piece with a uniform temperature for its temperature to rise is thus the product of the mass, \(c\) and the change of \(T\). For a piece with cross-section area \(A\) and temperature \(T(x, t)\) the mass is spread along the length with density \(\rho A\), so the internal energy of the piece is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \rho A\,e(T)\,\mathrm{d}x\), and its derivative with respect to time is the stored power \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \rho c A\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) (derivative of an integral with respect to a parameter, lemma 4.19). The law of conservation of energy for the piece then gives the equation

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \rho c A\,T_{\mathrm{t}}(x, t)\,\mathrm{d}x = A\,q(a, t) - A\,q(b, t) + \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b A\,Q(x, t)\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{14.4}\]

in which we have added a possible source: \(Q\) is the power of heat generated in the material (for example by electric heating) per unit volume, in W/m\(^3\) (BARBER §14.2, PDF p. 235, CM §5.4.2, PDF p. 237). All terms have the unit W.

This is the balance for a bar. A body in more than one dimension has no cross-section that the flow crosses only twice. So we repeat the same calculation for a part \(V\) of an arbitrary body. Figure 14.6 shows such a part.

The part of the body \(V\) is a body made of boxes (definition 4.11), as in the divergence theorem. It has a surface \(S\) and an outward normal \(\vek n\) (a unit vector perpendicular to the surface, pointing out). The heat flux \(\vek q\) is a vector, so the amount of heat flowing outward through the surface per unit time is the integral of the component of the flux in the direction of the normal, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\) (definition 14.2). Where heat enters, \(\vek q\cdot\vek n < 0\), where it leaves, \(\vek q\cdot\vek n > 0\). Inside are the sources \(Q\).

Before we write the calculation we say what the model assumes. We name each idealization and give it a measure.

  1. The body is at rest: every part \(V\) consists at all times of the same material with the same density \(\rho\), and the mechanical work is zero. Because of thermal expansion the density changes at \(\Delta T = 30\) K by \(3\alpha\,\Delta T = 3\cdot 15\cdot 10^{-6}\cdot 30 = 1{,}35\cdot 10^{-3}\) (relative, steel of chapter 3, definition 3.13: for small strains the volumetric strain is three times the linear one), that is \(0{,}14\) %. The work of the stresses in this motion, which the model neglects, is the coupling term of thermoelasticity. SADD (§12.1, PDF p. 379, read) says that for most materials it is small under static or slow loading, and so we neglect it (the uncoupled problem). We do not prove an estimate of its size here, because we would need the specific heat of steel, which the book does not have (open question about material data at the end of the section).
  2. Heat is transferred only by conduction according to Fourier's law (definition 14.3). Transfer by radiation depends on the difference of the fourth powers of the absolute temperatures and is therefore not linear (COOK §12.1, PDF p. 469, read, treated in §12.3), our model does not have it.
  3. The material is isotropic (definition 3.4) and the conductivity \(k\) is constant. BARBER (§14.2, PDF p. 235, read) says that for real materials it depends on temperature, but the nonlinearity matters only over a large range of temperatures, and COOK (§12.1, PDF p. 469, read) says that dependence on temperature makes the conduction problem itself nonlinear. A measure: let \(k\) lie over the range of temperatures between \(0{,}95\,\bar k\) and \(1{,}05\,\bar k\), where \(\bar k\) is the middle value (an example, not a datum from a source). With the middle value we then misjudge the flux at a given gradient by at most \(5{,}3\) %. The error is largest at \(k = 0{,}95\,\bar k\), where \((\bar k - k)/k = 0{,}05/0{,}95 = 5{,}3\) %. This bound holds for the flux at a given gradient, not for the error of the computed temperature.
  4. The density \(\rho\) and the specific heat \(c\) are constant (definition 14.6), as in KREYSZIG §12.5 (PDF p. 583, read, assumption 1).
  5. The source \(Q\) is a given continuous function of place and time. It does not depend on the solution.
  6. The temperature is measured in kelvins or in degrees Celsius: only the derivatives \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(\nabla T\) occur in the equations, and they are the same for both units, because the two differ only by a shift of the zero (COOK §12.1, PDF p. 469). For radiation this would not hold.
Derivation 14.7 Heat balance of a part of the body (toplotna bilanca dela telesa)

Goal: for a part \(V\) of a body made of boxes and for time \(t\) write how the heat in \(V\) changes, with integrals over \(V\) and its surface \(S\). The assumptions are idealizations 1 to 5. We also need the temperature \(T(\vek x, t)\) to have a continuous derivative \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\) and continuous second partial derivatives in the coordinates on an open set \(D\) that contains \(V\), at all times in an open interval \(I\).

1
\[U(t) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho\,e\big(T(\vek x, t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
Hint

The material has density \(\rho\) and internal energy \(e\) per unit mass (definition 14.6), so its internal energy per unit volume is \(\rho e\). The energy of the part is the sum (integral) over \(V\).

2
\[\frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t} = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
Hint

By definition 4.11 the integral over \(V\) is the sum of the integrals over the cells, each cell is a box. For a cell we use lemma 8.31 (the parameter is the time): the function \(\rho\,e(T)\) is continuous, its derivative with respect to time \(\rho\,e'(T)\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = \rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\) is continuous, since \(e' = c\). The derivative of a finite sum is the sum of the derivatives.

3
\[\text{heat entering through } S \text{ per unit time:} \quad -\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
Hint

Through the surface flows outward \(\vek q\cdot\vek n\) per unit area (definition 14.2), and what enters is the opposite value. The expression has the unit \(\text{W/m}^2\cdot\text{m}^2 = \text{W}\).

4
\[\text{heat generated in } V \text{ per unit time:} \quad \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
Hint

\(Q\) is power per unit volume, in W/m\(^3\) (idealization 5).

5
\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}V = -\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{14.5}\]
Hint

The first law: the rate of change of the total energy equals the power of the external forces plus the heat supplied per unit time (CM §5.4.2, PDF p. 236). The total energy is kinetic and internal. For a body at rest (idealization 1) the kinetic energy and the power of the external forces are zero, since nothing moves, what remains is \(\mathrm{d}U/\mathrm{d}t\) from step 2 on the left and the heat from steps 3 and 4 on the right.

6
\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}V = k\int_{\mathrm{S}} \nabla T\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{14.6}\]
Hint

By Fourier's law (definition 14.3) \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T\) with constant \(k\) (idealization 3).

Source: CM §5.4.2 (PDF pp. 236 to 238, read), KREYSZIG §12.5 (PDF pp. 583 to 584, read), BARBER §14.2 (PDF p. 235, read). CM takes a volume element \(\mathrm{d}x\) and KREYSZIG and BARBER a small cube, we take a part \(V\) of finite size, as in theorem 13.3. The derivation step by step is not from the sources.

Equation (14.6) holds for every part \(V\). Does the equation at every point follow from it? Yes, because \(V\) is arbitrary: a continuous function that has integral zero over every box is zero everywhere. Why must this be shown and not just stated? Because the argument uses the continuity of the function under the integral, and that needs continuous second derivatives of the temperature. Where a second derivative does not exist, the equation at a point has no meaning, while the balance still holds (example 14.12 below).

Theorem 14.8 Heat equation (enačba prevajanja toplote)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points of the body, \(I\) an open time interval and \(T(\vek x, t)\) a temperature with continuous \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\) and continuous second partial derivatives in the coordinates on \(D\times I\). Let the material be as in idealizations 1 to 5, with constant \(\rho > 0\), \(c > 0\) and \(k > 0\), and let \(Q\) be continuous on \(D\times I\). Then equation (14.6) holds for every body \(V\) made of boxes in \(D\) and every time \(t \in I\) if and only if at every point \(\vek x\) of \(D\) and at every time \(t\) of \(I\)

\[\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = k\,\nabla^2 T + Q , \tag{14.7}\]

where \(\nabla^2\) is the Laplace operator (definition 11.5).

Proof

We must show that equation (14.6) for all parts \(V\) is one and the same equation as (14.7) at all points. We write the difference of the two sides as an integral of one continuous function over \(V\). Then we use that a continuous function with integral zero over every box cannot differ from zero at any point.

  1. Let \(f = \rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} - k\,\nabla^2 T - Q\). The function \(f\) is continuous on \(D\times I\), because \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\), the second derivatives of \(T\) and \(Q\) are continuous.
  2. The field \(\vek v = k\,\nabla T = k\,(T_{\mathrm{x}}, T_{\mathrm{y}}, T_{\mathrm{z}})\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), because \(T\) has continuous second derivatives. Its divergence (definition 4.13) is \(k\,(T_{\mathrm{xx}} + T_{\mathrm{yy}} + T_{\mathrm{zz}}) = k\,\nabla^2 T\). By the divergence theorem 4.14, item 2, \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,\nabla^2 T\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} k\,\nabla T\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  3. By step 2 and linearity of the integral (lemma 4.10, item 1) the difference of the left and right sides of equation (14.6) equals \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). For \(V\) the equation is thus \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).
  4. If (14.7) holds, then \(f = 0\) everywhere, so \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\) for every \(V\), and by step 3 (14.6) holds.
  5. Conversely, let (14.6) hold for every \(V\) and time \(t\). With \(t\) fixed assume that \(f(P, t) \neq 0\) at some point \(P\) of \(D\), say \(f(P, t) > 0\) (for \(< 0\) the calculation is the same with the signs exchanged). By continuity, and since \(D\) is open, there is a ball with centre \(P\) that lies in \(D\) and in which \(f(\cdot, t) > f(P, t)/2\). In it lies a box \(K\) that contains \(P\) (a cube with centre \(P\) and a small enough side). By monotonicity and the property of a constant function (lemma 4.10, items 2 and 4) \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \ge \tfrac12 f(P, t)\,V_{\mathrm{K}} > 0\), where \(V_{\mathrm{K}}\) is the volume of the box. This contradicts \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\) from step 3 for \(V = K\). So \(f = 0\) everywhere and (14.7) holds.

Source: KREYSZIG §12.5 (PDF p. 584, read): "Since this holds for any region in the body, the integrand (if continuous) must be zero everywhere." BARBER (14.15) (PDF p. 235), CM (8.3.3) (PDF p. 402), SADD (12.1.8) (PDF p. 379, without the coupling term). The proof with a box and continuity is not from the sources.

The theorem holds for bodies made of boxes. A round bar or a plate is not one, but by corollary 4.40 on a body cut into pieces equation (14.6) holds also for every part that we can cut into pieces between graphs, and we use this for the bar. If the conductivity \(k\) is not constant but a function with continuous first derivatives, the same proof with \(\vek v = k\,\nabla T\) gives \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = \nabla\cdot(k\,\nabla T) + Q\). A layered body, however, has a jump of \(k\), and there the equation at a point does not hold, as example 14.12 below shows.

The units are in order: \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\) has the unit \(\text{J/(m}^3\text{K)}\cdot\text{K/s} = \text{W/m}^3\), and \(k\,\nabla^2 T\) the unit \(\text{W/(m K)}\cdot\text{K/m}^2 = \text{W/m}^3\). Both sides are power per unit volume. Since \(\rho c\) stands with the derivative in time and \(k\) with the second derivative in place, we divide by \(\rho c\) and get an equation with a single number of the material.

Definition 14.9 Thermal diffusivity (temperaturna prevodnost)

The thermal diffusivity of a material with conductivity \(k\), density \(\rho\) and specific heat \(c\) is the number

\[\kappa = \frac{k}{\rho c} , \tag{14.8}\]

in m\(^2\)/s. The heat equation (theorem 14.8) is then \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = \kappa\,\nabla^2 T + Q/(\rho c)\).

Explanation

The name has its reason in \(\kappa\) combining two opposite properties: \(k\) says how well the material conducts heat, \(\rho c\) how much heat is needed to raise the temperature. A larger \(k\) means a faster flow, a larger \(\rho c\) slower warming, so \(\kappa\) is a measure of how fast a temperature disturbance spreads. The unit m\(^2\)/s is area per time (BARBER §14.2, PDF p. 236). "Diffusivity" is the same word as in diffusion, because the same equation holds for the mixing of one substance with another (KREYSZIG §12.5, PDF p. 584, read).

Source: BARBER (14.17) (PDF pp. 235 to 236, read), KREYSZIG §12.5 (PDF p. 584, read).

For the bar of figure 14.5 we get the equation directly from the balance (14.4), with a finite piece and the fundamental theorem of calculus, as for the string (theorem 13.3).

Corollary 14.10 Heat conduction in a bar (prevajanje toplote v palici)

Let a bar of constant cross-section of area \(A\) lie along \([0, L]\), insulated on its whole mantle. Let the temperature \(T(x, t)\) and the source \(Q(x, t)\) be constant over every cross-section. Let \(I\) be an open time interval and let \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(Q\) be continuous on \([0, L]\times I\) (\(T_{\mathrm{x}}\) continuously differentiable in \(x\)). Let \(\rho\), \(c\), \(k\) be constant. Then the balance (14.4) with \(q = -k\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\), that is

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \rho c A\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = k A\,\big(T_{\mathrm{x}}(b, t) - T_{\mathrm{x}}(a, t)\big) + \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b A\,Q\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{14.9}\]

holds for all \(0 \le a < b \le L\) and every \(t \in I\) if and only if for every \(x \in [0, L]\) and every \(t \in I\)

\[\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = k\,T_{\mathrm{xx}} + Q . \tag{14.10}\]
Proof

We must show that (14.9) for all pieces is the same equation as (14.10) at all points. We write the difference as an integral of a continuous function over a piece, as in the proof of theorem 13.3.

  1. Let \(f = \rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} - k\,T_{\mathrm{xx}} - Q\). Fix \(t\). The function \(f(\cdot, t)\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), because \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(Q\) are continuous.
  2. The function \(T_{\mathrm{x}}(\cdot, t)\) is differentiable with continuous derivative \(T_{\mathrm{xx}}\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40, item 1) \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b T_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = T_{\mathrm{x}}(b, t) - T_{\mathrm{x}}(a, t)\).
  3. By step 2 and linearity (lemma 3.39) the difference of the left and right sides of equation (14.9), divided by \(A\), equals \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,\mathrm{d}x\). Equation (14.9) for the piece \([a, b]\) is thus \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\).
  4. If (14.10) holds, then \(f = 0\), so \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for every piece.
  5. Conversely, let (14.9) hold for every piece. By step 3 \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for all \(a < b\), so \(G(x) = \int_0^x f\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) for \(x \in (0, L]\) and \(G(0) = 0\). The function \(G\) is differentiable with \(G' = f\) (theorem 3.40, item 2), because \(f\) is continuous, and it is zero everywhere, so \(f = G' = 0\).

Source: KREYSZIG §12.6 (PDF p. 585, read) takes the bar equation \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = c^2 u_{\mathrm{xx}}\) from the equation of the body, CM (8.3.7) (PDF p. 403) for the fin. The proof with a finite piece is not from the sources.

The form is the same as for the string, with one difference: for the string the second derivative in time occurs and so two initial conditions are needed, here the first derivative occurs, so one initial condition suffices (section 14.3). The explanation lies in what the flux determines: the string accelerates, because the force determines the acceleration, in heat the flux determines only the rate of change of the temperature.

Let us test the theorem on numbers. We take the copper bar for which KREYSZIG (§12.6, example 1, PDF p. 587) gives data, in the units of the source (cm, s, cal, degrees Celsius). The book has no conductivity and specific heat of steel (open question about material data at the end of the section), so for a numerical test we take copper.

Example 14.11 Copper bar: balance of a piece (bakrena palica: bilanca kosa)

The bar has length \(L = 80\) cm, conductivity \(k = 0{,}95\) cal/(cm s °C), specific heat \(c = 0{,}092\) cal/(g °C) and density \(\rho = 8{,}92\) g/cm\(^3\) (KREYSZIG, PDF p. 587). So \(\rho c = 0{,}82064\) cal/(cm\(^3\) °C), and the thermal diffusivity is \(\kappa = k/(\rho c) = 1{,}1576\) cm\(^2\)/s. The ends are held at \(0\) °C. Let the temperature be \(T = 100\,\sin(\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma t}\) with a decay rate \(\gamma\), at time \(0\) thus \(100\,\sin(\pi x/L)\). We ask which \(\gamma\) satisfies equation (14.10) and how we test the balance of a piece. We compute powers per unit cross-section area (SymPy, num-02.py).

Figure 14.7 shows on the left the temperature profile at time \(t = 0\), with the position \(x\) on the horizontal axis and the temperature \(T\) on the vertical one. The curve is half a sine, zero at both ends. In blue is the piece between \(a = 20\) cm and \(b = 40\) cm. The two orange segments are tangents to the profile at \(a\) and \(b\): at \(a\) the slope is \(T_{\mathrm{x}}(a) = 100\,(\pi/L)\cos(\pi/4) = 2{,}777\) °C/cm, at \(b\) it is zero, because the peak is there.

  1. The right \(\gamma\): from equation (14.10) without a source \(\rho c\,(-\gamma) = k\,(-(\pi/L)^2)\), so \(\gamma = \kappa\pi^2/L^2 = 1{,}7852\cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/s. The decay rate is not arbitrary, it is determined by the material and the length of the bar.
  2. The piece \([20, 40]\) at time \(0\): the left side of the balance, the stored power per area, is \(\int_{20}^{40}\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -2{,}638\) cal/(cm\(^2\) s). The right side, from the slopes of the orange tangents, is \(k\,(T_{\mathrm{x}}(40) - T_{\mathrm{x}}(20)) = 0{,}95\,(0 - 2{,}777) = -2{,}638\) cal/(cm\(^2\) s). The equality is exact (SymPy), negative because the piece is cooling. The flux at \(a\) points in the direction of decreasing \(x\) (\(q(a) = -k\,T_{\mathrm{x}}(a) < 0\)): heat flows out of the piece toward the cold end.
  3. The whole bar \([0, 80]\), under the whole profile: \(-7{,}461\) on both sides. The bar as a whole loses heat through both ends.

So the balance holds for every piece and for the right \(\gamma\). The test also shows when it does not hold.

Near miss 1: a wrong decay rate. Let \(\gamma' = 1{,}2\,\gamma\), with the same shape \(\sin(\pi x/L)\). The left side for the piece \([20, 40]\) is then \(-3{,}166\), the right stays \(-2{,}638\) (the slopes of the tangents do not change), the difference is \(-0{,}528\) cal/(cm\(^2\) s). For the whole bar \(-8{,}954\) against \(-7{,}461\). The residual \(f = \rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} - k\,T_{\mathrm{xx}}\) at time \(0\) is \(f = -0{,}0293\,\sin(\pi x/L)\) cal/(cm\(^3\) s), so at \(x = 40\) cm it is \(-0{,}0293\), which is \(1/6\) of the term \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\). The residual differs from zero at every interior point \(0 < x < L\), so the equation fails at every interior point. A bar that decayed faster than conduction demands would lose more heat than can flow out through its ends.

Near miss 2: the whole bar holds, a piece does not. Let \(T = 100\,\sin(2\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma t}\) with the same \(\gamma\) as before (the right one for \(\sin(2\pi x/L)\) would be four times larger, \(4\gamma\)). This is the right profile. Its axis \(T\) reaches below zero too, because the temperature on the right half of the bar is negative. For the whole bar both sides are zero: the stored power is \(0\), because the positive and the negative part of the sine cancel, and \(k\,(T_{\mathrm{x}}(80) - T_{\mathrm{x}}(0)) = 0\), because \(T_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the same at both ends. For the piece \([0, 20]\), however, the stored power is \(-1{,}865\). The right side takes the slopes of the orange tangents at \(0\) and \(20\) cm and is \(k\,(T_{\mathrm{x}}(20) - T_{\mathrm{x}}(0)) = 0{,}95\,(0 - 7{,}854) = -7{,}461\) cal/(cm\(^2\) s). The residual at the point \(x = 20\) cm is \(0{,}4395\) cal/(cm\(^3\) s), with the terms \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = -0{,}1465\) and \(k\,T_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}5860\), a ratio of \(4{,}0\), which is the ratio of the right and the used decay rate. For the whole bar the residuals of the two halves cancel, in a piece they do not. That is why theorem 14.8 demands the balance for every piece, not only for the whole bar.

The theorem also has the hypothesis that the second derivatives are continuous. What happens without it is shown by the junction of two materials.

Example 14.12 A bar of two layers: the balance holds, the equation at a point does not (palica iz dveh plasti)

A bar of length \(L\) has conductivity \(k\) on the left half and \(2k\) on the right half (figure 14.8, top). Its ends are held at \(100\) and \(0\) °C, the temperature does not change with time and there is no source. Then the balance (14.4) for every piece, divided by \(A\), is \(0 = q(a) - q(b) = k_{\text{at } \mathrm{b}}\,T_{\mathrm{x}}(b) - k_{\text{at } \mathrm{a}}\,T_{\mathrm{x}}(a)\), where \(q = -k\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\) with the conductivity at the place of the cross-section. So the flux \(q = -k\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\) must be constant along the bar. The left half therefore has a slope twice as large as the right.

  1. In each half \(k\) is constant, the temperature does not change with time and there is no source, so there \(T_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) by corollary 14.10 and the profile is a straight line. Let \(T_{\mathrm{m}}\) be the temperature at the junction. The flux through the left half is \(k\,(100 - T_{\mathrm{m}})/(L/2)\), through the right \(2k\,T_{\mathrm{m}}/(L/2)\). Equality gives \(100 - T_{\mathrm{m}} = 2\,T_{\mathrm{m}}\), so \(T_{\mathrm{m}} = 33{,}33\) °C.
  2. The slopes are \(T_{\mathrm{x}} = -133{,}33\) °C per \(L\) on the left and \(-66{,}67\) °C per \(L\) on the right (SymPy). The two orange segments continue the two straight lines across the junction and do not match the profile on the other side. The profile therefore has a kink at the junction, so the second derivative \(T_{\mathrm{xx}}\) does not exist at the point of the junction.
  3. The balance holds for every piece, also for one that contains the junction: the flux \(q = -k\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\) is \(k\cdot 133{,}33\) °C\(/L\) on the left and \(2k\cdot 66{,}67\) °C\(/L\) on the right, so it is the same \(133{,}33\,k\) °C\(/L\) on both sides, and the left side of the balance is zero. The equation at a point, however, is not satisfied at the junction, because \(T_{\mathrm{xx}}\) does not exist.

This is not a failure of the theorem, since the example does not satisfy its hypothesis: the theorem demands continuous second derivatives. Without it the balance is still valid, but the equation at a point is no longer described by \(k\,\nabla^2 T\). The balance holds also across the junction, which means that the flux \(q = -k\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuous at the junction, not the slope \(T_{\mathrm{x}}\). Such a condition at the junction of layers is continued in section 14.3.

In this chapter there are several symbols that have other meanings elsewhere in the book. The temperature \(T\) is in chapter 13 the tension force of the string, here it is the temperature (in chapter 3 the change of temperature is \(\Delta T\)). The conductivity \(k\) is in chapter 5 the shear factor of the cross-section. The specific heat \(c\) is in chapter 13 the wave speed, the thermal diffusivity \(\kappa\) is in chapter 5 the curvature, and the heat flux \(\vek q\) is in chapter 5 a distributed load. In this chapter these symbols never occur together with the other meaning, and where this would occur we say so explicitly (curvature will be written \(v''\), element length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\)).

The summary of the section is short. We showed that the same law of conservation of energy, written for a part of a body, gives an integral equation, and that from it, because the part is arbitrary, the equation at a point follows, \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = k\,\nabla^2 T + Q\), under assumptions that we named and gave a measure. The test on the copper bar showed that the equation selects the decay rate and that the balance must hold for every piece. In the next section we write what determines the solution: the initial condition and the conditions on the surface of the body (section 14.3).

14.3 Boundary conditions and uniqueness

In section 14.2 we obtained the heat equation (enačba prevajanja, theorem 14.8) from the heat balance of every finite part of a body, \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = \nabla\cdot(k\nabla T) + Q\), where \(T(P, t)\) is the temperature at the point \(P\) at time \(t\), \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\) its derivative with respect to time and \(Q\) the heat source per unit volume. Now we ask whether this equation alone determines the temperature. We shall show that it does not, and that it is determined once we also know what happens on the surface of the body and what the temperature was at the start. We shall arrange these data into a boundary value problem and prove that it has at most one solution, as for the boundary value problem of elasticity in chapter 11. The proof is the same as there: the difference of two solutions is estimated by an energy, only that the energy is now \(\tfrac12\int\rho c\,w^2\) and no longer a strain energy.

Notation. In this chapter \(k\) is the thermal conductivity (in chapter 5 \(k\) is the shear factor), \(c\) the specific heat (in chapter 13 \(c\) is a wave speed), \(\vek q\) the heat flux vector (in chapter 5 \(q\) is a distributed load), \(\kappa\) the thermal diffusivity (in chapter 5 \(\kappa\) is a curvature) and \(h\) the heat transfer coefficient, introduced below (in chapters 6 and 7 \(h\) is the length of an element). The meaning of each letter is always restated where it is used.

14.3.1 What the equation does not say

Take the steel bar of chapter 3, diameter \(10\) mm, cross section \(A = 78{,}54\) mm², length \(L\). Let its lateral surface be insulated, which means that no heat flows through it (section 14.3.2 below says exactly what this means). Let the temperature be the same at all points of each cross section. Hence by corollary 14.10 the temperature \(T(x, t)\) obeys the heat equation of the bar. Look at the steady state, in which the temperature does not change with time and there is no source: \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) and \(Q = 0\), so \(T'' = 0\). The function \(T'\) has derivative zero on an interval, so by the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84) it is constant, \(T' = a\), and the function \(T - a x\) has derivative zero, so it is constant and equal to its value at \(x = 0\): \(T(x) = T(0) + a x\). Every straight line is a solution. In the lower part of the figure the temperature \(T\) is drawn over the axis \(x\), and the three blue lines \(T_1\), \(T_2\) and \(T_3\) are three of these solutions. The equation leaves two numbers, \(T(0)\) and \(a\), to us.

Which line the bar follows is decided by what we do to its ends. Through the left end we supply a heat flux of \(1000\) W/m² with a heating foil, through the right end we remove an equally strong flux by cooling. The heat flux vector \(\vek q\) (toplotni tok, definition 14.2) has by Fourier's law (definition 14.3) the component \(q_{\mathrm{x}} = -k\,T'\). The flux that leaves the bar is \(\vek q\cdot\vek n\) with the outward normal \(\vek n\). At \(x = L\) the normal \(\vek n\) points in the direction \(+x\), so \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = -k\,T'(L)\), at \(x = 0\) it points in the direction \(-x\) and \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = k\,T'(0)\). The prescription at the left end is \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = -1000\) W/m² (the flux enters), at the right end \(+1000\) W/m². Hence \(T'(0) = -1000/k\) and \(T'(L) = -1000/k\). The two requirements give the same slope \(-q/k\), where \(q = 1000\) W/m², so every line of the family satisfies them, also the one that is \(50\) K higher. The datum \(T(0)\) remains unknown: the equation together with the two conditions does not determine the temperature. We shall explain this example in detail at the end of the section and set it next to the uniqueness theorem. Now we look at what kinds of data there are at all.

14.3.2 Three kinds of conditions on the surface

For an elastic body we divided the surface into a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), where supports prescribe the displacement, and a part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where a known force acts (definition 11.1). For heat it is similar, except that there are three possibilities. Take a body \(V\) and its surface \(S\), drawn in cross section in figure 14.10. We denote its outward normal by \(\vek n\), and the flux through the surface per unit area is \(\vek q\cdot\vek n\) (definition 14.2), positive when heat flows out of the body.

The first possibility arises if we press the body against a wall whose temperature we hold, for example against a large bath whose temperature is practically not changed by the heat the body gives or takes. On this part \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) the temperature is known, \(T = \bar T\), and we call it a prescribed temperature (predpisana temperatura). The second possibility arises if we know the heat flux through the surface, on the part \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\). With a heating foil on the lower face, insulated on its outer side so that all its power goes into the body, we measure the flux as the electric power divided by the area of the foil. The flux enters, so \(\bar q_{\mathrm{n}} < 0\). A special case is insulation (foam, the vacuum between the walls of a thermos flask), which heat does not cross: the flux \(\int\vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\) through every piece of the surface is zero, so on this part \(\bar q_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\). The condition is

\[\vek q\cdot\vek n = \bar q_{\mathrm{n}} \quad\text{or}\quad -k\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial n} = \bar q_{\mathrm{n}} , \tag{14.11}\]

where \(\partial T/\partial n = \nabla T\cdot\vek n\) is the derivative of the temperature in the direction of the normal (definition 14.3). With insulation, \(\partial T/\partial n = 0\): the temperature does not change in the direction of the normal and the isotherms (surfaces of constant temperature) meet the surface at a right angle, which COOK (PDF p. 482) gives as a check of an insulated edge. That the flux is zero at every point follows from continuity: a continuous function \(\vek q\cdot\vek n\) with integral zero over every piece is zero everywhere (otherwise it would be positive or negative on a piece around some point and the integral over that piece would not be zero).

The third possibility is the most common. The body is surrounded by air or water, whose temperature we do not hold constant, and we do not know the flux. But we can say what the flux depends on. Heat flows out if the surface is warmer than the fluid far from it, and flows in if it is colder, so \(\vek q\cdot\vek n\) will be positive for \(T > T_\infty\) and negative for \(T < T_\infty\), and zero for \(T = T_\infty\). Here \(T_\infty\) is the temperature of the fluid outside the thin boundary layer at the wall (COOK, PDF p. 469), in which the temperature changes. The simplest dependence with this sign is proportionality, and experiments support it approximately (KREYSZIG, PDF p. 41, more on this below in section 14.3.4): the flux is proportional to the temperature difference. The sources write this as a boundary condition with a name.

Definition 14.13 Newton's law of cooling (Newtonov zakon ohlajanja)

Let the part \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) of the surface of a body be in contact with a fluid whose temperature outside the boundary layer at the surface is \(T_\infty\), and let \(h \ge 0\). Newton's law of cooling is the boundary condition that requires at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\)

\[\vek q\cdot\vek n = h\,(T - T_\infty) \quad\text{or}\quad -k\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial n} = h\,(T - T_\infty) , \tag{14.12}\]

where \(\vek n\) is the outward normal and \(\vek q = -k\nabla T\) the heat flux (definition 14.3). The number \(h\) is the heat transfer coefficient (koeficient toplotne prestopnosti).

Source: COOK §12.1 (PDF p. 469): equation (12.1-1), "called Newton's law of cooling", \(T_\infty\) is the temperature of the fluid outside the boundary layer. CM §6.7.3 (PDF p. 282): "heat transfer coefficient or film conductance", the law "also defines h".

The sources do not say where the name comes from, and we do not tell a history of the law here. In the sources \(h\) is also called film conductance (CM, PDF p. 282). The unit of \(h\) is W/(m² K), because the flux per unit area is in W/m² and we get it by multiplying \(h\) by a temperature difference in K. The word film points to the thin layer of fluid at the wall, the boundary layer, in which the temperature changes from the temperature of the wall to \(T_\infty\) (COOK, PDF p. 469), that the name refers to exactly this layer is not stated in the sources. The coefficient \(h\) is not a property of a material but depends on the motion of the fluid, the roughness of the wall and more, so it is determined by experiment (COOK, PDF p. 469), for everyday bodies roughly between \(5\) and \(10^5\) W/(m² K), with large values for boiling and condensation. For radiation the flux is not proportional to a temperature difference but to the difference of the fourth powers of absolute temperatures (COOK, PDF p. 469), so we leave it out: the assumption of this chapter is that \(h\) and \(T_\infty\) are known.

What equation (14.12) means for the temperature we show on a slab of thickness \(L\). We hold the left face at \(x = 0\) at \(T_0 = 30\) K above the surroundings. We measure temperatures as the difference from the temperature of the surroundings \(T_\infty\), so on this scale the surroundings have the value \(T_\infty = 0\). The right face at \(x = L\) passes heat to the surroundings. The steady state is a line \(T(x) = T_0 + a\,x\) as before, drawn in the figure over the axis \(x\). The condition (14.12) at \(x = L\) is \(-k\,a = h\,(T_0 + a L - T_\infty)\), from which

\[a = -\frac{h\,(T_0 - T_\infty)}{k + h L} , \qquad T(L) = T_0 - (T_0 - T_\infty)\,\frac{\mathrm{Bi}}{1 + \mathrm{Bi}} , \qquad \mathrm{Bi} = \frac{h L}{k} . \tag{14.13}\]

The number \(\mathrm{Bi}\) (the symbol is ours) is the ratio of two temperature drops for the same flux \(q\): in the slab the temperature drops by \(q L/k\), in the fluid film by \(q/h\), the ratio is \(hL/k\). For \(\mathrm{Bi} = 1\) the drop in the slab and in the film are equal, the right face has \(15\) K, half the way to the surroundings. The line, continued beyond the right face, reaches \(T_\infty\) at \(x = L + k/h\), that is a distance \(k/h\) to the right of the face, which for \(\mathrm{Bi} = 1\) is exactly \(2L\): the tangent at \(x = L\) is the condition (14.12) written as a picture, since \(-k\,T' = h\,(T - T_\infty)\) is exactly \(T - T_\infty = -T'\,(k/h)\). Two more extremes:

  • \(\mathrm{Bi} = 10\): \(T(L) = 2{,}73\) K, the tangent reaches \(T_\infty\) already at \(1{,}1\,L\). The film hardly holds back any drop, the right face is close to \(T_\infty\) (for \(\mathrm{Bi} = 100\) only \(0{,}297\) K above it) and the condition (14.12) becomes the prescribed temperature \(T = T_\infty\). More precisely: \(T(L) - T_\infty = (T_0 - T_\infty)/(1 + \mathrm{Bi})\) tends to zero as \(h \to \infty\).
  • \(\mathrm{Bi} = 0{,}1\): \(T(L) = 27{,}27\) K, the difference \(T(0) - T(L)\) is \(9{,}1\) % of \(T_0 - T_\infty\), the tangent reaches \(T_\infty\) only at \(11\,L\), outside the figure. For \(h \to 0\) the value \(T(L)\) tends to \(T_0\) and the flux to zero: the condition becomes insulation.

Heat transfer is thus a bridge between the first two kinds of condition: a large \(h\) is a prescribed temperature, a small \(h\) is insulation. The values \(\mathrm{Bi} = 0{,}1\), \(1\) and \(10\) are in figure 14.11.

Heat transfer in this section is a model. We assume that \(h\) and \(T_\infty\) are known, constant along the surface and independent of the temperature, and that the surroundings are not warmed by the body. A real fluid, in which the temperature goes from the wall to the surroundings along a complicated profile, has these properties only approximately. KREYSZIG (PDF p. 41) says in this connection that such experimental laws are derived under idealized assumptions that rarely hold exactly.

One more property must hold for all three kinds. At each point of the surface we may prescribe only one. With \(T = \bar T\) and at the same time \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\) we would have too many data. COOK (PDF p. 472) says so: the temperature must not be prescribed on a part where the flux is prescribed. We check it on the slab. Let \(T(0) = 0\) and \(T(L) = 30\) K, steady, without source: the only solution of the equation \(T'' = 0\) with these two data is \(T = 30\,x/L\), its flux at the right end is \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = -k\,T'(L) = -30\,k/L\) and is thereby determined. If we also prescribed at the right end the flux \(\bar q_{\mathrm{n}} = -50\,k/L\), there is no solution, since \(-30\,k/L \ne -50\,k/L\). So the parts \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) must not overlap. Where two parts with different conditions meet, for example in a corner of a plate where two edges with different temperatures meet, the condition at the point of contact is not determined (COOK, PDF p. 482). We shall see this in the section on the plane field, on the example of a plate.

14.3.3 The initial state and the boundary value problem

In the heat equation time appears with one derivative, \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\). If we know the temperature at some instant everywhere in the body, the equation tells how fast it changes at each point, and thereby what it will be a little later. For a start one field is enough, the initial temperature \(T^0(P)\) at \(t = 0\), which we measure at all points of the body. In the equation of the string (theorem 13.3) time appears with a second derivative and we need two fields, the position and the velocity. COOK (PDF p. 482) writes, for transient computations, that all initial nodal temperatures must be prescribed.

Now we write everything at once, as for elasticity (definition 11.1).

Definition 14.14 Boundary value problem of heat conduction (robni problem prevajanja toplote)

Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes (definition 4.11) with surface \(S\) and outward normal \(\vek n\), whose interior points form a connected open set (definition 1.130) and each of whose points is a limit of a sequence of interior points. Let the surface \(S\) be the union of three parts \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) that do not overlap and are made of whole outer pieces of the surface (some parts may be empty). Let the material be homogeneous and isotropic, with constant \(k > 0\), \(\rho > 0\) and \(c > 0\). The data, all continuous, are the source \(Q\) on \(V \times (0, t_1]\), the temperature \(\bar T\) and the flux \(\bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\) on the parts \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) (functions of point and time), the coefficient \(h \ge 0\) and the temperature \(T_\infty\) on \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) and the initial temperature \(T^0\) on \(V\). For \(t_1 > 0\) a solution is a function \(T(P, t)\) of a point \(P\) of \(V\) and a time \(t\) in \([0, t_1]\) with the following requirements.

  1. The function \(T\) is continuous on \(V \times [0, t_1]\) and \(T(P, 0) = T^0(P)\) (initial condition, začetni pogoj).
  2. The function \(T\) is defined on \(D \times (0, t_1]\) for some open set \(D\) that contains \(V\), and has continuous partial derivatives there with respect to time and the space coordinates up to second order.
  3. At every point of the body and at every \(t \in (0, t_1]\) we have \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = \nabla\cdot(k\nabla T) + Q\) (theorem 14.8).
  4. At every point of the parts of the surface and at every \(t \in (0, t_1]\) the boundary conditions (robni pogoji) hold: \(T = \bar T\) on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(-k\,\partial T/\partial n = \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) and \(-k\,\partial T/\partial n = h\,(T - T_\infty)\) on \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) (equations (14.11) and (14.12)).

The steady boundary value problem has the same requirements 2 to 4 for a function \(T(P)\) that does not depend on time, with the equation \(\nabla\cdot(k\nabla T) + Q = 0\) and data independent of time. There is no requirement 1.

Source: COOK §12.1 (PDF pp. 469 to 472): the three kinds of boundary conditions (prescribed temperature, prescribed flux and heat transfer), "boundary temperature may also be prescribed, but not on the same portion of a boundary where \(f_{\mathrm{B}}\) is prescribed" (PDF p. 472), initial conditions (PDF p. 482). The requirements of continuous differentiability and the division of the surface are ours, so that the principles proved in chapter 4 apply, as in definition 11.1.

Requirement 2 is a simplification. It says that the solution is smooth up to the surface, and it excludes cases that we cannot treat in this section, for example an initial field with a jump (as \(t \to 0\) the solution has no derivatives at the jump) and boundary conditions that meet in a corner with different values. A full description of such solutions needs weak solutions in Sobolev spaces, as for the boundary value problem of elasticity (section 6.2.3 for Sobolev spaces). Later in the chapter we shall treat such cases as limits of smooth solutions and say each time in what sense they solve the problem.

14.3.4 Heat in the whole body

Before we prove uniqueness we need an identity that is the heat equation in integral form: what happens to the heat in the whole body. Section 14.2 derived the equation from the balance of an arbitrary finite part, and now we go the other way, from the equation to the balance of the whole. The stock of heat in the body is \(H(t) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho c\,T\,\mathrm{d}V\) (definition 14.6), up to an additive constant that depends on the choice of the zero of temperature.

Lemma 14.15 Heat in the whole body (toplota celega telesa)

Let \(T\) be a solution of the boundary value problem of heat conduction or of its steady version (definition 14.14) and \(H(t) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho c\,T\,\mathrm{d}V\). For the transient problem \(H\) is differentiable on \((0, t_1)\) and

\[H'(t) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad \vek q = -k\nabla T . \tag{14.14}\]

In the steady case, therefore, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V\).

Proof

We must show that the derivative of \(H\) is the integral of the right-hand side of the heat equation and that the integral of a divergence is the flux through the surface.
