  1. The function \(\rho c\,T\) and its partial derivative with respect to time are continuous on \(V \times (0, t_1)\) (requirement 2 of the definition). By lemma 8.31 on differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter, applied to the set with volume \(V\) (lemma 4.32, item 6) and the parameter \(t\) in an open interval, \(H'(t) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. By the heat equation (requirement 3 of the definition) \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = \nabla\cdot(k\nabla T) + Q\). By linearity of the integral (lemma 4.32, item 1) \(H' = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \nabla\cdot(k\nabla T)\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  3. The field \(\vek v = k\nabla T\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\) at every \(t\) (requirement 2). By the divergence theorem (theorem 4.14) \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \nabla\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = -\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\), because \(\vek q = -k\nabla T\).
  4. Steps 2 and 3 together give (14.14). For a steady field \(H' = 0\), since \(T\) does not depend on \(t\), and from \(\nabla\cdot(k\nabla T) + Q = 0\) step 3 gives the equality \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The heat balance of a body is treated by CM §5.4.2 (PDF pp. 236 to 238) and KREYSZIG §12.5 (PDF pp. 583 to 585) for a part of a body, here it is written for the whole body.

The lemma says: the heat in a body grows with the power of the sources, reduced by the flux through the surface. As for the force on the whole body in chapter 11 (lemma 11.2), this is a consequence of the equation, not an additional requirement. We check it on the slab at \(\mathrm{Bi} = 1\) of figure 14.11, where the source is zero, the lateral faces are insulated and \(T\) is a line. For \(\mathrm{Bi} = 1\) we have \(h = k/L\) and by equation (14.13) \(a\,L = -30\,\mathrm{K}/2 = -15\) K. At \(x = 0\) we have \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = k\,T'(0) = -15\,k/L\) (the flux enters), at \(x = L\) we have \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = -k\,T'(L) = 15\,k/L\). By the heat transfer law (14.12) it is there \(h\,T(L) = (k/L)\cdot 15 = 15\,k/L\), as it must be. Since the slab has the same cross section \(A\) everywhere, the fluxes through the left and the right face are opposite, \(-15\,k\,A/L\) and \(15\,k\,A/L\), zero together, as the lemma requires in the steady state (step 4).

The lemma has one more consequence, which is a view of heat transfer from the other side. Take a body that has almost the same temperature at every point (such, as KREYSZIG states on PDF p. 41, is a copper ball, which conducts heat well). In the model of uniform temperature we describe it by a single temperature \(T(t)\). Then \(H = \rho c\,V_{\mathrm{V}}\,T\) and the flux is \(h\,(T - T_\infty)\) everywhere on the surface, so by equation (14.14) without a source

\[\rho c\,V_{\mathrm{V}}\,T' = -h\,A_{\mathrm{S}}\,(T - T_\infty) , \tag{14.15}\]

where \(V_{\mathrm{V}}\) is the volume and \(A_{\mathrm{S}}\) the area of the surface. The rate of change of temperature is proportional to the difference from the surroundings, which is the form of Newton's law known from experiments on well conducting bodies (KREYSZIG, PDF p. 41). The model is only an approximation. If the temperature were really the same everywhere, its derivative in the direction of the normal would be zero, by Fourier's law so would the flux through the surface, and the body would not cool. The model is good when \(\mathrm{Bi}\) is small: for \(\mathrm{Bi} = 0{,}1\) the temperature in the slab of figure 14.11 changes from one face to the other by only \(9{,}1\) % of the difference between the left face and the surroundings, for \(\mathrm{Bi} = 1\) by \(50\) %, and there a uniform temperature is no longer a good description.

14.3.5 Uniqueness

For the boundary value problem of elasticity uniqueness followed from the fact that the difference of two solutions solves the problem with zero data and that the energy is not zero unless the field is free of strain. For heat we do the same. The difference of two solutions, \(w = \tilde T - T\), has zero source, zero boundary data and zero initial state. The energy we shall follow is not the energy of the body but \(E(t) = \tfrac12\int_{\mathrm{V}}\rho c\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}V\). Why exactly this one? Because on differentiation with respect to time \(w\) is multiplied by \(\rho c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\), which the heat equation replaces by a divergence, and by the divergence theorem this passes to the surface, where the boundary conditions tell exactly which signs we get. First we need a rule on integrals, which we shall use twice.

Lemma 14.16 Integral of a nonnegative continuous function (integral nenegativne zvezne funkcije)

Let \(V\) be a body as in definition 14.14 (a body made of boxes, every point is a limit of interior points) and \(g\) a continuous function on \(V\) with \(g \ge 0\). If \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} g\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\), then \(g = 0\) at every point of \(V\).

Proof

We must show that a positive value at one point gives a positive integral, as in steps 3 to 7 of item 2 of the proof of theorem 4.91.

  1. Suppose \(g(P) > 0\) at an interior point \(P\). By continuity (definition 1.67) with the error \(g(P)/2\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(g > g(P)/2\) at the points of the body that are less than \(\delta\) from \(P\).
  2. Since \(P\) is an interior point, a cube \(K_{\mathrm{P}}\) with edge \(d > 0\) lies in the body around it, whose vertices are less than \(\delta\) from \(P\). On it \(g > g(P)/2\).
  3. By monotonicity of the integral over a set (lemma 4.32, item 2) \(0 = \int_{\mathrm{V}} g\,\mathrm{d}V \ge \int_{\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{P}} g\,\mathrm{d}V \ge \tfrac12\,g(P)\,d^3 > 0\), because the cube has volume \(d^3\) (item 6 of the same lemma). This is a contradiction, so \(g = 0\) at every interior point.
  4. Every point of \(V\) is a limit of a sequence of interior points, and \(g\) is continuous, so by lemma 1.68 \(g = 0\) on the surface as well.

Source: The proof is not from the sources, it is the same inference as in steps 3 to 7 of item 2 of the proof of theorem 4.91.

Now the theorem. The question is whether one initial field and one kind of condition at each point of the surface are really enough.

Theorem 14.17 Uniqueness of the boundary value problem of heat conduction (enoličnost robnega problema prevajanja)

Let the boundary value problem of heat conduction be as in definition 14.14 and let \(T\) and \(\tilde T\) be solutions for the same data \(Q\), \(\bar T\), \(\bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(h\), \(T_\infty\) and possibly different initial fields \(T^0\) and \(\tilde T^0\). Then:

  1. for every \(t \in [0, t_1]\) the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}}\rho c\,(\tilde T - T)^2\,\mathrm{d}V\) at time \(t\) is at most as large as at \(t = 0\). If \(\tilde T^0 = T^0\), then \(\tilde T = T\) on \(V \times [0, t_1]\),
  2. if \(T\) and \(\tilde T\) are solutions of the steady problem for the same data, \(\tilde T - T\) is constant on \(V\), and the constant is zero if \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) is nonempty or if \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,\mathrm{d}A > 0\).
Proof

We must show that \(E(t) = \tfrac12\int_{\mathrm{V}}\rho c\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}V\) for \(w = \tilde T - T\) is nonnegative, does not grow, and is zero if the initial fields are equal. In the steady part the same computation shows that the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}V\) is zero.

  1. The difference \(w\) is continuous on \(V \times [0, t_1]\), has continuous derivatives up to second order on \(D \times (0, t_1]\) and satisfies the homogeneous problem: \(\rho c\,w_{\mathrm{t}} = \nabla\cdot(k\nabla w)\) (the source \(Q\) cancels), \(w = 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(\partial w/\partial n = 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) and \(-k\,\partial w/\partial n = h\,w\) on \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) (equation (14.12), in which \(T_\infty\) cancels). All equations are linear and derivatives of a difference are differences of derivatives.
  2. The function \(w^2\) is continuous on the closed bounded set \(V \times [0, t_1]\), so it is uniformly continuous (theorem 4.6). For every error \(\eta > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|w(P, t)^2 - w(P, s)^2| < \eta\) for every \(P \in V\) and \(|t - s| < \delta\). By the bound for the integral (lemma 4.32, item 3) \(|E(t) - E(s)| \le \tfrac12\rho c\,V_{\mathrm{V}}\,\eta\). The function \(E\) is therefore continuous on \([0, t_1]\).
  3. By lemma 8.31 with \(f = \tfrac12\rho c\,w^2\) and \(\partial f/\partial t = \rho c\,w\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\), both continuous on \(V \times (0, t_1)\), the function \(E\) is differentiable and \(E'(t) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \rho c\,w\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}V\). By step 1 this is \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,\nabla\cdot(k\nabla w)\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  4. By the product rule (lemma 1.81, componentwise) \(\nabla\cdot(w\,k\nabla w) = k\,|\nabla w|^2 + w\,\nabla\cdot(k\nabla w)\). So \(w\,\nabla\cdot(k\nabla w) = \nabla\cdot(w\,k\nabla w) - k\,|\nabla w|^2\). The field \(w\,k\nabla w\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), so by the divergence theorem (theorem 4.14) and linearity
    \[E'(t) = \int_{\mathrm{S}} w\,k\,\frac{\partial w}{\partial n}\,\mathrm{d}A - \int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  5. We divide the surface into three parts. On \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) we have \(w = 0\) and the product \(w\,k\,\partial w/\partial n\) is zero. On \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) we have \(\partial w/\partial n = 0\) and the product is zero. On \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) we have \(k\,\partial w/\partial n = -h\,w\) and the product is \(-h\,w^2\). So
    \[E'(t) = -\int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}A \le 0 , \tag{14.16}\]
    because \(k > 0\) and \(h \ge 0\) and the integrands are nonnegative.
  6. Let \(t \in (0, t_1]\). The function \(E\) is continuous on \([0, t]\) and differentiable on \((0, t)\), so by the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84) there is \(\tau \in (0, t)\) with \(E(t) - E(0) = E'(\tau)\,t \le 0\). So \(E(t) \le E(0)\), which is the first claim of item 1.
  7. If \(\tilde T^0 = T^0\), then \(E(0) = 0\) and \(0 \le E(t) \le 0\). The integrand \(\rho c\,w^2\) is continuous and nonnegative, so by lemma 14.16 \(w(\cdot, t) = 0\) on \(V\) for every \(t\). This is the second claim of item 1.
  8. The steady case: the difference \(w\) solves \(\nabla\cdot(k\nabla w) = 0\) with the same conditions. The same computation without the term with time (steps 4 and 5, \(w \nabla\cdot(k\nabla w) = 0\)) gives \(0 = -\int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}A\). Both terms are nonnegative, so each is zero. By lemma 14.16 for \(g = k\,|\nabla w|^2\) we have \(\nabla w = \vek 0\) everywhere. By lemma 1.133 on the connected open set of interior points \(w\) is constant, and by continuity on all of \(V\), since every point is a limit of interior points.
  9. Let \(w = w_0\) be the constant. If \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) is nonempty, \(w = 0\) at some point of that surface, so \(w_0 = 0\). If \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,\mathrm{d}A > 0\), step 8 gives \(0 = \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,w_0^2\,\mathrm{d}A = w_0^2\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,\mathrm{d}A\), so \(w_0 = 0\).

Source: COOK §12.1 (PDF pp. 469 to 472) states the form of the problem, KREYSZIG §12.5 (PDF pp. 583 to 585) the equation. Uniqueness by energy is an adaptation of the proof of theorem 11.4, the proof is not from the sources.

What did the theorem show? The difference of two solutions has an energy \(E\) that is forced to fall both by the loss of flux in the interior, \(\int k|\nabla w|^2\), and by the loss at heat transfer, \(\int h\,w^2\). It starts at zero if the initial fields are equal, and so it never grows. One initial field, not two as for the string, because the equation contains one derivative with respect to time. The first item of the theorem is stronger than uniqueness alone: it says that for different initial fields the difference does not grow in the mean square (\(\int\rho c\,w^2\)). An error in the measurement of the initial temperature therefore does not grow with time, measured by this integral, which will be used with series in the section on the transient bar.

We test the derivative of the energy (14.16) on a slab with \(k = \rho c = L = h = 1\) (no units, \(\mathrm{Bi} = 1\)), whose left face at \(x = 0\) is held at \(w = 0\) and whose right face at \(x = L\) passes heat. In the figure the difference \(w\) is drawn over the axis \(x\). Such is the difference of two solutions if \(w(x, 0) = \sin(z x)\), where \(z = 2{,}02876\) is the first positive root of \(\tan z = -z\) (the condition \(-k\,w'(1) = h\,w(1)\), which \(\sin(zx)\) satisfies because \(-z\cos z = \sin z\) at \(z = 2{,}02876\): both sides are \(0{,}896956\)). A solution of the heat equation is \(w = \sin(z x)\,\mathrm{e}^{-z^2 t}\), since \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = -z^2 w\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -z^2 w\). Figure 14.12 shows \(w\) at \(t = 0\), \(0{,}05\) and \(0{,}1\). The energy is \(E(0) = 0{,}298868\) and falls at the rate \(-2{,}46018\) (computed by numerical differentiation of the energy \(E(t) = \tfrac12\int_0^1 w^2\,\mathrm{d}x\)). The right-hand side of (14.16) is \(-\int_0^1 w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x - w(1)^2 = -2{,}46019\). They agree to rounding. The same at \(t = 0{,}05\) (\(-1{,}63012\) for both) and \(0{,}1\) (\(-1{,}08012\)). The energy falls as \(\mathrm{e}^{-2z^2t}\) and \(2z^2 = 8{,}2317\). The tangent at the right end reaches \(w = 0\) at \(L + k/h = 2\), because \(w'(1) = -w(1)\).

The conditions of the theorem are not there for nothing, as the next lemma shows.

14.3.6 A body with fluxes only

The theorem says that the steady solution is unique up to a constant and that the constant is determined if the temperature is prescribed on some part or there is heat transfer there. What happens if we prescribe the flux on the whole surface, \(S = S_{\mathrm{q}}\)? An example is the bar of figure 14.9, where we left \(T(0)\) arbitrary.

Lemma 14.18 A body with prescribed flux on the whole surface (telo s predpisanim tokom po vsej površini)

Let \(S = S_{\mathrm{q}}\) (\(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) in definition 14.14 are empty) and \(T\) a solution of the steady problem. Then:

  1. \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V\). If this equality does not hold, there is no solution,
  2. for every number \(C\) the function \(T + C\) is also a solution, so the solution is not unique,
  3. for the transient problem with \(S = S_{\mathrm{q}}\) the solution is unique (theorem 14.17, item 1), and its heat \(H\) of lemma 14.15 has the derivative \(H' = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{S}} \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}A\).
Proof

We must show that the first equality is the condition for existence, that a constant does not affect the requirements of the definition and that the initial state determines the constant.

  1. By lemma 14.15 for a steady solution \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek q\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V\). On \(S = S_{\mathrm{q}}\) we have \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\) (equation (14.11)), so \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. The function \(T + C\) has the same partial derivatives as \(T\), so it satisfies requirements 2 to 4 of the definition: the equation and the condition (14.11) contain only derivatives.
  3. The transient problem has the initial field in requirement 1, which determines the constant: \(T + C\) has at \(t = 0\) the value \(T^0 + C \ne T^0\). Item 1 of theorem 14.17 holds, because \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) is empty and the surface term in equation (14.16) drops out, and the remaining term is nonpositive. The derivative \(H'\) is equation (14.14) with \(\vek q\cdot\vek n = \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The same inference for force is lemma 11.2.

A test with numbers is the bar of figure 14.9. With \(1000\) W/m² at both ends \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}A = (-1000 + 1000)\,A = 0 = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V\) (on the insulated lateral surface \(\bar q_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\)) and the solutions are the lines \(T(x) = T(0) - (1000/k)\,x\) for every value of \(T(0)\), which we can shift by an arbitrary constant (item 2). A case with the condition violated: with the same flux at the left end and \(900\) W/m² at the right, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}A = (-1000 + 900)\,A = -100\,A = -0{,}007854\) W, there is no source, so \(0 \ne -0{,}007854\) W and there is no steady solution. What happens in the body? By item 3, \(H' = +0{,}007854\) W, the heat in the bar grows steadily, and the mean temperature grows at the rate \(H'/(\rho c\,A\,L) = 100/(\rho c)\) K/s for \(L = 1\) m (without a value of \(\rho c\) for steel, for which the books have no source). The steady state does not exist because the heat has nowhere to go. With balanced fluxes \(H\) is constant, and this is the datum that determines \(T(0)\): the bar keeps the heat it had at the start. How the temperature approaches this line is shown by the section on the transient bar.

So we have seen what the theorem demands. Without a prescribed temperature or heat transfer we get no uniqueness in the steady state, and no existence either if the flux is not balanced by the sources. For the transient problem uniqueness remains, because the initial state guarantees it. In the next section we shall compute steady states with all three kinds of conditions.

14.4 Steady conduction in one dimension

So far we have introduced temperature (section 14.1), derived the heat equation from the heat balance of a part of the body (theorem 14.8), and settled what must be prescribed on the boundary (section 14.3). Chapter 5 took the temperature over the height of a beam to be linear when it treated bending caused by temperature, and sent the reader here for the real distribution. This section pays that debt and solves three more problems in which the temperature changes along one direction only: a wall in which heat is also produced, a fin that loses heat from its sides, and a tube. In all four the state is steady (stacionarno). The word is from the Latin stare, to stand: a steady state is one that stands still, because no temperature in the body changes with time, \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\). Then the energy of no part of the body changes, so by theorem 14.8 the heat that flows into a piece or is produced in it also flows out. This one thought, the balance of a piece \([a, b]\) at a temperature that stands still, is the whole section.

The model is the same everywhere. The body is at rest, made of a material with constant conductivity \(k\) (an idealization from section 14.2: over a large range of temperature \(k\) changes, which we do not take into account here), and the heat flux is \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T\) by Fourier's law (definition 14.3). In every case the temperature is a function of one coordinate only. For the wall that is an idealization, which is good when the wall is much longer in the other two directions than it is thick and we are far from its edges. Near an edge heat also flows along the face, and the one-dimensional calculation fails there. This section does not compute the size of that error, the plane field without this idealization is in section 14.6. For the fin it is an idealization that is good when the fin is thin (the subsection on the fin gives an estimate with a bound). For a tube with insulated ends, however, it is no idealization: the proof of the lemma on the tube shows that the temperature is indeed a function of the radius only.

Symbols that meet other meanings in the book (section 14.1 listed them): \(k\) is the conductivity here, the shear factor in chapter 5, \(q\) is the heat flux density here, a distributed load in chapter 5, and \(c\) is the specific heat, a wave speed in chapter 13. In this section \(k\) and \(q\) appear only as heat quantities.

14.4.1 The plane wall

Take a slab (plošča), say the wall of a furnace or the flange of the beam of chapter 5. It is \(L\) thick, made of a material with conductivity \(k\), and much larger in the other two directions. One face is held at temperature \(T_0\), the other at \(T_{\mathrm{L}} < T_0\), because they touch a warmer and a colder medium. Heat flows from the warmer face to the colder one, so we draw the flux as arrows in the direction of the axis \(x\) across the thickness. We write \(q(x)\) for the component of the heat flux density in the direction \(x\) (definition 14.2): how much heat flows per unit time through a unit of area perpendicular to the axis \(x\). Above the wall we draw the axes \(x\) and \(T\), to see the temperature as a graph, and enter the profile \(T(x)\) from \(T_0\) at \(x = 0\) to \(T_{\mathrm{L}}\) at \(x = L\). What shape this profile has is our question.

Why the flux must be the same everywhere is told by the balance. Look at the piece of the wall between \(x = a\) and \(x = b\), as a column with cross-section of area \(A\). Nothing flows through the sides of the column: the temperature does not depend on the coordinates along the faces, so by Fourier's law both components of the flux along the faces, \(-k\,T_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(-k\,T_{\mathrm{z}}\), are zero. There is no source in the wall. The state is steady, so heat does not accumulate in the piece (theorem 14.8 at \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\)). What flows through the section at \(a\) must therefore also flow through the section at \(b\).

Lemma 14.19 Temperature in a plane wall (temperatura v ravni steni)

Let the wall \(0 \le x \le L\) be made of a material with constant conductivity \(k > 0\), with no heat source, in a steady state, and let the temperature \(T(x)\) be a differentiable function of one coordinate with \(T(0) = T_0\) and \(T(L) = T_{\mathrm{L}}\). Then

\[T(x) = T_0 + (T_{\mathrm{L}} - T_0)\,\frac{x}{L} , \qquad q = \frac{k\,(T_0 - T_{\mathrm{L}})}{L} , \tag{14.17}\]

the flux \(q\) is the same at every point of the wall and flows from the warmer face to the colder one.

Proof

We must show that the derivative of the temperature is constant, and then compute the temperature from a derivative that is zero.

  1. Let \([a, b] \subset [0, L]\) and \(A\) the area of the cross-section. By the balance of a piece (theorem 14.8 at \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), \(Q = 0\), no flux through the sides, as above) \(A\,q(a) - A\,q(b) = 0\).
  2. By Fourier's law (definition 14.3) \(q = -k\,T'\), so \(T'(a) = T'(b)\) for all \(a < b\) in \([0, L]\). The derivative \(T'\) is therefore a constant number \(s\).
  3. The function \(x \mapsto T(x) - s\,x\) has derivative \(T' - s = 0\) on \((0, L)\) and is continuous, so it is constant (corollary 1.85): \(T(x) = c + s\,x\).
  4. From \(T(0) = T_0\) we get \(c = T_0\), from \(T(L) = T_{\mathrm{L}}\) we get \(s = (T_{\mathrm{L}} - T_0)/L\). This is the first equation (14.17).
  5. The flux is \(q = -k\,s = k\,(T_0 - T_{\mathrm{L}})/L\) by step 2, the same at every point. It is positive when \(T_0 > T_{\mathrm{L}}\), so it flows in the direction of increasing \(x\), from the warmer face to the colder one (lemma 14.4).

Source: Not from a source. BARBER §14.2 (PDF p. 235) is the heat equation it follows from, CM §8.3 (PDF p. 402) the one-dimensional form.

The proof showed what a constant flux means: the slope of the temperature is constant because \(k\) is constant, and so the profile is a straight line. Let us test it on chapter 5.

Example 14.20 Free curvature of a beam from a temperature difference (prosta ukrivljenost nosilca iz razlike temperatur)

The beam of chapter 5 is \(40\) mm high, the coordinate \(y\) runs along the height, the upper face (\(y = 20\) mm) is \(20\) K warmer than the lower. By lemma 14.19 (with \(y\) instead of \(x\) and \(L = 40\) mm) the temperature is linear, \(\theta = g\,y\) with \(g = 20\ \text{K}/0{,}040\ \text{m} = 500\) K/m (NumPy). The heat flux flows from the upper face toward the lower one and has the magnitude \(500\,k\) W/m\(^2\), with \(k\) in W/(m K). The book does not yet have a sourced value of \(k\) for steel, so we write no number for it here. The gradient \(g = 500\) K/m is exactly the one that theorem 5.37 took as given, and the free curvature \(\alpha g = 15\cdot 10^{-6}\cdot 500 = 7{,}5\cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/m is the one shown in figure 5.38. The linearity that chapter 5 assumed is thus a consequence of the steady balance, not an extra assumption, when the beam is of one material and the flux through the height is the only one.

The steel bar of chapter 3 (diameter 10 mm, between rigid walls) has, by this lemma, if its lateral surface is thermally insulated and one end is at \(+30\) K and the other at \(0\) K, a linear temperature with mean \(15\) K, because the mean of a linear function is its value at the midpoint. At a uniform warming by \(30\) K the stress there was \(-88{,}2\) MPa (chapter 3). What the stress is now, section 14.7 computes. The mean temperature is the number we shall need.

The lemma requires \(k\) to be the same everywhere. Take a wall of two layers, as in the right slab of figure 14.13: the first layer \(20\) mm thick with conductivity \(k\), the second layer \(20\) mm thick with conductivity \(3k\) (the ratio is chosen for the example, not taken from any material). The faces are \(20\) K apart. Step 1 of the proof stays: a piece that contains the layer interface has \(q(a) = q(b)\) by the balance, so the flux \(q\) is the same in both layers. Steps 2 to 4 however hold only inside each layer, where \(k\) is constant: in the first the slope is \(s_1 = -q/k\), in the second \(s_2 = -q/(3k)\), so \(s_2 = s_1/3\). The temperature drop is \(-s_1 \cdot 20\) mm in the first layer, \(-s_2 \cdot 20\) mm in the second, \(20\) K together. From that \(q = 20\ \text{K}/(0{,}020/k + 0{,}020/(3k))\ \text{m} = 750\,k\) W/m\(^2\), the slopes are \(-750\) K/m and \(-250\) K/m and the drops \(15\) K and \(5\) K (NumPy). The profile is no longer one segment: it has a kink at temperature \(T_*\) at the interface. What stays constant is the flux \(q\), not the slope. So the assumption of chapter 5 that the temperature is linear over the height holds only for a beam of one material. In a layered beam the temperature is linear only inside each layer, not over the whole height.

14.4.2 A wall with a heat source

What if heat is also produced in the wall, for instance because an electric current flows through it? Let \(Q\) denote the heat that the material produces per unit time in a unit of volume (theorem 14.8), constant over the wall. We hold both faces at the same temperature \(T_{\mathrm{s}}\). We draw the wall with dots that show the source, and above it the axis \(x\) and the axis \(T\).

In a wall without a source the inflow and outflow through a piece were equal. Now they differ by the contribution of the source: what flows into the piece \([a, b]\) at \(a\), plus what is produced in it, must flow out at \(b\). So the flux at the right end of the piece must be greater than at the left, by \(Q\,(b - a)\). The flux is no longer constant: right of the middle it flows in the direction of increasing \(x\), left of it toward smaller \(x\), because heat leaves through the nearer face. In the middle the flux is zero. At the faces it is largest. By Fourier's law heat flows in the direction of falling temperature. Since it flows from the middle toward both faces, the temperature is highest in the middle and falls toward the faces.

Lemma 14.21 Wall with a uniform source (stena z enakomernim virom)

Let the wall \(0 \le x \le L\) be made of a material with constant conductivity \(k > 0\), in a steady state, with a uniform source \(Q\) and a differentiable temperature \(T(x)\) with \(T(0) = T(L) = T_{\mathrm{s}}\). Then

\[T(x) - T_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{Q}{2k}\,x\,(L - x) , \qquad q(x) = Q\Big(x - \frac L2\Big) . \tag{14.18}\]

The largest temperature is \(T_{\mathrm{s}} + Q L^2/(8k)\) in the middle. Through each face \(Q L/2\) per unit area flows out, together as much as is produced in a section of the wall, \(Q L\).

Proof

We must show that \(T' + Q\,x/k\) is constant, and then use twice that a function with derivative zero has a constant value.

  1. Let \([a, b] \subset [0, L]\) and \(A\) the area of the cross-section. The balance of the piece (theorem 14.8 at \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\)): \(A\,q(a) - A\,q(b) + Q\,A\,(b - a) = 0\).
  2. By Fourier's law \(q = -k\,T'\). From step 1 we get \(-k\,T'(a) + k\,T'(b) + Q\,(b - a) = 0\), that is \(T'(b) + Q\,b/k = T'(a) + Q\,a/k\) for all \(a < b\).
  3. The function \(T' + Q\,x/k\) is therefore constant, \(= s\). So the function \(x \mapsto T(x) + Q\,x^2/(2k) - s\,x\) has derivative zero and is continuous, so it is constant (corollary 1.85): \(T = c + s\,x - Q\,x^2/(2k)\).
  4. From \(T(0) = T_{\mathrm{s}}\) we get \(c = T_{\mathrm{s}}\). From \(T(L) = T_{\mathrm{s}}\) we get \(s\,L = Q\,L^2/(2k)\), so \(s = Q\,L/(2k)\). Substituting: \(T - T_{\mathrm{s}} = Q\,x\,(L - x)/(2k)\).
  5. Because \(x\,(L - x) = L^2/4 - (x - L/2)^2\), the largest value is \(L^2/4\), at \(x = L/2\), so \(T_{\max} = T_{\mathrm{s}} + Q L^2/(8k)\).
  6. The flux is \(q = -k\,T' = -k\,(s - Q x/k) = Q\,(x - L/2)\). At \(x = 0\) it is \(q = -Q L/2\) (out of the wall, in the direction of decreasing \(x\)), at \(x = L\) it is \(q = +Q L/2\). Together \(Q L\) flows out.

Source: Not from a source. CM Example 8.3.2 (PDF p. 406) solves the same balance for a cylinder with a uniform source.

Numbers for a wall of thickness \(L = 40\) mm. Let the ratio be \(Q/k = 10^5\) K/m\(^2\) (chosen for the example, not taken from a material). Then the rise in the middle, the measure in figure 14.14, is \(Q L^2/(8k) = 10^5 \cdot 0{,}04^2/8 = 20\) K, and at a quarter and three quarters of the thickness it is \(15\) K above \(T_{\mathrm{s}}\) (\(x/L = 0\), \(\tfrac14\), \(\tfrac12\), \(\tfrac34\), \(1\) gives \(0\), \(15\), \(20\), \(15\), \(0\) K, NumPy). This temperature is not linear over the height, so theorem 5.37 of chapter 5 does not hold for it. The stresses of a beam with any temperature \(T(y)\), a parabola like this one included, are computed in section 14.7.

The hypothesis that the lemma needs is hidden in the boundary conditions. Take the same wall with a source \(Q > 0\), but let both faces be thermally insulated, \(q(0) = q(L) = 0\). Step 2 of the proof at \(a = 0\) and \(b = L\) gives \(0 + Q\,L = 0\), which is false. There is no steady solution, because the heat that is produced could go nowhere. The temperature indeed rises: the uniform temperature \(T_0 + Q\,t/(\rho c)\) satisfies the equation of theorem 14.8 (the left side is \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = Q\), the right side \(k\,T_{\mathrm{xx}} + Q = 0 + Q\)) and has slope zero at both faces. The same holds for the body treated by lemma 14.18. Without a source, \(Q = 0\), and with both faces insulated a steady solution exists, but it is not unique: any constant \(T\) will do. The difference from the walls of lemmas 14.19 and 14.21 is that here no face is prescribed by its temperature.

14.4.3 The fin

Now comes a problem in which heat leaves from the sides. The heat that a body gives to a fluid is proportional to the area of contact, because \(h\,(T - T_\infty)\) leaves per unit area (equation (14.12)). If that area is too small, thin strips or rods of a well-conducting material are attached to the body, fins (rebra), and the heat leaves through a larger area (CM §8.3.2, PDF p. 403). The name comes from a thin outgrowth that sticks out of a surface: the English word fin is the fin of a fish, the Slovenian rebro is a rib, as in the rib cage.

The model. A rod of length \(L\), with constant cross-section of area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\), made of a material with conductivity \(k\), is attached at \(x = 0\) to a wall that has temperature \(T_0\) and keeps it. The surroundings have temperature \(T_\infty\). Through the lateral surface heat leaves by Newton's law of cooling (equation (14.12)): per unit area \(h\,(T - T_\infty)\), where \(h\) is the heat transfer coefficient of section 14.3. Nothing leaves through the tip at \(x = L\), the surface is insulated. Inside the rod heat flows along the axis, the axial flux \(q = -k\,T'\).

For the idealizations hidden in the model we want a bound and a number, not only words.

  • The temperature over the cross-section is the same. In reality it is higher at the axis than at the surface, because heat has to flow there. An estimate for a round rod of radius \(R\): the heat that the rod gives off at the sides per unit length is \(2\pi R\,h\,\theta_{\mathrm{s}}\), where \(\theta_{\mathrm{s}}\) is the excess at the surface. If we imagine it is brought by a uniform source \(Q_{\mathrm{e}}\) over the cross-section \(\pi R^2\), then \(Q_{\mathrm{e}} = 2h\,\theta_{\mathrm{s}}/R\). The function \(T = T_{\mathrm{s}} + Q_{\mathrm{e}}\,(R^2 - r^2)/(4k)\) has \(T'' + T'/r = -Q_{\mathrm{e}}/(2k) - Q_{\mathrm{e}}/(2k) = -Q_{\mathrm{e}}/k\), so it satisfies the equation with source \(Q_{\mathrm{e}}\) (corollary 11.18) and equals \(T_{\mathrm{s}}\) at the surface. The difference between axis and surface is \(Q_{\mathrm{e}} R^2/(4k) = (hR/k)\,\theta_{\mathrm{s}}/2\). At \(hR/k \le 0{,}1\) that is at most \(5\,\%\) of the excess \(\theta_{\mathrm{s}}\). This is an estimate, not a proof, since the flux toward the surface is not uniformly distributed. The book does not yet have a sourced value of \(k\) for steel, so we give no estimate for steel.
  • The insulated tip. Its area \(A\) against the area of the lateral surface \(P\,L\) is, for a round rod of diameter \(d\), \((\pi d^2/4)/(\pi d\,L) = d/(4L)\), at \(L = 10\,d\) that is \(2{,}5\,\%\). For a shorter rod the error is larger. CM Example 8.3.1 (PDF p. 404) exposes the tip to the surroundings. Our case is its special case in which no heat leaves through the tip.
  • The coefficient \(h\) is constant over the surface and independent of temperature (an idealization that the sources adopt, COOK PDF p. 469: \(h\) depends on the fluid and is usually measured).

Let us look at the balance of a piece \([a, b]\) of the fin. Heat flows in at \(a\) with the axial flux \(A\,q(a)\), flows out at \(b\) with \(A\,q(b)\), and at the sides \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b h\,P\,(T - T_\infty)\,\mathrm{d}x\) leaves, because in every section the perimeter is \(P\) and per unit area \(h\,(T - T_\infty)\) leaves. The state is steady, so the inflow equals the outflow plus the loss at the sides. Why the profile is bent as figure 14.15 shows: heat escapes from the sides everywhere, so the axial flux shortens from the root toward the tip, and at the tip, which is insulated, it reaches zero. The flux is \(-k\,T'\), so the slope must shorten, which means that \(\theta\) bends upward toward the tip. The lateral arrows are shorter too, because \(\theta\) is smaller there.

We write \(\theta = T - T_\infty\), \(\theta_0 = T_0 - T_\infty\) and

\[m = \sqrt{\frac{h\,P}{k\,A}} , \tag{14.19}\]

in units 1/m. The numerator \(h\,P\) tells how much heat per unit length leaves at the sides per kelvin of excess, the denominator \(k\,A\) how well the rod conducts along its axis. A large \(m^2\) means that the heat escapes before it gets far. The length \(1/m\) is the scale on which the temperature changes appreciably, and the dimensionless number \(m L\) tells how many such lengths the fin has. At \(m L \ll 1\) little leaves at the sides and the fin is nearly uniformly warm. At \(m L \gg 1\) the heat is used up already near the root and there is almost none at the tip. A round rod of diameter \(d\) has \(P/A = 4/d\) and \(m^2 = 4h/(k\,d)\).

Theorem 14.22 Temperature and heat of a fin (temperatura in toplota rebra)

Let a rod of length \(L\) have constant cross-section \(A\), perimeter \(P\), conductivity \(k > 0\) and heat transfer coefficient \(h > 0\) at its sides. Let the temperature \(T(x)\) have continuous \(T'\) and \(T''\) on \([0, L]\), \(T(0) = T_0\), let the tip be insulated, \(T'(L) = 0\), and \(\theta = T - T_\infty\), \(m\) as in equation (14.19). Then:

  1. The balance of every piece \([a, b]\) is equivalent to \(\theta'' = m^2\,\theta\) at every point.
  2. The problem \(\theta'' = m^2\,\theta\), \(\theta(0) = \theta_0\), \(\theta'(L) = 0\) has exactly one solution,
    \[\theta(x) = \theta_0\,\frac{\cosh m\,(L - x)}{\cosh m L} . \tag{14.20}\]
  3. The heat that flows into the fin through the root is
    \[\Phi_0 = -k\,A\,T'(0) = k\,A\,\theta_0\,m\,\frac{\sinh m L}{\cosh m L} , \tag{14.21}\]
    and it equals the heat that leaves at the sides, \(\int_0^L h\,P\,\theta\,\mathrm{d}x\). The ratio of this heat to the heat \(h\,P\,L\,\theta_0\) that would leave if the whole fin were at the temperature of the root is \(\tanh(m L)/(m L)\), where \(\tanh s = \sinh s/\cosh s\). This ratio is the effectiveness of the fin (učinkovitost rebra).
Proof

We must show first that the balance gives a differential equation, then that the given function satisfies it and is the only one, and finally compute the heat.

  1. By the balance of a piece \(A\,q(a) - A\,q(b) - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b h\,P\,\theta\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). With \(q = -k\,T'\) this is \(k\,A\,\big(T'(b) - T'(a)\big) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b h\,P\,\theta\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40, item 1) \(T'(b) - T'(a) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b T''\,\mathrm{d}x\), because \(T''\) is continuous. Step 1 is therefore \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for every piece, where \(f = k\,A\,T'' - h\,P\,\theta\) is a continuous function (\(\theta' = T'\)).
  3. A continuous function with zero integral over every piece is zero everywhere, as in step 5 of theorem 13.3. So \(k\,A\,T'' = h\,P\,\theta\), that is \(\theta'' = m^2\,\theta\). Conversely, if this holds everywhere, \(f\) has all integrals zero and the balance holds for every piece. This shows item 1.
  4. By the chain rule and lemma 9.42 (item 1) the function \(x \mapsto \cosh m\,(L - x)\) has derivative \(-m\,\sinh m\,(L - x)\) and second derivative \(m^2\cosh m\,(L - x)\). The function in equation (14.20) therefore satisfies \(\theta'' = m^2\theta\), its value at \(x = 0\) is \(\theta_0\), and its derivative at \(L\) is \(-\theta_0\,m\,\sinh 0/\cosh m L = 0\) (lemma 9.42, item 2).
  5. Uniqueness. Let \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) be solutions and \(w = \theta_1 - \theta_2\). Then \(w'' = m^2 w\), \(w(0) = 0\), \(w'(L) = 0\). Multiply by \(w\) and integrate over \([0, L]\): \(\int_0^L w\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x = m^2\int_0^L w^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). By integration by parts (corollary 3.41) the left side is \(w(L)\,w'(L) - w(0)\,w'(0) - \int_0^L (w')^2\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int_0^L (w')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), because \(w'(L) = 0\) and \(w(0) = 0\). So \(-\int_0^L (w')^2 = m^2 \int_0^L w^2\). The left side is \(\le 0\), the right \(\ge 0\) (lemma 3.39, item 4), so both are zero, and since \(m^2 > 0\), \(\int_0^L w^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\).
  6. If \(w(x_0) \ne 0\), then by continuity \(w^2 \ge w(x_0)^2/2\) on some interval around \(x_0\), and by lemma 3.39 (items 2, 3 and 4) the integral would be positive. So \(w = 0\) everywhere and \(\theta_1 = \theta_2\).
  7. Heat at the root. By step 4 \(\theta'(x) = -\theta_0\,m\,\sinh m(L - x)/\cosh m L\), so \(\theta'(0) = -\theta_0\,m\,\sinh m L/\cosh m L\) and \(\Phi_0 = -k\,A\,\theta'(0)\) is equation (14.21).
  8. Heat at the sides. The function \(x \mapsto -\sinh m(L - x)/m\) has derivative \(\cosh m(L - x)\) (lemma 9.42, item 1), so by the fundamental theorem \(\int_0^L \cosh m(L - x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \sinh m L/m\) and \(\int_0^L h\,P\,\theta\,\mathrm{d}x = h\,P\,\theta_0\,\sinh m L/(m\cosh m L)\). Because \(h\,P = k\,A\,m^2\), this is \(k\,A\,\theta_0\,m\,\sinh m L/\cosh m L = \Phi_0\).
  9. The ratio: \(h\,P\,L\,\theta_0 = k\,A\,m^2 L\,\theta_0\), so \(\Phi_0/(h\,P\,L\,\theta_0) = (m \sinh m L/\cosh m L)/(m^2 L) = \tanh(mL)/(mL)\).

Source: CM Example 8.3.1 (PDF pp. 404 and 405, equations (8.3.10) and (5)), a fin whose tip is exposed to the surroundings. The solution with an insulated tip is a special case of its solution (5) at zero tip coefficient. CM defines after this example the effectiveness of a fin as the ratio of the heat given off to the heat that the surface would give off at the temperature of the root (PDF p. 405). The proof by steps, with a piece of finite length and uniqueness by energy, is not from the sources.

A test on two numbers (NumPy). The lower part of figure 14.15 shows the axis \(x\) and the excess \(\theta\) and the profiles for \(m L = 1\) and \(m L = 2\). At \(m L = 1\) the tip is at \(1/\cosh 1 = 0{,}648\) of the temperature excess at the root, and at a quarter, half and three quarters of the length at \(0{,}839\), \(0{,}731\) and \(0{,}668\). The heat at the root is \(k A \theta_0/L \cdot m L \tanh m L = 0{,}7616\; k A\theta_0/L\) and the effectiveness \(0{,}762\). At \(m L = 2\) the tip is at \(1/\cosh 2 = 0{,}266\), the heat at the root \(1{,}928\; k A\theta_0/L\) and the effectiveness \(0{,}482\). If the whole fin were at the temperature of the root, the heat would be \((m L)^2\,k A\theta_0/L\), that is \(1\) at \(m L = 1\) and \(4\) at \(m L = 2\). The real heat is \(76\,\%\) and \(48\,\%\) of that, because the excess \(\theta\) along the fin is smaller than at the root. The effectiveness is the mean of \(\theta/\theta_0\) over the length of the fin (step 8 of the proof): at \(m L = 1\) \(\theta\) is everywhere at least \(0{,}648\,\theta_0\), at \(m L = 2\) the far half of the fin is only at \(0{,}27\) to \(0{,}41\) of the value at the root and contributes little. A consistency check (step 8): at \(m L = 1\) \((m L)^2\int_0^1\theta/\theta_0\,\mathrm{d}\xi = 0{,}76159\), where \(\xi = x/L\), the same number as \(m L\tanh m L\).

Let us also test what the proof of uniqueness really needs. Without losses at the sides, \(h = 0\), we have \(m = 0\) and step 5 gives only \(\int (w')^2 = 0\), so \(w\) is constant. Since the root is prescribed, \(w(0) = 0\), we get \(w = 0\) and uniqueness holds. But if both ends are insulated (\(w'(0) = 0 = w'(L)\)) and \(h = 0\), every constant \(T\) is a solution, the solution is not unique, as in the wall with insulated faces in the previous section. For uniqueness it is therefore enough that one end is prescribed by temperature or that \(h > 0\) (then \(m^2\int w^2\) is a positive term that also removes a constant difference).

14.4.4 A tube: temperature along the radius

The last problem has an area that changes with the radius. A tube (cev) with inner radius \(a\) and outer radius \(b\), of length \(\ell\), is made of a material with constant \(k\) and has its flat ends thermally insulated. The inner surface is at \(T_{\mathrm{a}}\), the outer at \(T_{\mathrm{b}}\), there is no source in the wall. We take the tube of chapter 11: \(a = 40\) mm, \(b = 60\) mm, the inner surface \(100\) K warmer than the outer. In this tube chapter 11 computed the stresses from the oil pressure and promised the stresses from temperature as well. Section 14.8 computes those, and it needs the temperature along the radius.

We draw two circles with radii \(a\) and \(b\) and the heat flux that flows outward from the inner surface, where it is warmer. Through the lateral surface of a cylinder of radius \(r\) and length \(\ell\) (a circle in the cross-section) there flows, by the definition of the flux (definition 14.2), \(q_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot 2\pi r\,\ell\), since the flux is radial and constant on that surface. In a steady state without a source the same heat flows through every such surface, because nothing accumulates between two of them. The area of the surface, \(2\pi r\,\ell\), grows in proportion to \(r\), so \(q_{\mathrm{r}}\) must fall like \(1/r\). In the figure this is drawn as a shorter arrow at the outer surface. We also draw the axes \(r\) and \(T\) and in them the profile \(T(r)\). It falls faster where the flux is larger, so at the inner surface. What function it is, the lemma shows.

Lemma 14.23 Radial conduction through a tube (radialno prevajanje skozi cev)

Let the tube \(a < r < b\) of length \(\ell\) be made of a material with constant conductivity \(k > 0\), with flat ends thermally insulated, \(T = T_{\mathrm{a}}\) at \(r = a\) and \(T = T_{\mathrm{b}}\) at \(r = b\), with no source, steady. Then the temperature is a function of \(r\) only,

\[T(r) = T_{\mathrm{a}} + (T_{\mathrm{b}} - T_{\mathrm{a}})\,\frac{\ln(r/a)}{\ln(b/a)} , \tag{14.22}\]

and the heat per unit length that flows through every circle of radius \(r\) is the same,

\[\Phi' = \frac{2\pi k\,(T_{\mathrm{a}} - T_{\mathrm{b}})}{\ln(b/a)} . \tag{14.23}\]
Proof

We must show that the function of equation (14.22) solves the problem and that the solution is unique. We find the form of the function from the Laplace operator in polar coordinates.

  1. Let the temperature \(T(r)\) be a function of the radius only. By theorem 14.8 at \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), \(Q = 0\) and constant \(k\) the equation is \(k\,\nabla^2 T = 0\), and by corollary 11.18 \(\nabla^2 T = T'' + T'/r\), because \(T\) does not depend on the polar angle and on \(z\).
  2. Multiply by \(r\): \(r\,T'' + T' = (r\,T')' = 0\) by the product rule. The function \(r\,T'\) has derivative zero, so it is constant (corollary 1.85), \(r\,T' = C\) and \(T' = C/r\).
  3. By lemma 9.11 (item 1) \(\ln r\) has derivative \(1/r\), so \(T - C\ln r\) has derivative zero and is constant: \(T = A + C \ln r\).
  4. From the boundary conditions \(T(a) = T_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(T(b) = T_{\mathrm{b}}\) we get \(C = (T_{\mathrm{b}} - T_{\mathrm{a}})/\ln(b/a)\) and \(A = T_{\mathrm{a}} - C\ln a\), which gives equation (14.22) (lemma 9.11, item 2: \(\ln r - \ln a = \ln(r/a)\)).
  5. The function of step 4 satisfies the equation at every point (step 1 in the reverse direction), both boundary conditions on the surfaces, and at the flat ends \(T_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), so the flux \(-k\,T_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), as the insulation requires. By theorem 14.17 (item 2, the steady case, \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) nonempty) it is the only solution, so the temperature is indeed a function of \(r\) only (without the assumption of step 1).
  6. The flux is \(q_{\mathrm{r}} = -k\,T' = -k\,C/r\). Through the lateral surface of a cylinder of radius \(r\) and length \(\ell\) there flows \(q_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot 2\pi r\,\ell = -2\pi k\,C\,\ell\), which does not depend on \(r\). Per unit length that is \(-2\pi k\,C = 2\pi k\,(T_{\mathrm{a}} - T_{\mathrm{b}})/\ln(b/a)\).

Source: CM §8.3.3 (PDF pp. 405 and 406): an axisymmetric cylinder, equation (8.3.11), Example 8.3.2 with a source. SADD (12.7.10) to (12.7.12) (PDF pp. 390 and 391): the same equation and the solution \(T_{\mathrm{i}}\,\ln(r_{\mathrm{o}}/r)/\ln(r_{\mathrm{o}}/r_{\mathrm{i}})\) for an annular plate (Example 12.2), the equation with the logarithm. The proof by steps and uniqueness is not from the sources.

Numbers for the tube \(a = 40\) mm, \(b = 60\) mm, \(T_{\mathrm{a}} - T_{\mathrm{b}} = 100\) K, \(T_{\mathrm{b}} = 0\) (NumPy): \(\ln(b/a) = 0{,}4055\). The temperature is \(T(r) = 100\ln(60/r)/\ln 1{,}5\) and at \(r = 40\), \(45\), \(50\), \(55\), \(60\) mm it is \(100\), \(70{,}95\), \(44{,}97\), \(21{,}46\) and \(0\) K. The slope is \(-6{,}17\) K/mm at \(r = 40\) mm and \(-4{,}11\) K/mm at \(60\) mm, the ratio is \(1{,}5 = b/a\), as it must be (\(r\,T'\) constant). The heat per unit length is \(\Phi' = 2\pi k \cdot 100/0{,}4055 = 1549{,}6\,k\) W/m (\(k\) in W/(m K)).

COOK (PDF p. 484, equation (12.6-1)) estimates the flux through a pipe wall as if the wall were plane: \(q = k\,\Delta T/\Delta r\). For our tube that is \(k\cdot 100\ \text{K}/20\ \text{mm} = 5\,k\) K/mm. The true flux is \(6{,}17\,k\) K/mm at the inner and \(4{,}11\,k\) K/mm at the outer surface, the estimate lies between them. COOK calls it an upper limit because it takes the temperatures of the fluids at the surfaces, whose difference is larger than that of the surfaces themselves. With prescribed surface temperatures, as here, the estimate is not an upper bound of the flux at the inner surface. If we multiply it by the perimeter of the middle circle (\(r = 50\) mm), we get \(2\pi\cdot 50\cdot 5 = 1570{,}8\,k\) W/m, which is \(1{,}4\,\%\) more than the true value. The difference is in the radius: the true value corresponds to the radius \((b - a)/\ln(b/a) = 49{,}33\) mm instead of the arithmetic mean \(50\) mm. For a thin wall, \(b/a \to 1\), the ratio of the fluxes at the surfaces, \(b/a\), tends to \(1\) and the estimate from a plane wall is good. This is an estimate of the size of the error, not a proof.

Why not use lemma 14.19 here as well? Let \(T\) be linear in \(r\) between \(T_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{b}}\). The flux \(q_{\mathrm{r}} = -k\,T'\) would then be the same everywhere. Through the circle of radius \(60\) mm there would flow \(1{,}5\) times as much heat as through the circle of radius \(40\) mm, because the perimeter is \(1{,}5\) times larger, and half of the first value would be created from nothing. The linear profile does not satisfy the balance, because in a wall the area along the flow is constant, and in a tube it grows. The linear profile in figure 14.16 shows it: at \(r = 50\) mm it gives \(50\) K, the true value is \(44{,}97\) K.

What we have seen. In all four problems the idea was one and the same: the balance of a piece at a steady temperature, then Fourier's law, a derivative zero means a constant value, and the boundary conditions fix the constants. A wall without a source has a constant flux and a linear temperature (and so the linear \(\theta\) of chapter 5), a wall with a source a parabola, the fin a hyperbolic cosine with the scale \(m L\), the tube a logarithm, and in each the result is unique, by the balance or by energy uniqueness. What we use later: the temperature of the tube is the datum for the stresses in the tube in section 14.8, the parabola of the wall for a beam with any temperature in section 14.7, and the fin is a case that we shall solve with finite elements in section 14.10 and compare with the function \(\cosh\). The next section drops the steadiness: what happens to the temperature of a bar while it changes with time.

14.5 Unsteady conduction in a bar

Unsteady (nestacionarno) means that the temperature changes with time, in contrast to the steady state of section 14.4, where it stays put (Latin stare, to stand).

We heat a copper bar of length \(80\) cm and then dip both ends in ice water, which holds them at \(0\) °C. How long does the bar take to cool, and how does the shape of the temperature along the bar change while it cools? For the string (chapter 13) we answered a similar question with modes of vibration, that is with shapes that time only multiplies. We try the same idea for heat and see where it differs.

The model is the bar of section 14.2 (corollary 14.10): a straight bar of length \(L\) with constant cross-section of homogeneous material, perfectly insulated along its sides, so that heat flows only along the axis \(x\). The side insulation is an idealization: a real bar also loses heat through its lateral surface, which the fin of section 14.4 includes. We measure the temperature \(T(x, t)\) of the point \(x\) at time \(t\) from the temperature of the ends, as the change \(\Delta T\) of chapter 3. The ends have temperature zero, the initial temperature \(h(x)\) is known. By corollary 14.10 and definition 14.9,

\[T_{\mathrm{t}} = \kappa\,T_{\mathrm{xx}} \qquad (0 < x < L,\ t > 0) , \tag{14.24}\]

with \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = \partial T/\partial t\) and \(T_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2 T/\partial x^2\) and the thermal diffusivity \(\kappa = k/(\rho c)\). The boundary and initial conditions are

\[T(0, t) = T(L, t) = 0 \quad (t \ge 0) , \qquad T(x, 0) = h(x) \quad (0 \le x \le L) . \tag{14.25}\]

The letter \(\kappa\) here means the diffusivity, not the curvature of chapter 5, and the letter \(c\) means the specific heat, not the wave speed of chapter 13. We call this triple of equations a boundary value problem of heat conduction (definition 14.14), here for a bar.

Let us draw this problem. The bar is a rectangle of length \(L\) on the axis \(x\). At both ends a thermal contact with temperature \(0\) holds it: the blackwhite line is the edge of the bar, the hatching is the surroundings, which keep a fixed temperature at the contact, ice water for instance. Above the bar we draw the initial temperature \(h(x)\) as a height over the zero level, and the distance \(L\) measures the length of the bar. In the figure \(h\) is a triangle with its peak in the middle and with a kink. The kink is deliberate: for the string we saw that a kink in the initial shape travels along the string as a wave, and the question is what heat does with it.

For the string a mode was a shape \(\varphi(x)\) multiplied by \(\cos\omega t\) (definition 13.6). We try the same for heat, only the time factor is not known in advance. We look for a solution of the form \(T = \varphi(x)\,g(t)\) (separation of variables, since place and time sit in two separate factors) that satisfies equation (14.24) and both boundary conditions. The question is which \(\varphi\) and \(g\) can do this.

Lemma 14.24 Heat modes of the bar (načini prevajanja po palici)

Let \(L > 0\) and \(\kappa > 0\). Let \(\varphi : [0, L] \to \mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable and not identically zero, and \(g : [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) continuously differentiable and not identically zero. The function \(T(x, t) = \varphi(x)\,g(t)\) satisfies equation (14.24) and the boundary conditions (14.25) if and only if there are a natural number \(n\) and numbers \(C \ne 0\), \(A \ne 0\) with

\[\varphi(x) = C\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} , \qquad g(t) = A\,\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2} . \tag{14.26}\]
Proof

We must show that the equation gives an ordinary equation for each factor separately, that the boundary conditions pick out sine shapes as for the string, and that an energy computation (integration by parts) rules out growth.

  1. If \(T = \varphi g\), then \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = \varphi g'\) and \(T_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varphi'' g\), so equation (14.24) says \(\varphi(x)\,g'(t) = \kappa\,\varphi''(x)\,g(t)\) for \(0 < x < L\) and \(t > 0\).
  2. Since \(g\) is continuous and not identically zero, \(g(t_0) \ne 0\) for some \(t_0 > 0\) (if it were zero for every \(t > 0\) it would be zero at \(0\) too by continuity). Likewise \(\varphi(x_0) \ne 0\) for some \(x_0 \in (0, L)\), since a zero throughout the interior would give zeros at the ends.
  3. At \(x = x_0\) step 1 gives \(g' = \nu g\) with \(\nu = \kappa\varphi''(x_0)/\varphi(x_0)\) for every \(t > 0\). By the lemma on the equation of exponential growth and decay (9.14, item 1), \(g(t) = A\,\mathrm{e}^{\nu t}\) with \(A = g(t_0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\nu t_0} \ne 0\), and by continuity also at \(t = 0\).
  4. At \(t = t_0\) step 1 gives \(\nu\,\varphi(x) = \kappa\,\varphi''(x)\), so \(\varphi'' = \mu\varphi\) with \(\mu = \nu/\kappa\). From the boundary conditions \(\varphi(0)\,g(t_0) = 0\) and \(\varphi(L)\,g(t_0) = 0\), hence \(\varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0\).
  5. Multiply \(\varphi'' = \mu\varphi\) by \(\varphi\) and integrate. By integration by parts (corollary 3.41), \(\int_0^L\varphi\varphi''\,\mathrm{d}x = [\varphi\varphi']_0^L - \int_0^L\varphi'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int_0^L\varphi'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), since \(\varphi\) is zero at the ends. So \(\mu\int_0^L\varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int_0^L\varphi'^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le 0\). The integral \(\int_0^L\varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) is positive, because \(\varphi\) is continuous and not identically zero (lemma 6.10, item 3), hence \(\mu \le 0\).
  6. If \(\mu = 0\), then \(\int_0^L\varphi'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\), so \(\varphi' = 0\) (same lemma), \(\varphi\) is constant and by \(\varphi(0) = 0\) zero everywhere, which we excluded. So \(\mu = -k^2\) with \(k > 0\) and \(\varphi'' = -k^2\varphi\) with \(\varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0\). This is equation (13.7), so steps 3 to 5 of the proof of the theorem on the modes of the string (13.7) give \(kL = n\pi\) and \(\varphi = C\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with \(C \ne 0\).
  7. Then \(\nu = \kappa\mu = -\kappa n^2\pi^2/L^2\) and step 3 gives \(g = A\,\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2}\). This is the direction "only if".
  8. Conversely, for \(T = CA\sin(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2}\) the theorem on the derivatives of sine and cosine (8.12) and the lemma on the equation of exponential growth (9.14, item 1) give \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = -\kappa(n\pi/L)^2\,T\) and \(T_{\mathrm{xx}} = -(n\pi/L)^2\,T\), so \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = \kappa T_{\mathrm{xx}}\). At \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) we have \(\sin 0 = \sin n\pi = 0\) (lemma 8.10, item 2), so the boundary conditions hold.

Source: KREYSZIG section 12.5 (PDF p. 585-586) separates the variables, says that the separation constant must be negative, and obtains \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}^2 t}\). The proof by integration by parts in step 5, which rules out \(\mu \ge 0\), and the use of lemma 9.14 are not from the source.

In the exponent of the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2}\) stands the ratio \(\kappa t/L^2\), which has no unit, since \(\kappa\) is in m²/s. We call it the Fourier number (Fourierovo število) and write \(\mathrm{Fo} = \kappa t/L^2\). It is named after Fourier, who treated the spread of heat in solid bodies in his book La Théorie analytique de la chaleur of 1822 (section 14.1). It tells how much time has passed, measured in units of \(L^2/\kappa\). This unit is the time scale of conduction along a bar of length \(L\): at \(\mathrm{Fo} = 1\) the first mode has only \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi^2} = 5{,}2\cdot 10^{-5}\) of its initial height left. Mode \(n\) has the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-n^2\pi^2\,\mathrm{Fo}}\) after the time \(\mathrm{Fo}\).

For the string the time factor is \(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\): an oscillation that does not shrink. Here it is \(\mathrm{e}^{-n^2\pi^2\mathrm{Fo}}\): the shape stays, the amplitude decays and never changes sign. Figure 14.18 shows both, the shapes on the left and the decay on the right.

On the left are the shapes of the first, second and third mode at time zero (grey dashed line) and after \(\mathrm{Fo} = 0{,}01\) (blue line). The shape is the same, the height smaller, but not equally: the first mode kept \(0{,}906\) of its height, the second \(0{,}674\), the third only \(0{,}411\). On the right, on axes with \(\mathrm{Fo}\) horizontal and the factor vertical, are the decay curves \(\mathrm{e}^{-n^2\pi^2\mathrm{Fo}}\) for the first, second and third mode. Half of the initial amplitude is reached by mode \(1\) at \(\mathrm{Fo} = \ln 2/\pi^2 = 0{,}0702\), by mode \(2\) at \(0{,}0176\) and by mode \(3\) at \(0{,}0078\). The time to half is shorter by the factor \(n^2\) for mode \(n\) than for the first mode.

Why \(n^2\)? The law of conduction of corollary 14.10 says that the rate of change of temperature at a point is proportional to the curvature \(T_{\mathrm{xx}}\) there: a point that is warm between two cooler neighbours gives heat away and cools. Mode \(n\) has \(n\) times as many half-waves, so at the same height its slope is \(n\) times larger and its curvature \(n^2\) times larger, and it levels out that much faster. For the string the curvature determined the acceleration and so gave oscillation, here it determines the rate and so gives decay.

We write a general initial shape \(h\) as a sum of modes. Since equation (14.24) is linear (a sum and a multiple of solutions is a solution, by the rules of differentiation, lemma 1.81), the sum

\[T(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{n}=1}^{\infty}h_{\mathrm{n}}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2} \tag{14.27}\]

is a candidate for the solution, if the \(h_{\mathrm{n}}\) are the sine coefficients of the initial temperature (equation (13.8): at \(t = 0\) the series is the sine series of the function \(h\)). The formula for \(h_{\mathrm{n}}\) makes sense for every piecewise continuous function (definition 6.8), not only for a continuous one with zeros at the ends as in definition 13.9, and we use it so. We must justify two things: whether the series converges, and whether we may differentiate the sum term by term. For the string the answers depended on the smoothness of the initial shape. Here the exponential factor will provide them. Term-by-term differentiation needs a lemma that the book did not have so far.

Lemma 14.25 Continuity and derivative of a uniformly convergent series (zveznost in odvod enakomerno konvergentne vrste)

Let \(I\) and \(J\) be intervals (definition 1.43) and \(f_{\mathrm{n}} : I \times J \to \mathbb{R}\) functions for \(n = 1, 2, \dots\) that are continuous in both variables together, and \(M_{\mathrm{n}} \ge 0\) numbers with \(|f_{\mathrm{n}}| \le M_{\mathrm{n}}\) everywhere and \(\sum M_{\mathrm{n}} < \infty\).

  1. The sum \(s = \sum f_{\mathrm{n}}\) is continuous on \(I \times J\).
  2. Let every \(f_{\mathrm{n}}\) have at every point a partial derivative \(\partial f_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial x\) (one-sided at the endpoints of \(I\)) that is continuous on \(I \times J\) and of absolute value at most \(M_{\mathrm{n}}'\), and let \(\sum M_{\mathrm{n}}' < \infty\). Then \(s\) has a partial derivative in \(x\) at every point and \(\partial s/\partial x = \sum \partial f_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial x\), which is a continuous function.
  3. The same holds with \(t\) in the role of \(x\), if \(t\) is the variable on \(J\).
Proof

We must show that the remainder of the series is small uniformly everywhere (the Weierstrass test), so that passing to the limit keeps continuity, and obtain the derivative through an integral: we write the difference of the sums as an integral of the derivatives and take the limit under the integral.

  1. Let \(s_{\mathrm{N}} = f_1 + \dots + f_{\mathrm{N}}\) be the partial sum and \(R_{\mathrm{N}} = \sum_{\mathrm{n} > \mathrm{N}}M_{\mathrm{n}} \to 0\). By the Weierstrass test (theorem 9.85, item 2, whose proof does not use that the domain is an interval), \(|s(p) - s_{\mathrm{N}}(p)| \le R_{\mathrm{N}}\) at every point \(p\).
  2. Let \(p\) be a point and \(\eta > 0\). Choose \(N\) with \(R_{\mathrm{N}} < \eta/3\). The function \(s_{\mathrm{N}}\) is continuous as a finite sum of continuous functions, so there is \(\delta > 0\) with \(|s_{\mathrm{N}}(q) - s_{\mathrm{N}}(p)| < \eta/3\) for every point \(q\) near \(p\) (distance less than \(\delta\)). For such \(q\), \(|s(q) - s(p)| \le |s(q) - s_{\mathrm{N}}(q)| + |s_{\mathrm{N}}(q) - s_{\mathrm{N}}(p)| + |s_{\mathrm{N}}(p) - s(p)| < \eta\). This is item 1.
  3. Let \(g = \sum\partial f_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial x\). By item 1 applied to the functions \(\partial f_{\mathrm{n}}/\partial x\) with bounds \(M_{\mathrm{n}}'\), \(g\) is continuous and \(|g - \partial s_{\mathrm{N}}/\partial x| \le R_{\mathrm{N}}'\) with \(R_{\mathrm{N}}' = \sum_{\mathrm{n} > \mathrm{N}}M_{\mathrm{n}}' \to 0\).
  4. Let \(t \in J\) and \(x_0 < x\) in \(I\). The function \(y \mapsto s_{\mathrm{N}}(y, t)\) has a continuous derivative, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus (3.40, item 1) \(s_{\mathrm{N}}(x, t) - s_{\mathrm{N}}(x_0, t) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x}\frac{\partial s_{\mathrm{N}}}{\partial x}(y, t)\,\mathrm{d}y\).
  5. By the estimate of the integral (lemma 9.31), \(\big|\int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x}\big(g - \frac{\partial s_{\mathrm{N}}}{\partial x}\big)\mathrm{d}y\big| \le (x - x_0)\,R_{\mathrm{N}}' \to 0\). Since the left side of step 4 tends to \(s(x, t) - s(x_0, t)\), we get \(s(x, t) - s(x_0, t) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x}g(y, t)\,\mathrm{d}y\).
  6. The function \(y \mapsto g(y, t)\) is continuous (step 3), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus (3.40, item 2) the integral is differentiable in \(x\) with derivative \(g(x, t)\). So \(\partial s/\partial x = g\), continuous. This is item 2, and item 3 is the same proof with \(t\).

Source: LEBL1 theorems 6.2.2 (PDF p. 235), 6.2.4 (PDF p. 237) and 6.2.10 (PDF p. 239) give the continuity, integral and derivative of the uniform limit of a sequence of functions of one variable. The formula of item 2 for two variables and the proof with the fundamental theorem of calculus and the Weierstrass test are not from the source.

The condition on the sum \(\sum M_{\mathrm{n}}'\) is not a formality. Take the sine series of the function \(h(x) = x\) on \([0, 1]\) from section 13.2: \(h_{\mathrm{n}} = 2(-1)^{n+1}/(n\pi)\), the terms have the bound \(2/(n\pi)\), whose sum is not finite, and the series has the sum \(h\) pointwise on \((0, 1)\) (theorem 9.94). The term-by-term differentiated series has terms \(2(-1)^{n+1}\cos n\pi x\), which at \(x = 0\) give \(2, -2, 2, \dots\), with partial sums \(2, 0, 2, 0, \dots\) that have no limit, although \(h' = 1\). Differentiating term by term is wrong here, since the smallest bounds \(M_{\mathrm{n}}' = 2\) have no finite sum. For heat the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2}\) creates a finite sum of bounds: at every \(t > 0\) it shrinks the terms of the \(n\)th mode more than any power of \(n\).

Theorem 14.26 Expansion of the temperature of the bar in modes (razvoj temperature palice po načinih)

Let \(L > 0\), \(\kappa > 0\), \(h\) a piecewise continuous function on \([0, L]\) and \(h_{\mathrm{n}}\) its sine coefficients (equation (13.8)). Then:

  1. For every \(t > 0\) the series (14.27) converges. Its sum \(T\) is defined on \(\mathbb{R} \times (0, \infty)\) (sines are defined everywhere) and has continuous derivatives \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{xx}}\) there, obtained term by term, and \(T\) solves equation (14.24) and the boundary conditions \(T(0, t) = T(L, t) = 0\) for \(t > 0\).
  2. If \(h\) is moreover continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11) with \(h(0) = h(L) = 0\), then \(T\) is continuous on \([0, L] \times [0, \infty)\), \(T(x, 0) = h(x)\), and \(T\) is the only solution of the boundary value problem (14.24), (14.25) with continuous derivatives on a neighbourhood of the bar for \(t > 0\) and continuity up to \(t = 0\) (theorem 14.17, which we read for the bar in one dimension).
Proof

We must show that every term of the series and of the series of derivatives has a bound that is independent of \(x\) and \(t\) and has a finite sum, and then use lemma 14.25. The last part follows from the sine series of a function on an interval and from uniqueness.

  1. Let \(M\) be the maximum of \(|h|\) (a piecewise continuous function is bounded, since its pieces are continuous on closed intervals). By the estimate of the integral (lemma 9.31), \(|h_{\mathrm{n}}| \le \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L|h|\,|\sin|\,\mathrm{d}x \le 2M\).
  2. Let \(t_0 > 0\), \(a = \kappa\pi^2 t_0/L^2\) and \(k \in \{0, 1, 2\}\). Choose an integer \(m \ge (k + 2)/2\). By the lemma on the growth of the exponential function (9.15, item 2), \(s^m\,\mathrm{e}^{-as} \to 0\) as \(s \to \infty\), so it is less than \(1\) for every \(s > s_*\) and bounded by a number \(C\) for all integers \(s = n^2 \ge 1\) (finitely many terms up to \(s_*\)). So \(n^k\,\mathrm{e}^{-an^2} = n^{k - 2m}\,(n^2)^m\,\mathrm{e}^{-an^2} \le C/n^2\), since \(2m \ge k + 2\).
  3. A term of the series is \(f_{\mathrm{n}} = h_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2}\). By the theorem on the derivatives of sine and cosine (8.12) and lemma 9.14, \(\partial_{\mathrm{x}} f_{\mathrm{n}} = h_{\mathrm{n}}(n\pi/L)\cos(\cdot)\,\mathrm{e}^{\dots}\), \(\partial_{\mathrm{xx}}f_{\mathrm{n}} = -h_{\mathrm{n}}(n\pi/L)^2\sin(\cdot)\,\mathrm{e}^{\dots}\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}} f_{\mathrm{n}} = -\kappa(n\pi/L)^2 f_{\mathrm{n}}\) are continuous. On \(\mathbb{R} \times [t_0, \infty)\) we have \(\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2} \le \mathrm{e}^{-an^2}\), so by steps 1 and 2 each of \(|f_{\mathrm{n}}|\), \(|\partial_{\mathrm{x}} f_{\mathrm{n}}|\), \(|\partial_{\mathrm{xx}}f_{\mathrm{n}}|\), \(|\partial_{\mathrm{t}} f_{\mathrm{n}}|\) is at most \(c_{\mathrm{k}}\,2M\,C/n^2\) with \(c_{\mathrm{k}} = (\pi/L)^k\) or \(\kappa(\pi/L)^2\). The sum \(\sum 1/n^2\) is finite (lemma 9.83, item 3).
  4. By lemma 14.25 (items 1 to 3, repeated for \(\partial_{\mathrm{x}} f_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}} f_{\mathrm{n}}\)), \(T\) is continuous, has continuous \(T_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{xx}}\) on \(\mathbb{R} \times [t_0, \infty)\) and is differentiated term by term. Since \(t_0 > 0\) is arbitrary, this holds on \((0, \infty)\).
  5. By lemma 14.24 every term is a solution, and term by term \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = -\kappa\sum(n\pi/L)^2 f_{\mathrm{n}} = \kappa T_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The boundary conditions hold for every term, so for the sum. This is item 1.
  6. Let \(h\) be as in item 2. By the lemma on the sine series of a function on an interval (13.10), \(\sum|h_{\mathrm{n}}| < \infty\) and \(\sum h_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(n\pi x/L) = h(x)\). On \([0, L] \times [0, \infty)\) we have \(|f_{\mathrm{n}}| \le |h_{\mathrm{n}}|\), so by lemma 14.25, item 1, \(T\) is continuous up to \(t = 0\), and \(T(x, 0) = h(x)\).
  7. The bar is a body with boundary \(\{0, L\}\), where the temperature \(0\) is prescribed. The solution has continuous derivatives on the open set \(\mathbb{R}\) that contains \([0, L]\) (step 4) and is continuous up to \(t = 0\) (step 6), so uniqueness is guaranteed by theorem 14.17, where the integral over the body becomes an integral over \([0, L]\).

Source: KREYSZIG section 12.5 (PDF p. 586-587) writes the series \(\sum B_{\mathrm{n}}\sin(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}^2 t}\) and says it is the solution for piecewise continuous \(f\) with one-sided derivatives, but postpones the proof to uniform convergence (PDF p. 587). The proof with the bound \(n^k\,\mathrm{e}^{-an^2} \le C/n^2\) and lemma 14.25 is not from the source.

The theorem differs for heat from that for the string. For the string (theorem 13.11) the initial shape had to be twice continuously differentiable with zero curvature at the ends for the sum to solve the equation. Here any piecewise continuous \(h\) will do, even one with a jump, and the solution is smooth for every \(t > 0\). The same computation for higher powers \(n^k\) gives higher derivatives too.

Figure 14.19 shows this on the triangle of figure 14.17. The coefficients are \(h_{\mathrm{n}} = 8H\sin(n\pi/2)/(\pi^2 n^2)\) (KREYSZIG has the same shape in example 3, PDF p. 588), which fall off as \(1/n^2\), so the kink at \(t = 0\) is the effect of all modes together.

The grey line is the bar of length \(L\) with its ends at zero. The blackwhite line with the kink is the initial temperature and its height is \(H = 1\). Already after \(\mathrm{Fo} = 0{,}001\) the kink is rounded, the peak has fallen to \(0{,}929\). With growing time the curve sinks and approaches the shape of the first mode, because the higher modes die out sooner: the triangle has only odd modes, and at \(\mathrm{Fo} = 0{,}2\) the ratio of the third mode to the first is \(\frac19\,\mathrm{e}^{-8\pi^2\cdot 0{,}2} = 1{,}5\cdot 10^{-8}\). The curvature in the middle at \(\mathrm{Fo} = 10^{-5}\), \(10^{-4}\), \(10^{-3}\) is \(-357\), \(-113\), \(-35{,}7\) (\(H/L^2\)) and its size is proportional to \(\mathrm{Fo}^{-1/2}\): it tends to \(-\infty\) as time tends to zero, which says that the initial shape has a kink, and it is finite at every \(t > 0\). The string would carry the kink along itself as a wave, heat smooths it at once.

Smoothness also tells where the limit is. A jump in the initial temperature is not a continuous initial temperature, so the solution at \(t = 0\) is not a continuous function at the point of the jump. Take \(T = 100\) on \(L/4 < x < 3L/4\) and \(T = 0\) elsewhere (figure 14.21, blackwhite step). The coefficients are \(h_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{200}{n\pi}\big(\cos\frac{n\pi}{4} - \cos\frac{3n\pi}{4}\big)\), that is \(90{,}03\), \(0\), \(-30{,}01\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3\). For \(\mathrm{Fo} = 10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-3}\) we get \(T(L/4, t) = 50{,}000\), the mean of the one-sided values \(0\) and \(100\) (SymPy and NumPy, num-05.py), and in the middle \(T(L/2, t) = 100{,}000\). The root of the mean square distance from the initial step is \(8{,}13\) K at \(\mathrm{Fo} = 10^{-4}\), \(14{,}46\) K at \(10^{-3}\) and \(25{,}71\) K at \(10^{-2}\): it tends to zero, but slowly, since near the jump \(T\) is far from the value \(0\) or \(100\) in a band that narrows only like \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Fo}}\). So the distance falls off like \(\mathrm{Fo}^{1/4}\): at a ten times shorter time it is \(10^{-1/4} = 0{,}562\) times as large. That the distance tends to zero for every piecewise continuous \(h\) would follow from the Parseval equality for piecewise continuous functions (the remainder of the sum \(\sum h_{\mathrm{n}}^2(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\dots})^2\)), which the book does not prove: lemma 13.12 has it only for continuous piecewise continuously differentiable functions. LEBL2 theorem 11.8.13 (PDF p. 204) proves the equality for every Riemann integrable function, we do not prove this point. The value \(50\) at the point of the jump is the same as the Fourier series gives at a point of a jump (theorem 9.94), but that \(T(L/4, t)\) has it as \(t \to 0\) we do not prove either, this is only a computation.

The series that was the subject of the dispute about the string (history in section 9.11) is thus less sensitive for heat: the exponential factor gives it the convergence that the string demands from the initial shape.

Example 14.27 Cooling of a copper bar (hlajenje bakrene palice)

A copper bar of length \(L = 80\) cm is insulated along its sides, its ends are held at \(0\) °C, the initial temperature is \(h(x) = 100\sin(\pi x/80)\) °C. The data for copper are \(\rho = 8{,}92\) g/cm³, \(c = 0{,}092\) cal/(g °C), \(K = 0{,}95\) cal/(cm s °C) (KREYSZIG section 12.5, PDF p. 587, where the conductivity is written \(K\)). When does the maximum temperature fall to \(50\) °C? Example 14.11 checked the balance of a piece for the same bar, with a given shape and decay rate. Here we derive the solution from the initial temperature.

  1. By definition 14.9, \(\kappa = K/(\rho c) = 0{,}95/(8{,}92\cdot 0{,}092) = 1{,}1576\) cm²/s.
  2. Sine coefficients: \(h = 100\sin(\pi x/L)\) is the first mode itself, so by the orthogonality of the sines (lemma 9.87) \(h_1 = 100\) and \(h_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) for \(n \ge 2\).
  3. By theorem 14.26, \(T(x, t) = 100\sin(\pi x/80)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\) with \(\lambda = \kappa\pi^2/L^2 = 1{,}1576\cdot\pi^2/6400 = 1{,}7852\cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/s.
  4. The maximum temperature is at \(x = 40\) cm: \(100\,\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\). It falls to \(50\) at \(t = \ln 2/\lambda = 388{,}3\) s, that is \(6{,}47\) min. It falls to \(1\) °C at \(t = \ln 100/\lambda = 2580\) s, that is \(43{,}0\) min, and to \(16{,}8\) °C at \(1000\) s.
  5. For the initial temperature \(100\sin(3\pi x/80)\) the first mode is replaced by the third, so \(\lambda_3 = 9\lambda = 0{,}016067\) 1/s and the half is reached at \(t = 388{,}3/9 = 43{,}1\) s. KREYSZIG (PDF p. 587) gives \(43\) s and \(9\) times faster.

Source: KREYSZIG section 12.5, examples 1 and 2 (PDF p. 587): the data for copper, the question, and the results \(388\) s (\(6{,}5\) min) for the first and \(43\) s for the second example. The more precise \(388{,}3\) s is computed with the same data (num-05.py).

On the left of the figure is the bar of length \(80\) cm, above it the blackwhite half-sine, the initial temperature, and in blue the curves at the times \(388\), \(1000\) and \(2580\) s: the shape does not change, the height falls as \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\). On the right, on axes of time \(t\) and maximum temperature \(T_{\max}\), is the maximum temperature of the first mode and the orange line of the third, which falls to half, \(50\) °C, \(9\) times faster. Why \(9\) times? The third mode has three half-waves on the same length, so at the same height it is \(3\) times steeper and \(9\) times more curved, and by the law of corollary 14.10 heat levels it out that many times faster. The same \(n^2\) we saw in figure 14.18. In the third mode the points \(x = 80/3\) and \(160/3\) cm are at zero, because \(\sin(3\pi x/80) = 0\): the temperature there stays \(0\) °C all the time, since \(T(x, t) = \sin(3\pi x/80)\,g(t)\) and the first factor is zero at these points.

The insulated bar is an idealization that the model assumes: a real copper bar would also lose heat through its lateral surface, and the time to half would be shorter than \(6{,}47\) min.

So far the ends had temperature zero. What if they are insulated?

Corollary 14.28 Bar with insulated ends (palica z izoliranima koncema)

Let \(L > 0\), \(\kappa > 0\), \(h\) a piecewise continuous function on \([0, L]\) with \(|h| \le M\) and \(a_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L h(x)\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\mathrm{d}x\) for \(n \ge 0\). Then for \(t > 0\) the series

\[T(x, t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{\mathrm{n}=1}^{\infty}a_{\mathrm{n}}\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\kappa n^2\pi^2 t/L^2} \tag{14.28}\]

converges, \(T\) solves equation (14.24) and satisfies \(T_{\mathrm{x}}(0, t) = T_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = 0\), and:

  1. \(\int_0^L T(x, t)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L h(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) for every \(t > 0\) (heat is conserved).
  2. \(|T(x, t) - a_0/2| \le 2M\,q/(1 - q)\) with \(q = \mathrm{e}^{-\kappa\pi^2 t/L^2}\), so \(T \to a_0/2 = \frac1L\int_0^L h\,\mathrm{d}x\), the mean of the initial temperature.
  3. If \(h\) is continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable, \(T\) is continuous up to \(t = 0\) and \(T(x, 0) = h(x)\), with no condition at the ends.
Proof

We must show that the same computation as in theorem 14.26 holds with cosines, that the derivative of the cosine vanishes at the ends, and that conservation follows from the equation and not only from the series.

  1. As in steps 1 to 4 of theorem 14.26, \(|a_{\mathrm{n}}| \le 2M\) and the terms \(a_{\mathrm{n}}\cos(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{\dots}\) and all their derivatives have bounds \(\mathrm{const}\cdot C/n^2\). By lemma 14.25, \(T\) is differentiable term by term, \(T_{\mathrm{x}} = -\sum a_{\mathrm{n}}(n\pi/L)\sin(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{\dots}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = -\kappa\sum a_{\mathrm{n}}(n\pi/L)^2\cos(\cdot)\,\mathrm{e}^{\dots} = \kappa T_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  2. At \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) we have \(\sin 0 = \sin n\pi = 0\) (lemma 8.10, item 2), so \(T_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) at both ends.
  3. Conservation from the equation: by the lemma on the derivative of an integral with respect to a parameter (4.19) and the fundamental theorem of calculus (3.40, item 1), \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_0^L T\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \kappa\int_0^L T_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \kappa\,[T_{\mathrm{x}}]_0^L = 0\), so for \(t > 0\) the integral does not change with time. The series gives its value: \(\int_0^L\cos(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for \(n \ge 1\), and since the series converges uniformly, by the estimate of the integral (lemma 9.31) \(|\int_0^L(T - S_{\mathrm{N}})\,\mathrm{d}x| \le L\,R_{\mathrm{N}} \to 0\), so \(\int_0^L T\,\mathrm{d}x = (a_0/2)\,L = \int_0^L h\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  4. For \(n \ge 1\) we have \(n^2 \ge n\), so \(|T - a_0/2| \le \sum 2M\,\mathrm{e}^{-n^2\kappa\pi^2 t/L^2} \le 2M\sum_{\mathrm{n} \ge 1}q^n = 2M\,q/(1 - q)\) (lemma 9.83, item 2).
  5. For item 3 take the even extension \(h_{\mathrm{e}}(x) = h(|x|)\) on \([-L, L]\) with period \(2L\). It is continuous at \(0\) (the value \(h(0)\) from both sides) and at \(\pm L\) (the value \(h(L)\) from both sides) and piecewise continuously differentiable, with no condition \(h(0) = h(L) = 0\).
