In this section \(\vek q\) is the heat flux vector, not the distributed load of chapter 5, \(k\) is the thermal conductivity, not the shear factor, and the coefficient \(\kappa\) of the U piece in chapter 4 is now written as the product \(\alpha\,g\), because in this chapter \(\kappa\) is the thermal diffusivity, which this section does not need.

14.8.1 When a heated body stays free of stress

We state the theorem for two cases. The first is a body in which the temperature is a linear function of all three coordinates, like the U piece. The second is a long prism with cross-section \(R\) in which the temperature is a function of \(x\) and \(y\) only and has a vanishing Laplace operator (definition 11.5), \(\nabla^2 T = T_{\mathrm{xx}} + T_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\). With constant conductivity and no source this is exactly the steady equation by theorem 14.8: from \(\rho c\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = k\,\nabla^2 T + Q\) with \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) and \(Q = 0\) we get \(\nabla^2 T = 0\). For the prism we also need a model, which we call plane strain with temperature: the displacement along the axis \(z\) is zero, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) (definition 11.30). This is an idealization, and we name it: neighbouring cross-sections cannot shift relative to one another because a rigid wall holds them. A real wall is not rigid, and what happens near an end we do not estimate here. What happens when the cross-section is not simply connected is shown by lemma 14.45.

Why is a vanishing Laplace operator enough? Hooke's law with temperature says that at zero stress every piece of material has the strain \(\alpha\,T\) in all directions (theorem 3.15). The field \(\alpha\,T\,\mat I\) is a strain only if it satisfies the compatibility equations (theorem 1.127). The first equation, in the plane \(x\), \(y\), says \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx},\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy},\mathrm{xx}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{xy}}\), which for \(\alpha\,T\,\mat I\) means \(\alpha\,(T_{\mathrm{yy}} + T_{\mathrm{xx}}) = 0\). This is the Laplace condition. In the prism the rigid wall prevents the stretch along \(z\) and supplies the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -E\,\alpha\,T\). The strain is therefore \((1 + \nu)\,\alpha\,T\) in the plane and zero along \(z\) (step 2 of the proof below). For it the same first equation holds with \((1 + \nu)\,\alpha\) in place of \(\alpha\), and the others hold because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), there are no shear strains and nothing depends on \(z\). For the full three-dimensional field \(\alpha\,T\,\mat I\), however, the second equation gives \(\alpha\,(T_{\mathrm{yy}} + T_{\mathrm{zz}}) = 0\) and the third \(\alpha\,(T_{\mathrm{zz}} + T_{\mathrm{xx}}) = 0\), and together with them all six equations require all second derivatives of \(T\) to vanish, that is \(T\) must be linear. That is why the theorem has a linear temperature in the first case and a plane one in the second.

Theorem 14.43 Steady temperature without stress (stacionarna temperatura brez napetosti)

Let the body be isotropic, homogeneous and linearly elastic with \(E > 0\), \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\) (theorem 3.48) and a temperature expansion coefficient \(\alpha\) independent of temperature. Let \(T\) be the change of temperature from the temperature at which the body is free of stress. There is no body force and the surface of the body is free, in case 2 below only the lateral surface (no force acts on it). A solution of the thermoelastic problem is a displacement field \(\vek u\), continuously differentiable with continuous second derivatives, whose stresses by equation (3.17) satisfy the equilibrium equations and the given boundary conditions. Then:

  1. If the body is simply connected (definition 1.136) and \(T\) is a linear function of \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), all stresses are zero in every solution, and the solution is unique up to a small rigid motion.
  2. If the body is a prism \(R \times (-l, l)\) with simply connected cross-section \(R\), \(T = T(x, y)\) has a vanishing Laplace operator, there is no body force, no force on the lateral surface, and the force \(\mp E\,\alpha\,T\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) on the ends \(z = \pm l\) (which a rigid wall holding \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) supplies), then in every solution \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -E\,\alpha\,T\), and the solution is unique up to a small rigid motion.

In both cases the strains have this form: in the first \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \alpha\,T\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), in the second \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \hat\alpha\,T\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) and all shear strains zero, where \(\hat\alpha = (1 + \nu)\,\alpha\).

Proof

We must show that the stresses of the theorem, together with the strains they give by Hooke's law, belong to a displacement field that satisfies all conditions, and that this is the only solution. The route is: stresses, strains, compatibility, displacement, uniqueness.

1. Stresses and strains.

  1. Case 1: all stresses are zero. By equation (3.16), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \alpha\,T\) and the shear strains are zero.
  2. Case 2: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -E\,\alpha\,T\). By equation (3.16), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac1E\,(0 - \nu\,(0 - E\,\alpha\,T)) + \alpha\,T = (1 + \nu)\,\alpha\,T\), the same for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \tfrac1E\,(-E\,\alpha\,T) + \alpha\,T = 0\).

2. Compatibility.

  1. Case 1: all second derivatives of the strains \(\alpha\,T\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are zero, because second derivatives of a linear function are zero, so all six equations (1.68) hold as \(0 = 0\).
  2. Case 2: equations 2 to 6 hold, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), all shear strains are zero and nothing depends on \(z\) (every term contains a derivative in \(z\) or a component that is zero). Equation 1 is \(\hat\alpha\,(T_{\mathrm{yy}} + T_{\mathrm{xx}}) - 0 = \hat\alpha\,\nabla^2 T = 0\).

3. Displacement.

  1. The set \(D\) is the interior of the body in case 1, and the prism \(R \times (-l, l)\) in case 2. In case 2 it is simply connected: for a closed curve \((\gamma(s), z(s))\) in \(D\) we shrink the first part in \(R\) by a shrinking to a point (because \(R\) is simply connected) and the second part by \((1 - t)\,z(s)\), and all intermediate stages stay in \(D\).
  2. By theorem 4.119 there is a displacement field \(\vek u\), continuously differentiable with continuous second derivatives, whose strains are those of step 1.
  3. By theorem 3.15, equations (3.16) and (3.17) are inverse to one another, so the same strains give the same stresses. For the strains of step 1 these are the stresses of the theorem. In case 1 this is also the computation \(\ten\sigma = \lambda\,\tr(\ten\varepsilon - \alpha\,T\,\mat I)\,\mat I + 2\mu\,(\ten\varepsilon - \alpha\,T\,\mat I) = \mat 0\) from \(\ten\varepsilon = \alpha\,T\,\mat I\).

4. Equilibrium and boundary conditions.

  1. In case 1 the stresses are zero, so the equilibrium equation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{j}} = 0\) holds. In case 2 the only nonzero component is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -E\,\alpha\,T(x, y)\) and the equilibrium \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}/\partial z = 0\) holds, because \(T\) does not depend on \(z\).
  2. On the lateral surface the normal \(\vek n\) has only \(x\) and \(y\) components. By Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24), \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \vek 0\), since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\) are zero. At the end \(z = l\) the normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = -E\,\alpha\,T\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), at the end \(z = -l\) it is \(\ten\sigma\,(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = +E\,\alpha\,T\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). This is the force of the theorem.

5. Uniqueness.

  1. Let \(\tilde{\vek u}\) be another solution. By equation (3.17) the difference of the stresses is \(\lambda\,\tr(\ten\varepsilon - \tilde{\ten\varepsilon})\,\mat I + 2\mu\,(\ten\varepsilon - \tilde{\ten\varepsilon})\), in which \(T\) cancels. This is the stress of the field \(\vek u - \tilde{\vek u}\) by the ordinary Hooke's law, and it is in equilibrium with no forces on the surface. By theorem 11.4, item 2, the difference has zero stress and strain, so \(\vek u\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}\) have the same stresses and differ by a small rigid motion.

Source: BARBER §14.3 (PDF p. 236): a steady temperature field without a source causes no stress in a free, simply connected plane plate. SADD §12.5 (PDF p. 386): the same for the plane problem, and for multiply connected bodies a steady temperature field normally gives rise to in-plane stresses. The proof by compatibility, theorem 4.119 and uniqueness is not from the sources. BARBER gives only the plane problem. We split it into two cases, because the first holds in three dimensions and the second only with a rigid wall at the ends.

The proof showed three things. First, the reason is not in the physics of heat but in the geometry of strain: the strain that temperature gives the material without in-plane stress must satisfy the compatibility equations. In the plane of a prism exactly a temperature with a vanishing Laplace operator satisfies them, that is every steady one without a source, while in three dimensions only a linear one does. Second, simple connectedness of the body makes compatibility sufficient (theorem 4.119). Third, the uniqueness of chapter 11 says there is no other solution. In case 1 there is therefore no stress, however we look for it. In case 2 there is no stress in the plane of the cross-section, and the axial stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -E\,\alpha\,T\) is carried by the rigid wall.

Let us test the theorem on the U piece. The temperature \(T = g\,y\) is linear, so case 1 applies, and the piece is free of stress. Its strain \(\alpha\,g\,y\,\mat I\) is the same as in chapter 4, and the displacement of the point \(B\) relative to \(A\) computed there, \(\vek u(B) = (0{,}0105,\ -0{,}0030,\ 0)\) mm, is now the displacement of the free heated piece. The piece bends (after heating) so that the arms move apart and the foot arches upward. In the figure the displacement is magnified 400 times: the tops of the arms \(A\) and \(B\) move apart by \(0{,}0105\) mm, which at this magnification is \(4{,}2\) mm, and the middle of the foot rises relative to its ends. The grey outline shows the state before heating, and the points \(A\) and \(B\) are joined by a dashed line. The piece deforms and there is no stress. The everyday impression that a piece with an uneven temperature must be under stress is therefore wrong: stress does not depend on the temperature being uneven but on whether the stretch \(\alpha\,T\) is compatible.

The theorem has one condition that we must test with an example where it fails. What happens when the temperature is not steady? Take the beam of chapter 5 and raise its top face by 20 K at once and hold it. The temperature along the height is then not linear (\(T_{\mathrm{t}} \ne 0\), hence also \(\nabla^2 T = T_{\mathrm{yy}} \ne 0\)), and the stress at the top face is \(-53{,}04\) MPa at \(\mathrm{Fo} = \kappa t/h^2 = 0{,}0005\) (section 14.7, the example of the heated beam). Only after a long time, when the temperature along the height evens out into a linear field, does just the curvature of chapter 5 remain. The theorem therefore holds for the steady state and not for the way to it. A source in the body (\(Q \ne 0\)) or dependence on \(z\) in a thin plate also break it: in a plate with free faces \(z = \pm h\) a \(T(x, y)\) with nonzero \(T_{\mathrm{yy}}\) does not fit the second compatibility equation of the full three-dimensional strain, so plane stress (definition 11.32) is a model for a thin plate and not a solution (chapter 11). Such a model keeps the condition \(\nabla^2 T = 0\) for the plane and the in-plane stresses are zero (BARBER, §14.3, PDF p. 236), but we do not prove more precise statements here.

14.8.2 Edge curvature and heat flux (Dundurs' theorem)

The U piece bent. Can the bending be predicted from the heat flux, without computing displacements? In the piece the foot is cold and the arms warm. Does the curvature depend on the heat that flows through the edge? This is the content of the next corollary. It carries Dundurs' name because he was the first to prove it (BARBER, §14.3.1, PDF p. 237), so the name is the author's and not the subject's.

Corollary 14.44 Dundurs' theorem on edge curvature (Dundursov izrek o ukrivljenosti roba)

Let case 1 or case 2 of theorem 14.43 hold, let \(\hat\alpha\) be as in the theorem (equal to \(\alpha\) in case 1) and \(k\) the thermal conductivity (definition 14.3). Then at every point of the body the second derivative of the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) in \(x\), at fixed \(y\) and \(z\), is

\[\frac{\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x^2} = -\hat\alpha\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial y} = \frac{\hat\alpha}{k}\,q_{\mathrm{y}} , \tag{14.39}\]

where \(q_{\mathrm{y}}\) is the component of the heat flux in the direction \(y\).

Proof

We must show that the strains of theorem 14.43 give equation (14.39).

  1. By theorem 14.43, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), so \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = 0\) (definition 1.115). We differentiate in \(x\): \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x^2 = -\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\,\partial y\), where the order of differentiation can be exchanged because the second derivatives are continuous (theorem 1.125).
  2. By the theorem, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \hat\alpha\,T\). The derivative of this equality in \(y\) gives \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\,\partial y = \hat\alpha\,T_{\mathrm{y}}\). From step 1 follows the first equality in (14.39).
  3. By Fourier's law \(q_{\mathrm{y}} = -k\,T_{\mathrm{y}}\) (definition 14.3), so \(-\hat\alpha\,T_{\mathrm{y}} = \hat\alpha\,q_{\mathrm{y}}/k\).

Source: BARBER §14.3.1 (14.20), (14.21) (PDF p. 237) states the result under the name Dundurs' theorem and \(\delta = \alpha\,(1 + \nu)/k\) for the thermal distortivity. The proof is ours, since the book does not show it.

The derivative \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x^2\) is, to first order, the curvature of a line that was parallel to the axis \(x\) before heating (for small slopes the curvature is the second derivative, as for the beam in chapter 5). The corollary therefore says: an edge through which heat flows in the direction \(+y\) gets the curvature \(\hat\alpha\,q_{\mathrm{y}}/k\), and an edge without flux stays straight. On the U piece \(T_{\mathrm{y}} = g = 1\) K/mm and \(\alpha = 15 \cdot 10^{-6}\) 1/K, so \(\partial^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x^2 = -\alpha\,g = -1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-5}\) 1/mm, the radius of curvature is \(66{,}7\) m, and the middle of a segment of length 20 mm rises above the chord through its ends by \(\alpha g \cdot 20^2/8 = 7{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\) mm. A negative second derivative means that the edge arches upward, like the foot of the piece in the figure. In chapter 4 the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(B) = -0{,}0030\) mm includes the rotation of the piece as a whole, so it is not directly comparable with this number. The beam of chapter 5 has the same relation \(\alpha g\): at \(g = 500\) K/m its curvature is \(v'' = -\alpha g = -7{,}5 \cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/m (section 5.5.4). There we obtained it from the stretch of the fibres, now it is expressed by the heat flux \(k\,g\) through the beam.

Dundurs' theorem is therefore useful as a signpost: the curvature of an edge follows from the heat flux through the edge, without computing displacements. Where does it fail? Equation (14.39) is written for the field that theorem 14.43 allows. The next section shows what happens when the cross-section has a hole.

14.8.3 A ring with a hole: the jump of displacement at a cut

Now we remove what the theorem requires. Take the ring of chapters 4 and 11, radii \(a = 40\) mm and \(b = 60\) mm, with the inner wall 100 K warmer than the outer, no force on the surfaces. The ring is exactly the body that by corollary 4.113 is not simply connected. Heat flows outward through the wall, as the arrows \(\vek q\) show, and the isotherms are circles. From the Laplace operator in polar coordinates (corollary 11.18) it follows that the field \(T(r) = A + B\,\ln r\) is steady and without a source, since \(T'' + T'/r = -B/r^2 + B/r^2 = 0\). With our boundary condition \(T = 100\,\ln(b/r)/\ln(b/a)\), so \(B = -100/\ln 1{,}5 = -246{,}63\) K, and \(T = 100\) K at \(r = 40\) mm, \(70{,}95\) K at \(45\) mm, \(44{,}97\) K at \(50\) mm, \(21{,}46\) K at \(55\) mm and \(0\) at \(60\) mm. The flux through every circle per unit thickness is the same, \(2\pi\,k\,|B| = k \cdot 1549{,}6\) K, because \(q_{\mathrm{r}} = -k\,B/r\) and the circumference is \(2\pi\,r\).

Is the ring free of stress nevertheless? Theorem 14.43 does not say, because the ring is not simply connected. Let us see what would happen if it were free of stress, and make the cut that turns the ring into a simply connected body.

Lemma 14.45 A ring with a logarithmic temperature field (obroč z logaritemskim temperaturnim poljem)

Let the ring \(a \le r \le b\), \(|z| < c\) be as in lemma 1.131, with the material of theorem 14.43, and \(T = A + B\,\ln r\) with \(B \ne 0\). Let \(\hat\alpha = (1 + \nu)\,\alpha\) and \(S\) the cut, the set of points of the ring with \(y = 0\) and \(x > 0\). Then:

  1. the displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = \hat\alpha\,r\,(T - B)\), \(u_\theta = \hat\alpha\,B\,r\,\theta\) for \(0 < \theta < 2\pi\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) has on the cut ring the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = \hat\alpha\,T\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) and all shear strains zero, which are the strains of theorem 14.43, case 2,
  2. the jump of the displacement across the cut is \(\vek u^+ - \vek u^- = -2\pi\,\hat\alpha\,B\,r_{\mathrm{C}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) at a point of the cut at distance \(r_{\mathrm{C}}\) from the axis, so it is different from zero, and its size grows linearly with the radius,
  3. on the whole ring there is no displacement field with these strains, and therefore no solution of the thermoelastic problem on the ring with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) has zero stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).
Proof

We must show that the field of item 1 gives the stated strains, then compute the jump and use lemma 4.120.

  1. Strains in cylindrical coordinates (corollary 11.21): \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r = \hat\alpha\,(T - B) + \hat\alpha\,r\,T' = \hat\alpha\,(T - B) + \hat\alpha\,B = \hat\alpha\,T\), because \(r\,T' = B\). Further \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = u_{\mathrm{r}}/r + (1/r)\,\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta = \hat\alpha\,(T - B) + \hat\alpha\,B = \hat\alpha\,T\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_\theta/\partial r - u_\theta/r + (1/r)\,\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial\theta) = \tfrac12\,(\hat\alpha\,B\,\theta - \hat\alpha\,B\,\theta + 0) = 0\). The remaining three components are zero, since \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) and nothing depends on \(z\). This is item 1.
  2. At a point of the cut \(C = (r_{\mathrm{C}}, 0)\), \(\theta \to 0\) for neighbours above the cut and \(\theta \to 2\pi\) for neighbours below it. The displacement above the cut has \(u_\theta = 0\), below it \(u_\theta = 2\pi\,\hat\alpha\,B\,r_{\mathrm{C}}\), and \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the same on both sides. Since \(\vek e_\theta = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) at \(\theta = 0\) and \(\theta = 2\pi\), \(\vek u^+ - \vek u^- = (0 - 2\pi\,\hat\alpha\,B\,r_{\mathrm{C}})\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). This equals \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{C}}\) of lemma 4.120 with \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(W_{\mathrm{yx}} = -2\pi\,\hat\alpha\,B \ne 0\).
  3. Lemma 4.120 needs strains with continuous first and second derivatives that satisfy the compatibility equations at every point of the whole ring. The strains of item 1 are \(\hat\alpha\,(A + B\,\ln r)\) or zero, at \(r \ge a > 0\) they have continuous derivatives of all orders, and they are the strains of case 2 of theorem 14.43 with \(T = A + B\,\ln r\), which has a vanishing Laplace operator (corollary 11.18). By step 4 of the proof of the theorem they therefore satisfy all six compatibility equations at every point of the ring, on the cut too, since that computation does not need simple connectedness. By lemma 4.120, item 3, a displacement field on the whole ring with strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) exists exactly when \(\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W = \mat 0\). Here \(\mat W \ne \mat 0\), so there is no such field. A solution with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) would by Hooke's law with temperature have the strains of item 1 (step 2 of the proof of theorem 14.43), hence a displacement field on the whole ring.

Source: BARBER §14.3 (PDF p. 236) and SADD §12.5 (PDF p. 386) state that for multiply connected bodies stresses arise, and BARBER connects them with a dislocation in the hole. The derivation with the displacement of item 1 and the jump from lemma 4.120 are ours.

Let us see what the jump says. The cut is drawn in the ring in orange, and the thin grey circle shows the ring before heating. If we cut the ring while rigid walls hold its faces \(z = \pm c\) (\(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) as in the prism), the faces of the cut turn relative to one another by the angle \(2\pi\,\hat\alpha\,|B| = 0{,}03022\) rad (\(1{,}73°\)). The gap at the radius \(r\) is therefore \(2\pi\,\hat\alpha\,|B|\,r\), at the radius 50 mm \(1{,}511\) mm. This is with \(\hat\alpha = (1 + \nu)\,\alpha\). For a free thin ring (plane stress) the in-plane stretch would be \(\alpha\,T\) and we would get \(0{,}02324\) rad and \(1{,}162\) mm. The factor \(1 + \nu = 1{,}3\) between the numbers comes from the axial strain: in the prism with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) the opposing \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) raises the in-plane strain from \(\alpha\,T\) to \((1 + \nu)\,\alpha\,T\), in a plate with free faces there is no such stress. In the figure the gap is drawn magnified 12 times, the shape of the rest of the ring is not to scale, and only the angle between the faces is computed.

Why, then, can the whole ring not be free of stress? Whoever wanted it free of stress would have to hold the faces of the cut together, and that needs a force. The ring therefore gets stresses from a steady heat flow through the wall, even if no force acts from outside. Theorem 14.43 was not broken, but its assumption of simple connectedness is essential. The link with the flux is that \(2\pi\,B\) is exactly the flux through a closed curve around the hole divided by \(-k\): in a simply connected body this flux is zero by the divergence theorem (theorem 4.14, theorem 14.8, \(\nabla^2 T = 0\)), around a hole it is not, because heat enters through the inner wall and leaves through the outer. For a hole through which no flux flows \(B = 0\) and there would be no stress. So much for the reason. How large the stresses are we compute in the next section.

14.8.4 A tube with a steady radial temperature

We know the temperature of the tube. The question is what stresses it causes. The tube of chapter 11, \(a = 40\) mm, \(b = 60\) mm, was loaded there with oil at 30 MPa, which gave a hoop stress of 78 MPa at the inner wall. Now the tube has no pressure and its inner wall is warmer than the outer. We shall compare the stress we get with the stress from the oil, and, more interesting, add them.

From history

The thermal stresses in a cylinder and a sphere, where the temperature is a function only of the distance from the axis or the centre, were investigated by Duhamel and Neumann, whom chapter 3 already met. Timoshenko writes that C. W. Borchardt, among Neumann's pupils, contributed to the theory of thermal stresses: for both cases he gave solutions in the form of integrals for any temperature distribution (TIMO, PDF p. 286). This is the reason why for the tube we are interested in a general \(T(r)\) and not in one special case: the solution we shall write down contains an integral of the temperature over the radius, so it has that form.

So take a general temperature \(T(r)\) and write the solution as an integral. Let \(J(r) = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^r s\,T(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) (here \(s\) is the auxiliary variable of the integral), \(\zeta = \alpha\,(1 + \nu)/(1 - \nu)\) and \(\Gamma = E\,\alpha/(1 - \nu)\). Then \(J' = r\,T\) by the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40), because \(T\) is continuous.

Theorem 14.46 A tube with a steady radial temperature (cev s stacionarno radialno temperaturo)

Let the body be the tube \(a \le r \le b\), \(-l \le z \le l\) as in theorem 11.27, with a material that has \(E\), \(\nu\) and \(\alpha\) independent of temperature, no body force and no pressure on either lateral surface. The temperature \(T = T(r)\) is a continuously differentiable function on \([a, b]\) (change from the stress-free temperature). Let \(\varepsilon_0\) be a constant axial strain. Let

\[A_{\mathrm{T}} = \frac{\Gamma\,J(b)}{b^2 - a^2} , \qquad B_{\mathrm{T}} = A_{\mathrm{T}}\,a^2 . \tag{14.40}\]

Then:

  1. the displacement field
    \[\vek u = \Big(\zeta\,\frac{J(r)}{r} + \Big(\frac{(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)\,A_{\mathrm{T}}}{E} - \nu\,\varepsilon_0\Big)\,r + \frac{(1 + \nu)\,B_{\mathrm{T}}}{E}\,\frac1r\Big)\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} + \varepsilon_0\,z\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} \tag{14.41}\]
    is a solution of the thermoelastic problem, with stresses in local axes
    \[\begin{aligned} &\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A_{\mathrm{T}} - \frac{B_{\mathrm{T}}}{r^2} - \Gamma\,\frac{J(r)}{r^2} , \\ &\sigma_{\theta\theta} = A_{\mathrm{T}} + \frac{B_{\mathrm{T}}}{r^2} + \Gamma\,\Big(\frac{J(r)}{r^2} - T(r)\Big) , \\ &\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 2\nu\,A_{\mathrm{T}} + E\,\varepsilon_0 - \Gamma\,T(r) , \\ &\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rz}} = \sigma_{\theta \mathrm{z}} = 0 , \end{aligned} \tag{14.42}\]
    and the force on the ends \(z = \pm l\) is \(\pm\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\),
  2. the radial and hoop stresses are independent of \(\varepsilon_0\), and every solution of this problem has the same stresses and strains and differs by a small rigid motion,
  3. at \(\varepsilon_0 = 0\) (the ends held by a rigid wall) this is plane strain, and at \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\,(1 - \nu)\,A_{\mathrm{T}}/E\) the resultant axial force is zero, \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,2\pi\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = 0\), and on both lateral surfaces \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\theta\theta}\).
Proof

We must show that the field (14.41) satisfies the three requirements of a solution (definition 11.1, with Hooke's law with temperature), and then use uniqueness. The route is that of theorem 11.27: strains, stresses, equilibrium, boundary conditions. We use the constants \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) (definition 3.10) and \(\beta = (3\lambda + 2\mu)\,\alpha = E\,\alpha/(1 - 2\nu)\).

1. Strains and stresses.

  1. The field (14.41) is \(u = \zeta\,J/r + C_1\,r + C_2/r\) with \(C_1 = (1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)\,A_{\mathrm{T}}/E - \nu\,\varepsilon_0\) and \(C_2 = (1 + \nu)\,B_{\mathrm{T}}/E\). By corollary 11.21, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = u' = \zeta\,(T - J/r^2) + C_1 - C_2/r^2\) (since \(J' = rT\)), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = u/r = \zeta\,J/r^2 + C_1 + C_2/r^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_0\) and the remaining three components are zero as in step 1 of the proof of theorem 11.27.
  2. Hooke's law with temperature, equation (3.17), gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = (\lambda + 2\mu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} + \lambda\,(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}) - \beta\,T\) and similarly for \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The terms with \(T\) in \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) are \((\lambda + 2\mu)\,\zeta\,T - \beta\,T = 0\), because \(\zeta = \beta/(\lambda + 2\mu)\), which we check from \(\lambda + 2\mu = E\,(1 - \nu)/((1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu))\). The terms with \(J/r^2\) are \(-(\lambda + 2\mu)\,\zeta\,J/r^2 + \lambda\,\zeta\,J/r^2 = -2\mu\,\zeta\,J/r^2\), and since \(2\mu\,\zeta = E\,\alpha/(1 - \nu) = \Gamma\) we get \(-\Gamma\,J/r^2\). The remaining terms make up \(A_{\mathrm{T}} - B_{\mathrm{T}}/r^2\) with \(A_{\mathrm{T}} = 2(\lambda + \mu)\,C_1 + \lambda\,\varepsilon_0\) and \(B_{\mathrm{T}} = 2\mu\,C_2\) (SymPy, as in step 9 of the proof of theorem 11.27). So \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is the one of (14.42).
  3. Likewise: the terms with \(T\) in \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) are \(\lambda\,\zeta\,T - \beta\,T = (\lambda - \lambda - 2\mu)\,\zeta\,T = -\Gamma\,T\), the terms with \(J/r^2\) are \(-\lambda\,\zeta\,J/r^2 + (\lambda + 2\mu)\,\zeta\,J/r^2 = \Gamma\,J/r^2\), and the rest is \(A_{\mathrm{T}} + B_{\mathrm{T}}/r^2\). In \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) the terms with \(T\) are \(\lambda\,\zeta\,T - \beta\,T = -\Gamma\,T\), the rest \(2\lambda\,C_1 + (\lambda + 2\mu)\,\varepsilon_0\) is constant and equals \(2\nu\,A_{\mathrm{T}} + E\,\varepsilon_0\) (from \(\lambda/(\lambda + \mu) = 2\nu\) and \(\mu\,(3\lambda + 2\mu)/(\lambda + \mu) = E\), as in step 6 of the proof of theorem 11.27). The shear stresses are \(2\mu\) times zero shear strains.

2. Equilibrium and boundary conditions.

  1. The radial equilibrium equation (corollary 11.24, \(\vek b = \vek 0\)) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' + (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r = 0\). The derivative from (14.42) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' = 2B_{\mathrm{T}}/r^3 - \Gamma\,T/r + 2\Gamma\,J/r^3\) (since \(J' = rT\)), and the difference is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta} = -2B_{\mathrm{T}}/r^2 - 2\Gamma\,J/r^2 + \Gamma\,T\). The sum \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' + (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r\) is \(2B_{\mathrm{T}}/r^3 - \Gamma\,T/r + 2\Gamma\,J/r^3 - 2B_{\mathrm{T}}/r^3 - 2\Gamma\,J/r^3 + \Gamma\,T/r = 0\). The second and third equilibrium equations are as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 11.27, because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) does not depend on \(z\).
  2. The lateral surfaces are free. At \(r = a\), \(J = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a) = A_{\mathrm{T}} - B_{\mathrm{T}}/a^2 = A_{\mathrm{T}} - A_{\mathrm{T}} = 0\). At \(r = b\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(b) = A_{\mathrm{T}} - A_{\mathrm{T}}\,a^2/b^2 - \Gamma\,J(b)/b^2 = A_{\mathrm{T}}\,(b^2 - a^2)/b^2 - \Gamma\,J(b)/b^2 = 0\) by the definition of \(A_{\mathrm{T}}\). Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24) gives zero force on both lateral surfaces, because the shear stresses are zero.
  3. At the ends, by Cauchy's formula the force is \(\pm\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The field is thus a solution of the problem in which the force at the ends is this one.

3. Uniqueness and the axial condition.

  1. The difference of two solutions has by equation (3.17) the stress of the ordinary Hooke's law and is in equilibrium with no forces on the surface (as in step 10 of the proof of theorem 14.43). By theorem 11.4, item 2, they have the same stresses and strains. Steps 2 and 3 show that \(\varepsilon_0\) does not enter \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) (the constants \(A_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(B_{\mathrm{T}}\) do not contain it). This is item 2.
  2. The integral of the axial stress: \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b (2\nu A_{\mathrm{T}} + E\,\varepsilon_0 - \Gamma\,T)\,2\pi\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = \pi\,(b^2 - a^2)\,(2\nu A_{\mathrm{T}} + E\,\varepsilon_0) - 2\pi\,\Gamma\,J(b)\). With \(\Gamma\,J(b) = A_{\mathrm{T}}\,(b^2 - a^2)\) this is \(\pi\,(b^2 - a^2)\,(2\nu A_{\mathrm{T}} + E\,\varepsilon_0 - 2A_{\mathrm{T}})\), which is zero at \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\,(1 - \nu)\,A_{\mathrm{T}}/E\). At this value \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 2A_{\mathrm{T}} - \Gamma\,T\). At \(r = a\), by (14.42) (\(J = 0\), \(B_{\mathrm{T}} = A_{\mathrm{T}}\,a^2\)) \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a) = 2A_{\mathrm{T}} - \Gamma\,T(a)\), and at \(r = b\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(b) = A_{\mathrm{T}}\,(1 + a^2/b^2) + \Gamma\,J(b)/b^2 - \Gamma\,T(b) = 2A_{\mathrm{T}} - \Gamma\,T(b)\), because \(\Gamma\,J(b)/b^2 = A_{\mathrm{T}}\,(1 - a^2/b^2)\). This is item 3.

Source: SADD §12.7 (PDF pp. 388-392) for a thin ring (plane stress), equations (12.7.8) to (12.7.14), and example 12.2 (PDF p. 391) for comparing a number. TIMO (PDF p. 286) for the history. The proof by guessing the field and checking is ours, after the model of theorem 11.27. SymPy checked the equations of steps 2 to 4 and the equilibrium.

The proof showed that the solution for any radial temperature has the same two "Lamé" terms as for pressure, \(A_{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(B_{\mathrm{T}}\), plus an additional term with the integral of the temperature. Let us test it on a constant temperature: \(T = T_0\) gives \(J = T_0\,(r^2 - a^2)/2\), \(A_{\mathrm{T}} = \Gamma\,T_0/2\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) of (14.42) are zero (\(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \tfrac{\Gamma T_0}{2}\,(1 - a^2/r^2 - (r^2 - a^2)/r^2) = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \tfrac{\Gamma T_0}{2}\,(1 + a^2/r^2 + (r^2 - a^2)/r^2 - 2) = 0\)), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is zero at \(\varepsilon_0 = \alpha\,T_0\), the free thermal strain. That is again theorem 14.43, case 1, since \(T_0\) is a linear function. For the stresses that the solution gives at the actual data, the temperature falls from \(100\) K at the inner wall to \(0\) at the outer.

Now we insert the logarithmic temperature of the previous section. From the computation (SymPy, num-08.py): \(J(b) = 43\,315\) K mm², for the steel of chapter 3 (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(\alpha = 15 \cdot 10^{-6}\) 1/K) \(\Gamma = E\,\alpha/(1 - \nu) = 4{,}2\) MPa/K and \(A_{\mathrm{T}} = 90{,}96\) MPa. The stresses are in the table. The tube here is open (\(\varepsilon_0 = 2(1 - \nu)\,A_{\mathrm{T}}/E = 6{,}497 \cdot 10^{-4}\)): the resultant axial force at the ends is zero, but the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) at the ends is not, since it goes from \(-238{,}08\) to \(181{,}92\) MPa. The difference from a free end with no force at all is a self-equilibrated load, so this solution describes a free end only far from the end, by Saint-Venant's principle (section 11.11).

\(r\) (mm) \(T\) (K) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) (MPa) \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) (MPa) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) (MPa)
40 100.00 0.00 \(-238{,}08\) \(-238{,}08\)
45 70.95 \(-18{,}33\) \(-97{,}74\) \(-116{,}07\)
50 44.97 \(-20{,}51\) 13.58 \(-6{,}93\)
55 21.46 \(-13{,}13\) 104.92 91.79
60 0.00 0.00 181.92 181.92

The axes of the figure show radius and stress, the hoop stress goes from \(-238\) MPa at the hot inner wall to \(+182\) MPa at the cold outer wall, the radial is compressive everywhere and does not exceed \(-21{,}1\) MPa, and the axial behaves like the hoop stress. Why is the hoop stress compressive at the hot wall? If the inner wall were free it would expand more than the cooler outer wall, but the outer ring holds it, so it squeezes it. The outer wall is stretched for exactly the opposite reason. In plane strain (\(\varepsilon_0 = 0\)) the hoop and radial stresses are the same as for open ends (item 2 of the theorem), and the axial stress is \(-365{,}42\) MPa at the inner and \(54{,}58\) MPa at the outer wall. For a thin plate (plane stress, \(\Gamma\) replaced by \(E\,\alpha\)) the hoop stress is \(-166{,}65\) MPa at \(r = 40\) mm and \(127{,}35\) MPa at 60 mm, which is a factor \(1 - \nu = 0{,}7\) less than in plane strain, because the expressions contain \(E\,\alpha\) instead of \(\Gamma = E\,\alpha/(1 - \nu)\). Comparison with the source: SADD example 12.2 (PDF p. 391), a plate with \(b/a = 3\), \(E = 200\) GPa, \(\alpha = 13 \cdot 10^{-6}\) 1/K and \(100\) K, gives \(-174{,}17\) MPa by the same procedure, and the source writes "about 174 MPa".

The solution can be compared with the oil of chapter 11. The thermoelastic law is linear and the solution is unique, so the stress with pressure and temperature together is the sum of the stresses of the two separate problems. With open ends (the axial stress from oil is zero) the hoop stress from oil at the inner wall is \(78\) MPa and from heating \(-238{,}08\) MPa. If the inner wall is 100 K warmer, the hoop stress is \(-160{,}08\) MPa, the axial \(-238{,}08\) MPa and the radial \(-30\) MPa, by von Mises (chapter 2) \(182{,}07\) MPa, which is below the yield strength of 220 MPa. At the outer wall the hoop stress is \(229{,}92\) MPa and by von Mises \(210{,}08\) MPa, only \(4{,}5\,\%\) below yield. If the inner wall is 100 K colder (cooling under pressure, for example), the hoop stress is \(316{,}08\) MPa and by von Mises \(314{,}42\) MPa, which is above yield, where the linearly elastic model no longer holds. The tube alone under the oil pressure of 30 MPa has by von Mises only \(96{,}56\) MPa, so the stresses from the 100 K difference between the walls are, with these data, much larger than the stresses from the oil. Depending on the sign of the difference they subtract in one case and add in the other.

Is the model reasonable? The total strain from temperature is \(\alpha\,\Delta T = 1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-3}\) at 100 K, and the elastic strain at the largest stress is \(238{,}08/196\,000 = 1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-3}\). Both are slightly above the bound \(0{,}001\) that we set for small strains in chapter 4, but they are still \(0{,}15\,\%\) and \(0{,}12\,\%\) of a length, and the model is linear in \(\Delta T\), so at 60 K (\(\alpha\,\Delta T = 9 \cdot 10^{-4}\)) all results scale with \(0{,}6\). Two more idealizations that we name: constant conductivity \(k\) and elastic constants independent of temperature (section 14.2), and the uncoupled treatment, where the deformation does not act back on the temperature (definition 14.38). What a correction for the dependence on temperature would change we do not estimate here. The last bound is yield. At the inner wall the hoop and axial stresses are \(-238{,}08\) MPa and the radial one is zero, which by von Mises is \(238{,}08\) MPa, above the yield strength of 220 MPa. Ends held by a rigid wall give the axial stress \(-365{,}42\) MPa instead of \(-238{,}08\) MPa and by von Mises \(321{,}27\) MPa. The stresses are linear in \(\Delta T\), so the elastic result holds with open ends only up to a difference of \(100 \cdot 220/238{,}08 = 92\) K, with a rigid wall up to \(100 \cdot 220/321{,}27 = 68\) K. At 100 K the inner wall already yields, and the linearly elastic model no longer holds there. So the order of loading matters too: oil and an inner wall 100 K warmer give together only \(182{,}07\) MPa, but if we first heat the tube and only then fill it with oil, the inner wall exceeds yield on the way.

What have we shown? Two results. A simply connected body with a linear temperature stays free of stress. A prism with a steady plane temperature stays free of stress in the plane of the cross-section, and the axial stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -E\,\alpha\,T\) is carried by the rigid wall at the ends. We showed both with compatibility and uniqueness. For a ring with heat flowing through the wall stresses arise, because the hole demands a jump of displacement that a field without stress cannot satisfy (the lemma on the jump at a cut). For the tube we computed them with a guessed displacement field that we checked: for the steel of chapter 3 and 100 K between the walls they reach a hoop stress of \(-238{,}08\) MPa, three times the \(78\) MPa that oil at 30 MPa gives, and by von Mises they already exceed yield.

14.9 The weak form of steady heat conduction

So far we found the temperature with series, in a bar and in a rectangular plate (sections 14.5 and 14.6). A series needs a body of simple shape, and for a casting, an engine head or a bracket with holes there is none. For displacements, chapter 6 showed the way for such bodies: we write the problem as an equality of integrals that holds for every test function (the weak form), and look for the best approximation in a chosen family (the Ritz and Galerkin methods), and chapter 7 built the family from finite elements. Does the same way work for temperature? Chapter 6 mentioned steady conduction only as a problem for which the Galerkin method works and "the Ritz method does not". That is not true, and in this section we show what is true: steady conduction has a weak form with the same structure as the bar, the beam and the body, a symmetric bilinear form and a functional that the solution minimizes, so the Ritz and Galerkin methods give the same equations (theorem 6.44). Along the way we must tell apart a problem that has exactly one solution from a problem that has none or infinitely many.

The path is this. First we write the strong form of the steady problem and test it on the fin of section 14.4. Then we derive the weak form from it, for the bar by integration by parts and for a body with the divergence theorem (theorem 4.14), and prove that the two forms are equivalent. Next we show that the bilinear form is positive and with it that the solution minimizes a functional. At the end we show what happens when only heat fluxes are prescribed.

New in this section are the weak form of conduction and its functional. Everything else comes from earlier chapters and sections: the bilinear and linear forms (definitions 6.4 and 6.5), the Ritz method and its properties (chapter 6), the divergence theorem (chapter 4) and the heat flux with the energy balance (sections 14.1 and 14.2).

The symbols are from those sections: temperature \(T\), heat flux \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T\) (definition 14.3), conductivity \(k\), heat source \(Q\) per unit volume and film coefficient \(h\) (equation (14.12)). Several of these letters meet letters of other chapters. Here \(k\) is the conductivity and not the shear factor of chapter 5, \(q\) is a heat flux and not a distributed load, in chapters 6 and 7 \(h\) is the element length while here it is the film coefficient (the element length will be written \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) later), and \(\Pi\) is here a functional and not the potential energy. The letters \(\ell\) and \(B\) are the forms of definitions 6.5 and 6.4. Steady (stacionarno) means that the temperature does not change with time, \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), as after a long wait.

14.9.1 Strong form and the fin

We start with the simplest body, a bar. Let the bar be a fin as in section 14.4: it lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\), has a constant cross-section of area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\), its conductivity \(k\) is constant, and along its side surface it exchanges heat with surroundings at temperature \(T_\infty\) by Newton's law (equation (14.12)): the heat flowing into the bar per unit of side area is \(h\,(T_\infty - T)\). The exchange is a model and not a law of nature: we assume that \(h\) is constant and that the temperature in each cross-section is a single number, \(T(x)\), as in section 14.4, where it is said when this is close to true.

The equation of the fin comes from the energy balance of a finite piece \([a, b]\) of the bar (section 14.2), with no small pieces. In the steady state the stored heat does not grow, so the sum of three contributions is zero. Along the axis, heat enters through \(a\) and leaves through \(b\), and the net gain is \(kA\,T'(b) - kA\,T'(a)\) (since the flux is \(q = -k\,T'\) and \(q\,A\) flows through a cross-section), which by the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40) equals \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b (kA\,T')'\,\mathrm{d}x\). Through the side surface \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b hP\,(T_\infty - T)\,\mathrm{d}x\) enters, and the source gives \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b A\,Q\,\mathrm{d}x\). Hence

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \Big( (kA\,T')' + hP\,(T_\infty - T) + A\,Q \Big)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 \qquad \text{for every piece } [a, b] \subseteq [0, L] . \tag{14.43}\]

The integrand \(g\) is continuous when \(T\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(Q\) is continuous, and by theorem 3.40 (part 2) the function \(G(x) = \int_0^x g\,\mathrm{d}t\) has derivative \(g\). By equation (14.43), \(G(b) - G(a) = 0\) for every \(a < b\), so \(G\) is constant and \(g = G' = 0\) everywhere. We get the equation of the fin

\[(kA\,T')' - hP\,T = -hP\,T_\infty - A\,Q , \tag{14.44}\]

which is equation (12.1-10) of COOK, PDF p. 471, without the time term.

At the ends we prescribe two conditions. At \(x = 0\) the fin is attached to a wall of temperature \(T_0\), so the temperature is prescribed, \(T(0) = T_0\). At \(x = L\) let a prescribed flux \(\bar q\) per unit of cross-section area flow into the bar from outside. Since \(-q(L)\,A = kA\,T'(L)\) flows into the bar, the condition is \(k\,T'(L) = \bar q\). For an insulated end \(\bar q = 0\).

We test this on the fin of section 14.4, with an insulated end, \(\bar q = 0\), \(Q = 0\), and with the excess over the surroundings \(\theta = T - T_\infty\), which writes equation (14.44) without a right-hand side, \(kA\,\theta'' = hP\,\theta\), and \(\theta(0) = \theta_0\). Let \(m^2 = hP/(kA)\) and \(mL = 1\). Section 14.4 gave \(\theta(x) = \theta_0\,\cosh m(L - x)/\cosh mL\), which after two differentiations indeed gives \(\theta'' = m^2\,\theta\) and has at \(x = L\) the derivative \(-\theta_0\,m\,\sinh 0/\cosh mL = 0\). The ratio of tip to base is \(1/\cosh 1 = 0{,}6481\).

14.9.2 The body

We write the same for a body. Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes (definition 4.11) with surface \(S\) and outward normal \(\vek n\), contained in an open set \(D\).

We draw the body \(V\) as a rectangle cut by a plane. Heat is produced in it by the source \(Q\) per unit volume (dots), for example by a current through a conductor. The surface \(S\) is divided into parts that do not overlap, and on each part one condition holds, since at the same point we cannot prescribe both the temperature and the flux (COOK, PDF p. 472). On the left face the temperature \(\bar T\) is prescribed, this is the part \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\). On the right the flux \(\bar q\) per unit area flowing into the body is prescribed, the part \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\). Here we count the flux, as COOK does (PDF p. 472), positive into the body, while in equation (14.11) we counted it outward, so \(\bar q = -\bar q_{\mathrm{n}}\). By Fourier's law heat flows in the direction \(\vek q = -k\,\nabla T\), so through a surface with outward normal \(\vek n\) there enters per unit area \(-\vek q\cdot\vek n = k\,\nabla T\cdot\vek n = k\,\partial T/\partial n\) (where \(\partial T/\partial n\) is the derivative of the temperature in the direction of the normal), and the condition is \(k\,\partial T/\partial n = \bar q\). On the top face there is convection, the part \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\), where \(h\,(T_\infty - T)\) enters the body by Newton's law, so \(k\,\partial T/\partial n = h\,(T_\infty - T)\). The bottom face is insulated, which is the flux condition with \(\bar q = 0\), and belongs to \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\). The normal points out of the body.

Definition 14.47 Strong form of steady heat conduction (močna oblika stacionarnega prevajanja toplote)

Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes with surface \(S\), which is the union of parts \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) that overlap only along the edges of faces, and let \(D\) be an open set containing \(V\). The conductivity \(k > 0\) and the film coefficient \(h \ge 0\) are numbers, the source \(Q\) is a continuous function on \(V\), and \(\bar T\), \(\bar q\) and \(T_\infty\) are continuous functions on the corresponding parts of the surface. The strong form is the problem: find a function \(T\), twice continuously differentiable on \(D\), that satisfies

\[-k\,\nabla^2 T = Q \ \text{ in } V , \qquad T = \bar T \ \text{ on } S_{\mathrm{T}} , \qquad k\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial n} = \bar q \ \text{ on } S_{\mathrm{q}} , \qquad k\,\frac{\partial T}{\partial n} = h\,(T_\infty - T) \ \text{ on } S_{\mathrm{h}} . \tag{14.45}\]

The Laplace operator \(\nabla^2\) is from definition 11.5.

Source: COOK §12.1, (12.1-8), (12.1-14) and (12.1-15) (PDF pp. 471-472), CM §8.3.1 (PDF p. 402). With theorem 14.8 the first equation is the steady case of the conduction equation at constant conductivity.

The first equation is the conduction equation (theorem 14.8) with \(T_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) and constant \(k\): \(0 = \nabla\cdot(k\,\nabla T) + Q = k\,\nabla^2 T + Q\). As idealizations, let us say what we assumed (section 14.2): the body is isotropic, \(k\) is constant over the range of temperatures that the problem covers (if \(k\) changes with temperature the problem is nonlinear, COOK, PDF p. 469), heat moves only by conduction and convection, radiation is outside the model (COOK, PDF pp. 476 to 478), and the body is at rest. The requirement "twice continuously differentiable on \(D\)" is a simplification: a body made of boxes has corners on its surface, where the solution is in general not so smooth. What the general theory does about it is said in section 6.2.3, here we stay with smooth solutions.

14.9.3 The weak form

The strong form asks for the second derivative of the temperature at every point. The trial fields of finite elements are piecewise linear and do not have one. How do we get rid of it? We multiply the conduction equation by a test function \(w\) and integrate over the body, as for the bar in chapter 6, and move one derivative onto \(w\). For the bar integration by parts moves it, for a body the divergence theorem does. The move also gives boundary terms, and these themselves tell which conditions are essential and which natural.

Definition 14.48 Weak form of steady heat conduction (šibka oblika stacionarnega prevajanja toplote)

Let the body, the conductivity, the film coefficient and the data be as in definition 14.47. An admissible field is a function \(T\), continuously differentiable on \(D\), with \(T = \bar T\) on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\). A test function is a function \(w\), continuously differentiable on \(D\), with \(w = 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\). The test functions form a vector space \(W\). For functions \(T\) and \(w\), continuously differentiable on \(D\), let

\[B(T, w) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,\nabla T\cdot\nabla w\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,T\,w\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{14.46}\]
\[\ell(w) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,w\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{q}} \bar q\,w\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,T_\infty\,w\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{14.47}\]

The weak form is the problem: find an admissible field \(T\) such that

\[B(T, w) = \ell(w) \qquad \text{for every test function } w \in W . \tag{14.48}\]

The form \(B\) is bilinear and symmetric and \(\ell\) is linear, which follows from the linearity of the derivative and the integral (definitions 6.4 and 6.5). So this is a weak form in the sense of definition 6.6. For the bar of section 14.9.1 it is

\[B(T, w) = \int_0^L \big( kA\,T'\,w' + hP\,T\,w \big)\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad \ell(w) = \int_0^L \big( A\,Q + hP\,T_\infty \big)\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + A\,\bar q\,w(L) , \tag{14.49}\]

with admissible fields \(T(0) = T_0\) and test functions with \(w(0) = 0\).

Source: COOK §12.2, (12.2-1) and §5.1 (PDF pp. 473, 194). The notation with the forms \(B\) and \(\ell\) is as in definition 6.6.

Let us see which condition sits where in the weak form. The temperature on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) is in the set of admissible fields, so it is an essential condition, like a displacement at a support, and therefore the test function \(w\) is zero there, as the curve below the body shows. The flux \(\bar q\) and the convection are in the forms \(B\) and \(\ell\) as terms over \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\), so they are natural conditions. For the fin \(\ell\) contains the term \(A\,\bar q\,w(L)\) and the value \(T_0\) is in the set of admissible fields. The pattern is the same as for the bar (section 6.1.2), except that the displacement is replaced by the temperature and the axial force by the heat flux.

We test the definition on the fin of section 14.9.1, in units \(kA = 1\) and \(L = 1\), so \(hP = m^2 = 1\) (since \(mL = 1\)), \(\bar q = 0\) and \(\theta(0) = \theta_0 = 1\). The form is \(B(\theta, w) = \int_0^1 (\theta'\,w' + \theta\,w)\,\mathrm{d}x\), \(\ell = 0\), and \(\theta = \cosh(1 - x)/\cosh 1\). The test function \(w = x\) is zero at \(x = 0\) and so it is admissible.

In the left part of the figure the derivative \(\theta' = -\sinh(1 - x)/\cosh 1\) is always negative and its area is \(\int_0^1 \theta'\,\mathrm{d}x = \theta(1) - \theta(0) = 0{,}6481 - 1 = -0{,}3519\). The product \(x\,\theta\) is positive and its area is \(\int_0^1 x\,\theta\,\mathrm{d}x = 0{,}3519\) (SymPy). The sum is zero, as it must be, and the same holds for \(w = \sin(\pi x/2)\) (zero at \(x = 0\), SymPy). The weak form holds.

Now let us choose \(w = 1\), which is not zero at the prescribed temperature and therefore is not a test function. Its derivative is \(w' = 0\), so in the right part of the figure the product \(\theta'\,w'\) is zero and only the area under \(\theta\) remains, \(B(\theta, 1) = \int_0^1 \theta\,\mathrm{d}x = \tanh 1 = 0{,}7616\), which is not zero and differs from \(\ell(1) = 0\). The weak form does not hold for this \(w\). The reason is in a step that the theorem below carries out: integration by parts leaves a boundary term \(-kA\,\theta'(0)\,w(0)\), and it is zero only when \(w(0) = 0\). For \(w = 1\) it equals \(-\theta'(0) = \tanh 1\) and it is exactly the heat that flows through the base (section 14.4, \(mL\tanh mL\) in units \(kA\,\theta_0/L\), with \(mL = 1\): \(0{,}7616\)). A prescribed temperature therefore requires \(w = 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\), and it takes along the heat that the weak form computes separately.

Theorem 14.49 Strong and weak form of heat conduction (močna in šibka oblika prevajanja toplote)

Let the body, the data and the forms be as in definitions 14.47 and 14.48.

  1. Bar: let \(T\) be twice continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\) and \(A\,Q\) continuous. The function \(T\) is a solution of the strong form, equation (14.44) with \(T(0) = T_0\) and \(k\,T'(L) = \bar q\), exactly when it is an admissible field and a solution of the weak form with the forms (14.49).
  2. Body: if \(T\) is a solution of the strong form (definition 14.47), it is a solution of the weak form (definition 14.48). Conversely, if \(T\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(D\) and a solution of the weak form, it satisfies the first equation at every interior point of the body, and the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) at every point that has a neighbourhood in \(S\) inside that part, and by continuity on the whole part. The condition on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) is in the admissibility.
Proof

We must show four things: that the weak form follows from the strong form in the bar and in the body, and that the equation and the boundary conditions follow from the weak form in both cases. The bar is treated with integration by parts, the body with the divergence theorem, which is the same step in three dimensions. For the converse in the body we use a test function that is nonzero only in a small ball.

  1. Bar, strong to weak. Let \(w\) be a test function, \(w(0) = 0\). We multiply equation (14.44), written as \((kA\,T')' - hP\,T + hP\,T_\infty + A\,Q = 0\), by \(w\) and integrate over \([0, L]\). The functions are continuous, so the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals (lemma 3.39).
  2. By integration by parts (corollary 3.41, with \(kA\,T'\) in place of \(f\), which is continuously differentiable, and \(w\) in place of \(g\)) we have \(\int_0^L (kA\,T')'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = kA\,T'(L)\,w(L) - kA\,T'(0)\,w(0) - \int_0^L kA\,T'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\). Here \(w(0) = 0\) and \(kA\,T'(L) = A\,\bar q\), so the right-hand side is \(A\,\bar q\,w(L) - \int_0^L kA\,T'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. We insert step 2 into step 1 and move the terms \(\int_0^L kA\,T'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\int_0^L hP\,T\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\) to the left: this gives equation (14.48) with the forms (14.49). The field \(T\) is admissible, since \(T(0) = T_0\).
  4. Bar, weak to strong. Let \(T\) be a solution of the weak form. By step 2 read backwards, for every test function \(B(T, w) - \ell(w) = \big(kA\,T'(L) - A\,\bar q\big)\,w(L) - \int_0^L R\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\), where \(R = (kA\,T')' - hP\,T + hP\,T_\infty + A\,Q\) is a continuous function. Let \(R(x_0) > 0\) at some interior point \(x_0\). By continuity there is \(\delta > 0\) with \(R > R(x_0)/2\) on \([a, b] = [x_0 - \delta, x_0 + \delta] \subset (0, L)\). The function \(w = (x - a)^2\,(b - x)^2\) on \([a, b]\) and zero elsewhere is continuously differentiable (its derivative is zero at \(a\) and \(b\) and continuous), zero at \(x = 0\), with \(w(L) = 0\), and positive inside \([a, b]\). Then \(\int_0^L R\,w\,\mathrm{d}x \ge \tfrac12 R(x_0)\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b w\,\mathrm{d}x > 0\) (lemma 3.39, monotonicity), a contradiction, because this integral is zero (since \(w(L) = 0\) it is all that remains in the equation). The same for \(R(x_0) < 0\) with \(-R\). So \(R = 0\) in the interior, by continuity everywhere, and this is equation (14.44).
  5. With \(R = 0\) what remains is \(\big(kA\,T'(L) - A\,\bar q\big)\,w(L) = 0\) for every test function. We choose \(w = x\), which is zero at \(0\) and has \(w(L) = L \ne 0\). We get \(k\,T'(L) = \bar q\). The condition \(T(0) = T_0\) is in the admissibility. This is part 1.
  6. Body, strong to weak. Let \(w\) be a test function. The field \(\vek v = w\,k\,\nabla T\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (a product of continuously differentiable functions, \(T\) is twice continuously differentiable), so by the divergence theorem (theorem 4.14) \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \nabla\cdot\vek v\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\). By the product rule \(\nabla\cdot\vek v = k\,\nabla w\cdot\nabla T + w\,k\,\nabla^2 T\), and \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = w\,k\,\partial T/\partial n\). Hence \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,\nabla T\cdot\nabla w\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} w\,k\,\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial n}\,\mathrm{d}A - \int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,k\,\nabla^2 T\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  7. The first equation of (14.45) gives \(-\int_{\mathrm{V}} w\,k\,\nabla^2 T\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,w\,\mathrm{d}V\). On \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) we have \(w = 0\) and the term drops out, on \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) we have \(k\,\partial T/\partial n = \bar q\), on \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) we have \(k\,\partial T/\partial n = h\,T_\infty - h\,T\). Inserting everything into step 6 we get \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,\nabla T\cdot\nabla w\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,T\,w\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,w\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{q}} \bar q\,w\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,T_\infty\,w\,\mathrm{d}A\), which is equation (14.48).
  8. Body, weak to strong. Steps 6 and 7 read backwards, for a solution of the weak form, give for every test function \(B(T, w) - \ell(w) = -\int_{\mathrm{V}} R\,w\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{q}} (k\,\partial T/\partial n - \bar q)\,w\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} (k\,\partial T/\partial n - h\,T_\infty + h\,T)\,w\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), where \(R = k\,\nabla^2 T + Q\). Let \(R(P) \ne 0\) at an interior point \(P\) of the body. For a small enough radius \(\rho\) the ball \(|X - P| < \rho\) lies in the interior of the body and \(R\) has the same sign in it. The function \(w(X) = (\rho^2 - |X - P|^2)^2\) in the ball and zero outside is continuously differentiable (the derivative \(-4\,(\rho^2 - |X - P|^2)\,(X - P)\) is zero on the surface of the ball), zero on all faces (the ball does not reach them) and positive inside. Then \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} R\,w\,\mathrm{d}V \ne 0\) for the same reason as in step 4, a contradiction. So \(R = 0\) in the interior, by continuity everywhere, and this is the first equation.
  9. With \(R = 0\) the surface terms remain. Let \(P\) be a point of \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\) that has a neighbourhood in \(S\) inside \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\), and \(g = k\,\partial T/\partial n - \bar q\), continuous on \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\), with \(g(P) \ne 0\). For small enough \(\rho\) the ball \(|X - P| < \rho\) meets the surface \(S\) only in this neighbourhood, so the function \(w\) of step 8 is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\), hence a test function, and the term over \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) is zero. What remains is \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{q}} g\,w\,\mathrm{d}A\). For small enough \(\rho\), \(g\) has the sign of \(g(P)\) on the part of the surface inside the ball, and \(w\) is positive there except on the boundary of the ball. So \(g\,w\) has the sign of \(g(P)\) everywhere on this part and is not zero over a part of the surface of positive area, and the integral is not zero. This is a contradiction, so \(g(P) = 0\) at every such point and, by continuity, everywhere on \(S_{\mathrm{q}}\). The same argument on \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) gives \(k\,\partial T/\partial n = h\,(T_\infty - T)\). This is part 2.

Source: COOK §12.2 (PDF p. 473) and §4.7 (PDF p. 165), EP §6.3.6.2 for the relation of the strong and weak form (pp. 323-327). The proof in steps is not from the sources.

What did the proof show? The two forms give the same temperature when it is smooth enough, and the weak one asks for one derivative less. Steps 2 and 6 showed what the conditions are: the boundary term that integration by parts brings is the heat flux times \(w\), so the flux is built into the weak form and the temperature is not. For the converse in the body we assumed that \(T\) is twice continuously differentiable. For a piecewise linear finite element field in the plane or in space the integral over the body splits into a sum over pieces (corollary 4.40) and steps 6 and 7 gain terms on the faces between the pieces, which we treat in chapter 15. For the bar we did this completely already in chapter 6 (lemma 6.13).

14.9.4 Positivity and the functional

The weak form is easy to write as an equation, but the solution need not be unique. The Ritz method (definition 6.32) and theorem 6.34 require \(B(w, w) > 0\) for every \(w \ne 0\). For displacements it is twice the strain energy (lemma 6.7). For temperature \(B(w, w) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,|\nabla w|^2\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} h\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), a sum of two nonnegative terms. When is it zero?

Lemma 14.50 Positivity of the conduction form (pozitivnost forme prevajanja toplote)

Let the interior of the body \(V\) be a connected open set (definition 1.130), \(h > 0\) constant on \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\), and let \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) or \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) have positive area. Then \(B(w, w) \ge 0\) for every test function \(w\), and \(B(w, w) = 0\) only for \(w = 0\).

Proof

We must show that a zero sum of two nonnegative terms means a zero field. First the gradient, then the constant.

  1. The first integrand \(k\,|\nabla w|^2\) is continuous and nonnegative, and so is the second, \(h\,w^2\), hence \(B(w, w) \ge 0\) (lemma 4.32, part 2).
  2. Let \(B(w, w) = 0\). Both nonnegative terms are zero, since their sum is zero. If \(|\nabla w|^2 > 0\) at some interior point, by continuity it would be positive and larger than some positive bound in a neighbourhood of that point, and the integral over the neighbourhood would be positive (as in step 1 of the proof of lemma 6.7), a contradiction. So \(\nabla w = \vek 0\) at every interior point.
  3. Let \(P\) and \(P'\) be interior points and \(P = A_0, \dots, A_{\mathrm{m}} = P'\) a broken line in the interior (definition 1.130). On every segment \(A_{\mathrm{j}-1}A_{\mathrm{j}}\) the function \(t \mapsto w(A_{\mathrm{j}-1} + t\,\overrightarrow{A_{\mathrm{j}-1}A_{\mathrm{j}}})\) is differentiable with derivative \(\nabla w\cdot\overrightarrow{A_{\mathrm{j}-1}A_{\mathrm{j}}} = 0\), so by corollary 1.85 it is constant. The values on consecutive segments agree at \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(w(P) = w(P')\). The field \(w\) is therefore constant, \(w = c\), in the interior, and by continuity on all of \(V\).
  4. If the part of \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) where \(w = 0\) has positive area, then \(c = 0\). If \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) has positive area, the second term is \(h\,c^2\) times this area, which is zero only for \(c = 0\) (and \(h > 0\)). In both cases \(w = 0\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. For displacements it is lemma 6.7, here is the scalar version.

The lemma gives what we need. The Ritz solution exists and is unique (theorem 6.34 and its corollary on the matrix \(\mat K\)), and theorem 6.44 says that the Ritz and Galerkin methods are the same, because \(B\) is symmetric. It says something more: the solution of the weak form is the lowest point of a functional.

Lemma 14.51 Functional of steady conduction (funkcional stacionarnega prevajanja)

Let the assumptions of lemma 14.50 hold. For an admissible field \(v\) let

\[\Pi(v) = \tfrac12\,B(v, v) - \ell(v) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \tfrac12\,k\,|\nabla v|^2 - Q\,v \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} \Big( \tfrac12\,h\,v^2 - h\,T_\infty\,v \Big)\,\mathrm{d}A - \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{q}} \bar q\,v\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{14.50}\]

Then \(T\) is a solution of the weak form exactly when \(\Pi(T) \le \Pi(v)\) for every admissible field \(v\). For the solution \(\Pi(v) - \Pi(T) = \tfrac12\,B(v - T, v - T)\), with equality at \(v = T\).

Proof

We must show the difference of the functionals and the converse. The first comes from bilinearity, the second from the quadratic term.

  1. Let \(T\) be a solution of the weak form and \(v\) an admissible field. The difference \(w = v - T\) is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) and is a test function. By theorem 6.34, part 1, \(\Pi(v) - \Pi(T) = \tfrac12\,B(w, w) \ge 0\), with equality only for \(w = 0\) (lemma 14.50).
  2. Converse. Let \(T\) be an admissible field with \(\Pi(T) \le \Pi(v)\) for all admissible fields \(v\). For a test function \(w\) and a number \(\alpha\) the field \(T + \alpha w\) is admissible, so \(\Pi(T + \alpha w) - \Pi(T) = \alpha\,\big( B(T, w) - \ell(w) \big) + \tfrac12\,\alpha^2\,B(w, w) \ge 0\) (from bilinearity and symmetry, as in section 6.1.5).
  3. Let \(w \ne 0\) and \(r = B(T, w) - \ell(w)\). We choose \(\alpha = -r/B(w, w)\), which is possible since \(B(w, w) > 0\) (lemma 14.50). Then \(\Pi(T + \alpha w) - \Pi(T) = -r^2/B(w, w) + \tfrac12\,r^2/B(w, w) = -\tfrac12\,r^2/B(w, w)\), which is negative if \(r \ne 0\), and this contradicts minimality. So \(r = 0\) for every \(w \ne 0\), and for \(w = 0\) the claim is trivial.

Source: COOK §12.2, (12.2-1) (PDF p. 473) has the same functional with all terms, for the flux \(f_{\mathrm{B}}\) into the body and the film coefficient. The proof is not from the sources.

It is called a functional because we give it a whole field \(v\) as input and get one number. How large is that number? The unit of \(\tfrac12 k\,|\nabla v|^2\) is W/(m K) · K²/m² = W K/m³, so \(\Pi\) is in W K. It is not the energy of any quantity stored in the body, and COOK says for nonstructural problems that a functional may have no clear physical meaning (PDF p. 193). It is enough that it is a number with its lowest value at the true temperature.

With the lemma we check a Ritz approximation on the fin, in units \(kA = 1\), \(L = 1\), \(mL = 1\), \(\theta(0) = 1\). The trial field with one term is \(\theta_1 = 1 + c\,x\), \(\psi_0 = 1\) and \(\psi_1 = x\) (zero at \(x = 0\)). The Ritz equation (definition 6.32) has \(K_{11} = B(x, x) = \int_0^1 (1 + x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = 4/3\) and \(f_1 = \ell(x) - B(1, x) = 0 - \int_0^1 x\,\mathrm{d}x = -1/2\), so \(c = -3/8\) and \(\theta_1 = 1 - 3x/8\).

In the figure the horizontal axis carries the position \(x\) along the fin and the vertical one the excess temperature \(\theta\), starting at \(0{,}5\) so that the difference shows. The true temperature is a curve that flattens to slope zero at the insulated end, and the Ritz approximation is a straight line that satisfies only the condition at the base. At the end \(x = 1\) the approximation is \(0{,}625\) against the true \(0{,}6481\), \(3{,}6\ \%\) too low, and the difference is modest. The natural condition, slope zero, the line does not satisfy, since its slope is \(-0{,}375\). The weak form does not impose it on the trial fields: the true solution satisfies it (theorem 14.49, step 5), an approximation only as far as its family of trial fields allows.

By lemma 14.51, \(\Pi(\theta_1) = \tfrac12\,B(\theta_1, \theta_1) = \tfrac12\int_0^1 (\theta_1'^2 + \theta_1^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0{,}40625\), and the true solution has \(\Pi(\theta) = \tfrac12\,B(\theta, \theta) = 0{,}38080\) (SymPy), so \(\Pi(\theta_1) \ge \Pi(\theta)\) and the difference \(0{,}02545\) is \(\tfrac12\,B(\theta_1 - \theta, \theta_1 - \theta)\), the energy of the error, as theorem 6.34 states. The true value is also \(\Pi(\theta) = \tfrac12 B(\theta, 1) = \tfrac12\tanh 1 = 0{,}3808\): since \(\theta - 1\) is a test function, \(B(\theta, \theta - 1) = 0\) and \(B(\theta, \theta) = B(\theta, 1)\), which is the heat through the base of section 14.4. For the Ritz field the same holds, \(B(\theta_1, 1) = B(\theta_1, \theta_1) = 0{,}8125\), and since \(\Pi(\theta_1) \ge \Pi(\theta)\), the heat through the base computed from the Ritz field as \(B(\theta_1, 1)\), \(0{,}8125\), is larger than the true one, \(0{,}7616\). This holds for this way of computing it. From the slope of the line at the base we would get \(-\theta_1'(0) = 0{,}375\), much less than the true value. For finite elements, which we treat later in the chapter, this finding says on which side we err in the heat through the base.

14.9.5 Heat fluxes only

What if we prescribe only fluxes, so \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) is empty and \(h = 0\)? For displacements this is a body with no supports, which cannot be held (chapter 11, part 2 of theorem 11.4). For heat it is similar, and the condition here is the heat balance.

Lemma 14.52 Problem with heat fluxes only (naloga s samimi toplotnimi tokovi)

Let \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) be empty and \(h = 0\) everywhere, so that only the source \(Q\) and the flux \(\bar q\) on \(S = S_{\mathrm{q}}\) are given (definition 14.48). Then:

  1. \(B(w, w) = 0\) for \(w = 1\), so lemma 14.50 does not hold.
  2. The weak form has a solution only if \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}} \bar q\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), that is, if the heat that is produced in the body and flows into it also flows out.
  3. If \(T\) is a solution, so is \(T + c\) for every number \(c\). For every admissible field \(v\) and every number \(c\), \(\Pi(v + c) = \Pi(v) - c\,\big(\int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}} \bar q\,\mathrm{d}A\big)\).
Proof

We must show that a constant is in the kernel of the form, and then derive the balance from its effect on both sides of the equation.

  1. The function \(w = 1\) is continuously differentiable and, since \(S_{\mathrm{T}}\) is empty, a test function. Its gradient is \(\vek 0\) and \(h = 0\), so \(B(1, 1) = 0\) and \(w \ne 0\).
  2. Let \(T\) be a solution. We insert \(w = 1\) into the weak form: \(B(T, 1) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} k\,\nabla T\cdot\nabla 1\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\) and \(\ell(1) = \int_{\mathrm{V}} Q\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}} \bar q\,\mathrm{d}A\). The equality gives claim 2.
  3. The gradient of \(T + c\) is the gradient of \(T\) and \(h = 0\), so \(B(T + c, w) = B(T, w)\) for every \(w\), and \(T + c\) is a solution. For the same reason \(B(v + c, v + c) = B(v, v)\) for an admissible field \(v\), and \(\ell(v + c) = \ell(v) + c\,\ell(1)\), so \(\Pi(v + c) = \Pi(v) - c\,\ell(1)\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK, PDF p. 474 stresses that temperature and flux cannot be prescribed at the same place.

Let us look at this on a bar of two linear elements, in units \(kA = 1\) and \(L = 1\). The nodes are at \(0\), \(1/2\) and \(1\). The element matrix is the matrix of a bar element from lemma 7.5 with \(kA\) in place of \(EA\) (we justify this later in the chapter), an element of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/2\) has \(kA/h_{\mathrm{e}} = 2\), and the assembled matrix is \(\mat K = 2\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) with eigenvalues \(0\), \(2\) and \(6\) (NumPy) and determinant zero. In the figure, in its left part, heat \(1\) enters the left end of the bar and \(1\) leaves the right one (the arrows), \(\vek f = (1, 0, -1)\). The equations \(\mat K\,\vek T = \vek f\) determine the differences \(T_0 - T_1 = 0{,}5\) and \(T_1 - T_2 = 0{,}5\), but not the sum: a family of broken lines shifted upwards is an equally good solution, as claim 3 says. This is not an error of the computation but the fact that the flux between two parts depends only on the temperature differences. But if \(1\) enters the left end and nothing leaves the right one, \(\vek f = (1, 0, 0)\), the sum of the rows of the matrix is zero and the sum of the right-hand side is \(1\), and the system has no solution (the smallest residual is \(0{,}577\), NumPy). In a body the temperature would keep rising, which is an unsteady problem. In the right part of the figure heat \(1\) enters the bar without leaving (the arrow), and the functional along the constant field is \(\Pi(c) = -c\), a straight line without a lowest point, as claim 3 says.

What mends this? We prescribe a temperature somewhere, or add convection. With convection \(hA = 1\) at both ends the matrix is \(\mat K + \mat H\) with \(\mat H = \mathrm{diag}(1, 0, 1)\), the determinant is \(12\) and the smallest eigenvalue \(0{,}628\) (NumPy), the matrix is positive definite, as lemma 14.50 requires with \(h > 0\) on a part of the surface. Prescribed fluxes alone are therefore not enough, just as for displacements forces alone are not enough when the supports do not hold the body and \(B(w, w) > 0\) of theorem 6.34 fails (section 6.4.4). A prescribed temperature or convection must anchor the temperature.

14.9.6 What we have gained

Steady conduction has a weak form of the same structure as the bar, the beam and the body (theorem 14.49, definition 14.48). The temperature and the heat flux are divided by essential and natural conditions like the displacement and the force. Because the form \(B\) is positive (lemma 14.50), the problem has a functional that the solution minimizes (lemma 14.51), the Ritz and Galerkin methods are the same (theorem 6.44), and theorem 6.34 holds with all its consequences. Without a prescribed temperature or convection what happens is what happens for displacements without supports: the solution is not unique, or does not exist at all (lemma 14.52). We tested what we showed on the fin, where the Ritz approximation is \(0{,}625\) against the true \(0{,}6481\) at the tip. The next task is to write the same by elements, which is the same procedure as for the bar of chapter 7, and chapter 15 continues in the plane and in space.

14.10 Finite elements for heat conduction (končni elementi za prevajanje toplote)

Section 14.9 showed that steady heat conduction has a weak form and a functional, both known from chapter 6. So for the temperature the same two methods apply as for the displacement of a bar, the Ritz and the Galerkin method, and by theorem 6.44 they coincide. How does a computation come from this, which matrices do we get, and what do we know about the result in advance? First we read when finite elements first turned to heat. Then we show that the matrix of a conduction element is the matrix of a bar element from chapter 7 with the letters given a new meaning. We add the loss through a lateral surface, which is new, and put everything together on the fin that section 14.4 solved exactly. This shows where the result is exact, where it is not, and on which side of the true value the heat at the root lies.

From history

The name "finite element" was coined in 1960, and new elements for stress analysis were soon developed largely by intuition and physical argument. In 1963 the method was recognized as a form of the Rayleigh-Ritz method, a classical approximation technique, and so it was no longer only a special trick for stress analysis but a widely applicable method with a sound mathematical basis (COOK, PDF p. 24). Two years later, in 1965, papers appeared on heat conduction and on seepage flow through a porous medium, done with finite elements (COOK, PDF p. 24). The reason why heat conduction came so early is the content of section 14.9: steady conduction has a functional, so the Ritz route of chapter 6 applies unchanged. We drew this link ourselves, the source does not state it.

Back to what we were looking at: steady conduction has a functional, and now we use it.

14.10.1 The model of the fin (model rebra)

We compute on a body that we have solved exactly, so that we can compare. It is the fin of section 14.4 (theorem 14.22): a straight bar of length \(L\) with a constant cross-section of area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\), of a material with conductivity \(k\) (chapter 5 uses \(k\) for the shear factor, here it is the material quantity of definition 14.3). The bar is attached at \(x = 0\) to a wall at temperature \(T_0\) above the surroundings, it gives off heat to the air through its lateral surface with heat transfer coefficient \(h\) (definition 14.13), and the end at \(x = L\) is insulated. We measure the temperature \(T(x)\) from the temperature of the surroundings, so the heat flux through the lateral surface is \(h\,T\). We take the idealizations of section 14.4 as given: the temperature is the same over the whole cross-section, \(k\) and \(h\) are constant, radiation is neglected. We write the element length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\), because the letter \(h\) is taken by the heat transfer coefficient (chapter 7 used it for the element length).

By theorem 14.22 the temperature solves \(kA\,T'' = hP\,T\) with \(T(0) = T_0\) and \(T'(L) = 0\), namely

\[T(x) = T_0\,\frac{\cosh m(L - x)}{\cosh mL} , \qquad m^2 = \frac{hP}{kA} . \tag{14.51}\]

The number \(m\) has the unit 1/m, and \(mL\) has no unit: it says how many times the distance \(L\) is longer than the length \(1/m\) over which the temperature of a long fin falls by the factor \(e\). The heat that the wall supplies to the fin is \(Q = -kA\,T'(0) = \dfrac{kA\,T_0}{L}\,mL\tanh mL\). The book has no source for the \(k\) of steel, so we compute with the dimensionless numbers \(mL = 1\) and \(mL = 2\) and measure heat in units of \(kA\,T_0/L\). At \(mL = 1\) the temperature of the tip is \(T(L)/T_0 = 1/\cosh 1 = 0{,}64805\) and \(Q = 0{,}76159\), at \(mL = 2\) it is \(T(L)/T_0 = 0{,}26580\) and \(Q = 1{,}92806\) (computation in num-10.py).

We get the weak form as follows: multiply the equation \(kA\,T'' = hP\,T\) by a test function \(w\) with \(w(0) = 0\) and integrate over \([0, L]\). By integration by parts (lemma 6.13) \(\int_0^L kA\,T''\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = kA\,T'(L)\,w(L) - kA\,T'(0)\,w(0) - \int_0^L kA\,T'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\). Both boundary terms are zero: the first because the end is insulated, \(T'(L) = 0\), the second because \(w(0) = 0\). The weak form is therefore

\[B(T, w) = \int_0^L \big(kA\,T'\,w' + hP\,T\,w\big)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 \qquad \text{for every } w,\ w(0) = 0 . \tag{14.52}\]

The form \(B\) is bilinear and symmetric, since both terms under the integral are symmetric in \(T\) and \(w\). It is positive, \(B(w, w) > 0\) for every \(w \ne 0\): both terms under the integral are non-negative, and \(hP\,w^2\) is positive on some interval around a point where \(w \ne 0\), because \(w\) is continuous. So the theorems of chapter 6 on the Ritz method hold, and the functional is \(\Pi(v) = \tfrac12\,B(v, v)\), since the right-hand side is zero (definition 6.32).
