14.10.2 The matrix of a conduction element (prevodnostna matrika elementa)

The mesh divides the interval \([0, L]\) into elements as in definition 7.1: on an element \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) the field is the straight line through the nodal temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), given by \(T_{\mathrm{h}} = \psi_1^e\,T_1 + \psi_2^e\,T_2\) with the shape functions of definition 7.2. What does this element do when we fix the temperatures of its nodes? We draw it together with the bar element, to see which quantity corresponds to which (figure 14.38).

First we draw the bar as an element with two nodes. If the nodes are displaced from the grey dashed position by \(d_1\) and \(d_2\), the surroundings must hold them with the forces \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), which by lemma 7.5 are \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\). Below we do the same with the conductor element: instead of node displacements we have temperatures, shown by the profile \(T_{\mathrm{h}}\) with the heights \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), and instead of forces the heat flows that the surroundings must supply or remove so that the nodes stay at these temperatures. The height of the profile is not a length but the temperature above the zero level. In the steady state the heat must flow through the element from the warm end to the cold end, and the arrow of the heat flux \(q\) shows the direction of this flow.

Before we state the claim, let us say what we expect. Steady state means that the temperature of the element does not change in time, so with no loss through the lateral surface and no source, all the heat that enters at the left end must leave at the right end (corollary 14.10 of section 14.2). By Fourier's law (definition 14.3) the heat flux is \(q = -k\,T_{\mathrm{h}}'\), and since \(T_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a straight line, \(q\) is constant along the element.

Lemma 14.53 Conductivity matrix of an element (prevodnostna matrika elementa)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be a finite element with two nodes and length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) (definition 7.1), \(kA\) constant on the element, and let there be no heat source on it and no loss through the lateral surface. Let \(\vek T_{\mathrm{e}} = (T_1, T_2)^\T\) be the column of nodal temperatures and \(\mat b_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac1{h_{\mathrm{e}}}(-1,\ 1)\). Then:

  1. The temperature gradient on the element is constant, \(T_{\mathrm{h}}' = \mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  2. The part of the functional \(\tfrac12\int kA\,(T_{\mathrm{h}}')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) that the element contributes is \(\tfrac12\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\) with
    \[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}} \mat b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,kA\,\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{14.53}\]
  3. The heat flows that the surroundings supply to the element at nodes \(1\) and \(2\) (positive when heat enters the element) are \(\vek Q_{\mathrm{e}} = (Q_1, Q_2)^\T = \mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\). So \(Q_1 = -Q_2 = \dfrac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(T_1 - T_2)\).
  4. For \(T_1 = T_2\) both flows are zero: \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,(1,\ 1)^\T = \vek 0\).
Proof

We must show four claims. The first and second are computations from lemma 7.5, the third is the balance of flow, the fourth a consequence of lemma 7.3.

  1. The shape functions are the same as for the bar, so by step 1 of the proof of lemma 7.5 \(T_{\mathrm{h}}' = (-T_1 + T_2)/h_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\), a number independent of \(x\).
  2. The product \(\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the matrix \(\frac1{h_{\mathrm{e}}^2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) (step 2 of the proof of lemma 7.5). The integrand \(\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,kA\,\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\) does not depend on \(x\), so the integral equals the integrand times \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 3.39). This is equation (14.53). Since \((T_{\mathrm{h}}')^2 = \vek T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\) is a number, the contribution of the element is \(\tfrac12\,kA\,h_{\mathrm{e}}\,(T_{\mathrm{h}}')^2 = \tfrac12\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  3. By definition 14.3 the heat flux in the direction \(+x\) is \(q = -k\,T_{\mathrm{h}}' = k\,(T_1 - T_2)/h_{\mathrm{e}}\), constant along the element. Through the cross-section \(A\) the flow \(A\,q\) goes in the direction \(+x\). At the left end this flow enters the element, so \(Q_1 = A\,q = \dfrac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(T_1 - T_2)\). At the right end the same flow leaves, so the element receives \(Q_2 = -A\,q\) from the surroundings. The sum \(Q_1 + Q_2 = 0\) is just the balance of the element in the steady state without source and loss. Comparison with \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(T_1 - T_2,\ T_2 - T_1)^\T\) gives the claim.
  4. For \(T_1 = T_2\) the gradient is zero by claim 1 and both flows are zero by claim 3.

Source: COOK §12.2, equations (12.2-4) (PDF pp. 473-474), where [k] is called the "conductivity matrix". The notation and the signs of claim 3 are ours.

The lemma is the same computation as for the bar, with \(EA\) replaced by \(kA\). So everything we know from chapters 6 and 7 carries over word for word. The table shows what corresponds to what (after COOK, PDF p. 474).

bar (chapter 7) heat conduction
displacement of a node \(d\) temperature of a node \(T\)
stiffness matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(EA\) conductivity matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(kA\)
force on a node \(F\) heat flow into a node \(Q\)
support with a prescribed displacement prescribed temperature
reaction of a support heat supplied by the support

The matrix is the same, but the sign means something different for each quantity. The axial force in a bar is \(N = EA\,u'\) and is positive when the bar stretches. The flow in the direction \(+x\) is \(-kA\,T'\) and is positive when the temperature falls along \(x\), because heat flows from warm to cold. In figure 14.38 the bar is stretched, \(d_2 > d_1\), and the temperature falls, \(T_1 > T_2\). So the force \(F_1\) equals \(\tfrac{EA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(d_1 - d_2) < 0\) and points out of the element, while the flow \(Q_1\) is \(\tfrac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(T_1 - T_2) > 0\) and points into it. At the right end both arrows point out of the element: the force \(F_2\), because we pull the bar, and the arrow \(-Q_2\), because heat leaves there. The directions at node \(1\) are opposite because of the values drawn, not because of the matrix: for \(T_2 > T_1\), \(Q_1\) would be negative too, and heat would leave the element at node \(1\).

A test. A fin with two elements has \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = L/2\) and conductivity matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = (2kA/L)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Its rows sum to zero, as claim 4 says, so the matrix is singular by itself, like a bar without a support (section 7.3.1). The physical reason is the same: if all nodes are at the same temperature, heat flows nowhere, and we can change this common temperature by any number without anything happening. In conduction without lateral loss, only the prescribed temperature of at least one node fixes it, here \(T_0\) at \(x = 0\). In the fin, the surroundings, which take heat away through the lateral surface, also act as a support (COOK, PDF p. 481): the matrix this loss adds is positive definite by the next lemma, so the matrix of the fin is not singular even without a prescribed temperature. A body without lateral loss and with only prescribed flows has a solution by lemma 14.18 only if the sum of the flows is zero, and then any constant may be added.

Lemma 14.54 Matrix of lateral heat loss (matrika izgube skozi stransko ploskev)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be a finite element with two nodes and length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\), let the cross-section have perimeter \(P\), let the heat transfer coefficient on the lateral surface be \(h\) and constant (definition 14.13), and let the temperature be measured from the surroundings. The part of the functional \(\tfrac12\int hP\,T_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) that the element contributes is \(\tfrac12\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat s_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\) with

\[\mat s_{\mathrm{e}} = \int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}} \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,hP\,\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{hP\,h_{\mathrm{e}}}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{14.54}\]

The matrix is symmetric and positive definite, and the sum of its entries \(hP\,h_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the heat transfer coefficient times the lateral surface of the element: at equal temperature \(T\) of both nodes the loss of heat through the lateral surface is \(hP\,h_{\mathrm{e}}\,T\).

Proof

We must show that the integral of the product of shape functions is the matrix of lemma 10.31, only with another constant.

  1. For \(T_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\) we have \(T_{\mathrm{h}}^2 = \vek T_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 1.101), and \(\vek T_{\mathrm{e}}\) does not depend on \(x\), so by linearity of the integral we take it out.
  2. The integrals \(\int\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) are \(h_{\mathrm{e}}/3\), \(h_{\mathrm{e}}/6\), \(h_{\mathrm{e}}/6\), \(h_{\mathrm{e}}/3\) (step 3 of the proof of lemma 10.31). The factor \(hP\) is constant and goes in front of the integral, which gives equation (14.54).
  3. Positive definiteness: for \((a, b) \ne (0, 0)\) we have \((a, b)\,\mat s_{\mathrm{e}}\,(a, b)^\T = \tfrac{hP\,h_{\mathrm{e}}}{6}\big(a^2 + b^2 + (a + b)^2\big) > 0\) (step 5 of the same lemma).
  4. The sum of the entries is \(\tfrac{hP\,h_{\mathrm{e}}}{6}\,(2 + 1 + 1 + 2) = hP\,h_{\mathrm{e}}\). Step 1 gives the same for \(T_1 = T_2 = T\): by lemma 7.3 \(T_{\mathrm{h}} = T\), so \(\int hP\,T^2\,\mathrm{d}x = hP\,h_{\mathrm{e}}\,T^2\).

Source: COOK §12.2, (12.2-4) and (12.2-6) (PDF p. 474), where the term with lateral convection is added to the matrix \([k]\) and where COOK compares it with the matrix of an elastic foundation. The proof in steps is ours.

We called the matrix the side matrix, because it comes from the loss through the lateral surface of the bar. Its integral is the same as for the consistent mass matrix of lemma 10.31, with \(\rho A\) replaced by \(hP\). There the matrix multiplies the acceleration, here it multiplies the temperature, so it plays the role of a stiffness, like an elastic foundation. In section 14.11 the same integral appears once more, there with the density and the specific heat, and it will multiply the time derivative. If the end of the fin were not insulated but gave off heat with heat transfer coefficient \(h\), we would add a term \(hA\) to the diagonal of node \(n\), as for a spring at a node (COOK, PDF p. 474). At \(mL = 1\) and \(hA\,L/(kA) = 1\) with two elements we get the temperatures \(0{,}6040\) and \(0{,}3656\) (in units of \(T_0\)) instead of \(0{,}7266\) and \(0{,}6428\) with the insulated tip. The difference is large because at \(mL = 1\) the number \(hL/k = 1\) means \(A = PL\) (divide \(hL/k\) by \((mL)^2 = hPL^2/(kA)\)): the tip has as much area as the whole lateral surface. For a slender fin with \(A = PL/20\), so \(hL/k = 0{,}05\), we get \(0{,}7162\) and \(0{,}6193\), close to the values with the insulated tip.

14.10.3 Assembly and comparison with the exact solution (sestavljanje in primerjava s točno rešitvijo)

Now we have everything. By theorem 7.13 the matrix of the structure is the sum of the expanded matrices \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} + \mat s_{\mathrm{e}}\), then we prescribe \(T_0\) at node \(0\) and solve the reduced system (theorem 7.18). With \(n = 2\) elements and \(mL = 1\) we have \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = L/2\). In units of \(kA/L\) we have \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mat s_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac{(mL)^2}{12}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\), because \(hP\,h_{\mathrm{e}}/6 = hP\,L/12 = (mL)^2\,\tfrac{kA}{12\,L}\). By SymPy the matrix of the structure is

\[\mat K = \begin{pmatrix} 13/6 & -23/12 & 0 \\ -23/12 & 13/3 & -23/12 \\ 0 & -23/12 & 13/6 \end{pmatrix} , \tag{14.55}\]

where for instance the middle entry is \(2 + 2 + \tfrac{2}{12} + \tfrac{2}{12} = \tfrac{13}{3}\), since both elements contribute to it, each with its term from \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) and from \(\mat s_{\mathrm{e}}\). The reduced system for \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) has the right-hand side \(-K_{10}\,T_0 = \tfrac{23}{12}\,T_0\) and \(0\) and the solution

\[T_1 = \tfrac{598}{823}\,T_0 = 0{,}72661\,T_0 , \qquad T_2 = \tfrac{529}{823}\,T_0 = 0{,}64277\,T_0 .\]

The heat that the support must supply is row \(0\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) times the vector of temperatures: \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} = K_{00}\,T_0 + K_{01}\,T_1 = \tfrac{637}{823}\,\tfrac{kA\,T_0}{L} = 0{,}77400\,\tfrac{kA\,T_0}{L}\). The exact value is \(0{,}76159\). The exact temperature of the tip is \(0{,}64805\,T_0\), and the approximation gives \(0{,}64277\,T_0\).

We build the figure with two coordinate axes: \(x\) along the fin and the temperature vertically, starting at \(T_0\) at \(x = 0\). First we draw the exact curve of equation (14.51) at \(mL = 2\). It falls ever more slowly, because by Fourier's law the slope is proportional to the heat flowing through the cross-section, and there is less and less of it towards the tip: part has already left through the lateral surface, and nothing flows through the insulated end. Over it we lay the piecewise linear field with two elements and the field with four elements. The segments are straight lines through the nodes, each with its own constant gradient by lemma 14.53. At the nodes both fields lie slightly below the exact curve, with two elements by \(0{,}023\,T_0\) at the tip. In the middle of the elements, however, they lie above it, with two elements by at most \(0{,}071\,T_0\) at \(x = 0{,}215\,L\). The exact curve bends upwards, so the straight line between two of its points lies above it, and this outweighs the small deficit at the nodes (NumPy). On the right is the heat at the root: the dots are the values \(Q_{\mathrm{h}}\) for more and more elements, the grey line is the exact value \(Q\). The dots lie above the line and approach it with every doubling of the number of elements.

The table gives these numbers, and also those at \(mL = 1\), computed in num-10.py. The last column is the error of the tip temperature \(T_{\mathrm{h}}(L) - T(L)\), in units of \(T_0\).

\(mL\) \(n\) \(Q_{\mathrm{h}}\) \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} - Q\) error \(T_{\mathrm{h}}(L) - T(L)\)
1 2 0,77400 0,01240 1,63 % \(-0{,}00528\)
1 4 0,76468 0,00308 0,40 % \(-0{,}00129\)
1 8 0,76236 0,00077 0,10 % \(-0{,}00032\)
1 16 0,76179 0,00019 0,03 % \(-0{,}00008\)
2 2 2,01942 0,09136 4,74 % \(-0{,}02308\)
2 4 1,95103 0,02298 1,19 % \(-0{,}00544\)
2 8 1,93381 0,00575 0,30 % \(-0{,}00134\)
2 16 1,92949 0,00144 0,07 % \(-0{,}00033\)

We notice two things. The heat is above the exact value in all eight computations, and the excess decreases by about a factor of \(4\) with each doubling of \(n\) (the ratios for \(n = 4, 8, 16\) are \(4{,}02\), \(4{,}01\), \(4{,}00\) at \(mL = 1\) and \(3{,}98\), \(3{,}99\), \(4{,}00\) at \(mL = 2\)). The tip temperature, however, is below the exact value in all these computations. We explain both observations in two claims. The first says where the result is exact, the second why the heat at the root is above the exact value.

14.10.4 When the result is exact (kdaj je rezultat točen)

For a bar, chapter 6 showed that nodal displacements are exact if \(EA\) is constant on every element (theorem 6.38). We expect the same claim for temperature. The fin does not satisfy it, because it has a lateral loss, so first we look at a body without it.

Corollary 14.55 Exact nodal temperatures (točne vozliščne temperature)

Let a bar of length \(L\) have a temperature prescribed at \(x = 0\), no loss through the lateral surface, a product \(kA > 0\) that is piecewise constant, a given heat source per unit length and a given flow at the end \(x = L\). Let the nodes of a mesh of linear elements also lie at every jump of \(kA\). Then the temperature at every node equals the true temperature.

Proof

We must show that the weak form of this bar is the weak form of the bar of theorem 6.38 and that its assumptions hold.

  1. By theorem 14.49 the weak form is \(B(T, w) = \ell(w)\) with \(B(T, w) = \int_0^L kA\,T'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) and a linear form \(\ell\) from the source and the end flow. By form this is the weak form of a bar in which \(kA\) stands for \(EA\) and the loads are the source and the end flow (chapter 6).
  2. The field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) of theorem 6.38 has \(kA\,G_{\mathrm{P}}' = 1\) on \((0, x_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(0\) after, and is continuous. Let \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) be a node. On every element \(kA\) is constant, so \(G_{\mathrm{P}}'\) is constant, hence \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) is a straight line on every element.
  3. A field that is continuous and a straight line on every element is a combination of tent functions (definition 6.25), so it lies in the trial family.
  4. By theorem 6.38, therefore, \(T_{\mathrm{h}}(x_{\mathrm{P}}) = T(x_{\mathrm{P}})\) at every node \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. Exact nodal values for a bar with two-node elements are stated by ONATE1 (PDF p. 363), see the source of theorem 6.38.

We test the corollary on two examples and then at its limit.

A layer with a jump of conductivity. A bar has \(kA = 1\) on \([0, 0{,}4]\) and \(kA = 4\) on \([0{,}4, 1]\) (in arbitrary units, \(L = 1\)), \(T(0) = 0\) and a flow \(1\) entering at the end \(x = L\). The temperature rises with slope \(1/kA\), so \(T(0{,}4) = 0{,}4\), \(T(0{,}5) = 0{,}4 + 0{,}1/4 = 0{,}425\) and \(T(1) = 0{,}55\). The mesh with nodes \(0\), \(0{,}4\) and \(1\) has a node at the jump and gives \(0{,}4\) and \(0{,}55\), exactly as the corollary predicts. The mesh with nodes \(0\), \(0{,}5\) and \(1\) has the jump inside the first element, whose mean \(kA\) is \((0{,}4\cdot 1 + 0{,}1\cdot 4)/0{,}5 = 1{,}6\) (as for the bar, section 7.1.2), and gives \(T(0{,}5) = 0{,}3125\) instead of \(0{,}425\) (error \(-26{,}5\,\%\)) and \(T(1) = 0{,}4375\) instead of \(0{,}55\) (\(-20{,}5\,\%\)). The condition that the node lies at the jump is therefore not a refinement: where it holds the result is exact, where it fails the error is a fifth or more. The reason is in step 2: the field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) has a kink at the jump and is not a straight line inside the element.

A heat source. A bar has \(kA = 1\), \(L = 1\), temperature \(0\) at \(x = 0\), an insulated end and a uniform source \(1\) per unit length. The exact temperature is \(T = x - x^2/2\). With two elements we get \(T_{\mathrm{h}}(0{,}5) = 0{,}375\) and \(T_{\mathrm{h}}(1) = 0{,}5\), which is exact. In the middle of an element, at \(x = 0{,}25\), we get \(T_{\mathrm{h}} = 0{,}1875\) instead of \(0{,}21875\), a difference \(0{,}03125 = g\,h_{\mathrm{e}}^2/(8\,kA)\) with source \(g = 1\) (computation in num-10.py). So the corollary concerns the nodes and no other points.

The fin, where the corollary does not hold. With the loss through the lateral surface the table above showed that the tip temperature is not exact (\(0{,}64277\) against \(0{,}64805\)). This does not contradict the corollary, because one assumption is missing. The field \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) with \(B(G_{\mathrm{P}}, w) = w(x_{\mathrm{P}})\) for every \(w\) now satisfies \(kA\,G_{\mathrm{P}}'' = hP\,G_{\mathrm{P}}\) on both sides of the point \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and is there a combination of \(\cosh\) and \(\sinh\), not a straight line, so it does not lie in the family of piecewise linear fields and step 3 fails.

14.10.5 The heat at the root is above the exact value (toplota ob korenu je nad točno)

So the nodal temperatures of the fin are not exact. The heat \(Q_{\mathrm{h}}\) that the support must supply, however, has by the table an important property: it is always above the true value. We see why if we write it with energy.

Lemma 14.56 Heat at the root of a fin (toplota ob korenu rebra)

Let \(T\) be the exact temperature of the fin of section 14.10.1, \(Q = -kA\,T'(0)\) the heat supplied by the wall, \(T_{\mathrm{h}}\) the finite element solution with linear elements on an arbitrary mesh with a node at \(x = 0\), and \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} = (\mat K\,\vek T)_0\) row \(0\) of the system, that is, the heat that the support must supply. Then

\[Q_{\mathrm{h}} - Q = \frac{B(T - T_{\mathrm{h}},\ T - T_{\mathrm{h}})}{T_0} \ge 0 , \tag{14.56}\]

with equality only for \(T_{\mathrm{h}} = T\). The heat at the root is thus never below the exact value.

Proof

We must show that \(B(T, T)\) and \(B(T_{\mathrm{h}}, T_{\mathrm{h}})\) are \(T_0\) times the heat, and then use theorem 6.34.

  1. By theorem 14.22 \(kA\,T'' = hP\,T\). Hence \(B(T, T) = \int_0^L \big(kA\,T'\,T' + kA\,T''\,T\big)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L (kA\,T'\,T)'\,\mathrm{d}x\). By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40) this is \(kA\,T'(L)\,T(L) - kA\,T'(0)\,T(0) = 0 + Q\,T_0\), because the end is insulated.
  2. By theorem 7.13 (claim 3) \(K_{\mathrm{IJ}} = B(\psi_{\mathrm{J}}, \psi_{\mathrm{I}})\). The theorem is stated for a bar without the side term, but the proof stays the same, because the side term is also an integral over \([0, L]\), the sum of the integrals over the elements that lemma 14.54 gives. For the field \(T_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} T_{\mathrm{I}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{I}}\), therefore, \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{J}} K_{0\mathrm{J}}\,T_{\mathrm{J}} = B(T_{\mathrm{h}}, \psi_0)\). The reduced system (theorem 7.18) says \(B(T_{\mathrm{h}}, \psi_{\mathrm{i}}) = 0\) for every node \(i \ne 0\), since the right-hand side is zero.
  3. Hence \(B(T_{\mathrm{h}}, T_{\mathrm{h}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} T_{\mathrm{I}}\,B(T_{\mathrm{h}}, \psi_{\mathrm{I}}) = T_0\,B(T_{\mathrm{h}}, \psi_0) = T_0\,Q_{\mathrm{h}}\), because all other terms are zero by step 2 and \(T_0\) is the temperature at node \(0\).
  4. The functional is \(\Pi(v) = \tfrac12\,B(v, v)\), and \(T\) and \(T_{\mathrm{h}}\) are admissible fields with the same temperature \(T_0\) at \(x = 0\). By claim 1 of theorem 6.34, \(\Pi(T_{\mathrm{h}}) - \Pi(T) = \tfrac12\,B(T_{\mathrm{h}} - T,\ T_{\mathrm{h}} - T)\).
  5. By steps 1 and 3 the left side equals \(\tfrac12\,T_0\,(Q_{\mathrm{h}} - Q)\). Dividing by \(\tfrac12\,T_0 > 0\) gives equation (14.56). The right side is non-negative, because \(B\) is positive (section 14.10.1), and zero only for \(T_{\mathrm{h}} = T\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. For the general theorem on the energy of the Ritz solution see the source of theorem 6.34.

The proof showed that the excess heat is exactly the square of the energy norm of the error (definition 6.18), divided by \(T_0\). This explains the numbers in the table: at \(mL = 1\), \(n = 2\) we have \(B(T - T_{\mathrm{h}}, T - T_{\mathrm{h}})/T_0 = 0{,}01240\), the same as \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} - Q\), and the same holds in all eight rows to the fifth decimal (num-10.py). Why the excess decreases by a factor of \(4\) when the elements are halved, the lemma does not say. Theorem 6.41 gives an upper bound for a bar without the side term: the square of the energy norm of the error is at most proportional to \(h^2\). The theorem does not cover the side term, and we do not prove a bound for it here. The table, however, shows ratios from \(3{,}98\) to \(4{,}02\), as for a decrease with \(h_{\mathrm{e}}^2\).

What does the lemma not say? It says nothing about the temperature of the tip. There \(T_{\mathrm{h}}\) is below the exact value in all eight computations, but this is an observation, not a theorem: the temperature at one point is not an energy, and the Ritz method bounds the energy (theorem 6.34), not every value (as for the hanging bar in chapter 6, where the work of the weight is too small and the displacement of the end too large). For design this means: the finite element model overestimates the heat that the fin gives off and underestimates the temperature of the tip. The first is on the safe side if we ask whether the fin removes enough heat, the second is not on the safe side if we ask about overheating of the tip. For these two values of \(mL\) the error of the heat is below \(5\,\%\) already at two elements and below \(1{,}2\,\%\) at four. The error of the tip temperature, divided by the exact tip temperature, is only \(0{,}8\,\%\) and \(0{,}2\,\%\) at \(mL = 1\), but \(8{,}7\,\%\) at two and \(2{,}0\,\%\) at four elements at \(mL = 2\).

What have we gained and what is left? The conduction element is the bar element with the letters given a new meaning, so assembly, supports and the reduced system carry over without a new proof. The side matrix \(\mat s_{\mathrm{e}}\) is new, and with it two results: exactness of the nodal temperatures where \(G_{\mathrm{P}}\) is a straight line, and an upper bound for the heat at the root, where there is a functional. Three steps remain. Temperature changing in time brings one more matrix, which section 14.11 will multiply by the time derivative. Plane and spatial elements for heat are in chapter 15, where temperature is the first field on triangles and tetrahedra. Radiation and temperature-dependent conductivity we did not treat, because then the problem is nonlinear and the functional is no longer quadratic (COOK, PDF pp. 476-478).

14.11 Transient response with finite elements (prehodni pojav s končnimi elementi)

Section 14.10 assembled the conductivity matrix of a bar from elements and used it to compute the steady (stacionarna) temperature, that is, the temperature that does not change in time. Most heat problems, however, depend on time. A bar that we clamp between two sources at time zero warms up over seconds or hours, and the question of when it reaches a given temperature is not a question about the steady state. Section 14.5 solved this for the bar with an exact series. Now we solve the same question with finite elements, which also exist for bodies that have no closed-form series. There are three questions: what time adds to the node equations, how a computer takes a step in time, and when that step fails.

The model is the bar of corollary 14.10 (figure 14.40 below): length \(L\), constant cross section \(A\), constant \(k\), \(\rho\) and \(c\) (section 14.2), lateral surface insulated and no source, so \(\rho c A\,\partial T/\partial t = \partial(kA\,\partial T/\partial x)/\partial x\). We hold both ends at temperature \(0\). Temperature is measured from this value, as the change \(\Delta T\) in chapter 3. The idealizations of section 14.2 stay: a rigid body at rest, constant \(k\) and \(c\), no coupling with deformation. We add two new ones: in space the temperature is linear within each element (section 14.10), and in time we compute it only at the times \(t_{\mathrm{s}} = s\,\Delta t\).

The letter \(k\) is the conductivity in this chapter, so we count the steps in time with \(s\) and not with \(k\) as in section 10.12 of chapter 10. We write the element length as \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) because \(h\) is the film coefficient (section 14.3), \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}}\) is an angle, and the parameter of the scheme will be \(\beta\). We measure time in the unit \(L^2/\kappa\) with \(\kappa = k/(\rho c)\) (section 14.2), which is a unit of seconds because \(\kappa\) has the unit m\(^2\)/s. Time \(t\) is then the Fourier number \(\mathrm{Fo} = \kappa t/L^2\), and we compute with \(L = 1\) and \(\kappa = 1\). The book has no sourced values of \(k\) and \(c\) for steel yet, so we do not use steel here. The results in \(\mathrm{Fo}\) hold for every material.

We draw the bar as in section 14.10. The straight bar with its nodes is cut into \(n = 8\) equal elements of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = L/n\), the nodes are \(x_{\mathrm{j}} = j\,h_{\mathrm{e}}\). We hold the two ends at temperature \(0\), like a clamp in mechanics, where a displacement is prescribed: here the temperature is prescribed and the flow through the end is not. At the start only node \(x_4\) is hot, the initial field has \(1\) K there and \(0\) at the other nodes. Between the nodes the field is linear, so the initial field is exactly the hat function \(\psi_4\) (definition 6.25) multiplied by \(1\) K. Such a sharp start is chosen on purpose: it contains all spatial shapes that are symmetric about the middle of the bar, from the longest to the shortest that eight elements can still describe. The scheme has to cope with all of them, so the start will show what the scheme does not cope with.

What does time add to the node equations? The element stores heat. By definition 14.6 a mass \(m\) needs the heat \(m\,c\,\Delta T\) to raise its temperature by \(\Delta T\). An element of mass \(\rho A h_{\mathrm{e}}\) therefore needs \(\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}\) joules per kelvin if we raise it uniformly. The question of how this capacity is divided among the nodes is the same as for mass in section 10.7.1 of chapter 10. There the kinetic energy \(\tfrac12\int\rho A\,\dot u^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) gave the mass matrix of an element, here the heat stored in the element will give a matrix with \(\rho c\) in place of \(\rho\). Look at the element of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the local coordinate \(\xi\) from its left end (we do not use the letter \(s\), which counts the steps). Its shape functions are \(\psi_1^e = 1 - \xi/h_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\psi_2^e = \xi/h_{\mathrm{e}}\). A simpler idea is to divide the capacity of the element into two lumped halves \(\tfrac12\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}\), one at each end.

Definition 14.57 Capacity matrix (kapacitivna matrika)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be an element of a bar of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\) (definition 7.1, figure 14.40), constant area \(A\), density \(\rho\) and specific heat \(c\), and let \(\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the row of its shape functions (definition 7.2). The heat capacity (toplotna kapaciteta) of the element is \(\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}\), the heat that raises its temperature by \(1\) K. The consistent capacity matrix (konsistentna kapacitivna matrika) of the element is the matrix of order \(2\)

\[\mat c_{\mathrm{e}} = \int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\rho c A\,\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} , \tag{14.57}\]

and the lumped capacity matrix (zbrana kapacitivna matrika) is \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}^{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac12\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat I\). The matrices of a bar with \(n\) elements, \(\mat C\) and \(\mat C^{\mathrm{z}}\), are obtained like the matrix \(\mat K\) in theorem 7.13: we add \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the selection matrices \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) (definition 7.11) and keep the rows and columns of the free nodes (theorem 7.18). Before the rows and columns of the prescribed nodes are removed, the sum of the entries of the assembled matrix is \(\rho c A L\) for both, the heat capacity of the whole bar.

Source: COOK (12.2-4) and the comment under (12.2-5), PDF p. 474: "specific heat (or capacity) matrix", analogous to the mass matrix, full when obtained from the integral and diagonal ("lumped") when the capacity of the element is divided among the nodes. The notation and the values for the bar are ours: the matrices are those of lemma 10.31 and definition 10.32 with \(\rho c\) in place of \(\rho\), since \(\rho\) is only a constant factor in the integral there.

The matrix is called capacity because its sum tells how much heat the bar takes in per kelvin, and it is called consistent because it uses the same shape functions as the conductivity matrix (lemma 14.53), like the consistent mass matrix (section 10.7.1 of chapter 10). A test on the element with \(\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}} = 1\) gives the numbers \(\tfrac26\) and \(\tfrac16\) in \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\) and the sum of all four entries \((2 + 1 + 1 + 2)/6 = 1\). The lumped matrix gives the same sum, so lumped and consistent differ only in how they divide the same heat. The following lemma shows how the equation of the bar appears in matrices. Its path is the same as for theorem 7.13: we multiply the equation by a test function, transform it by parts in the integral and insert a field made of shape functions.

Lemma 14.58 Node equations of the transient problem (enačbe vozlišč prehodnega pojava)

Let the bar be as above with \(n\) equal elements, \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) the hat functions of the nodes \(j = 1, \dots, n - 1\) (definition 6.25), \(T_{\mathrm{h}}(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n-1}T_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}(x)\) and \(\vek T = (T_1, \dots, T_{\mathrm{n}-1})^\T\). Let \(T(x, t)\) be a solution of \(\rho c A\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = (kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(T(0, t) = T(L, t) = 0\) that is continuously differentiable in \(t\) and twice continuously differentiable in \(x\). Then for every \(i = 1, \dots, n - 1\)

\[\int_0^L\rho c A\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 , \tag{14.58}\]

and if we replace \(T\) by \(T_{\mathrm{h}}\) in this equation (Galerkin method, definition 6.42, trial and test functions are \(\psi_1, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}-1}\)) we obtain the system

\[\mat C\,\dot{\vek T} + \mat K\,\vek T = \vek 0 , \tag{14.59}\]

where \(\mat C\) is the capacity matrix (definition 14.57) and \(\mat K\) the conductivity matrix of the bar with \(kA\) in place of \(EA\) (lemma 14.53). Both are symmetric and \(\mat C\) is positive definite.

Proof

We have to show that the equation turns into (14.58) by multiplying and integrating by parts, and that the Galerkin replacement gives the matrices we have already computed.

  1. We multiply the equation \(\rho c A\,T_{\mathrm{t}} = (kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{x}}\) by \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and integrate over \([0, L]\): \(\int\rho c A\,T_{\mathrm{t}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int (kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{x}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. The function \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous and piecewise linear, \(kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuously differentiable in \(x\), so both are piecewise continuously differentiable on a common partition. By lemma 6.13 with \(N = \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(w = kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\int (kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{x}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x = [kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}]_0^L - \int kA\,T_{\mathrm{x}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\). The term in the square bracket is zero because \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}(0) = \psi_{\mathrm{i}}(L) = 0\) for a free node \(i\). This proves equation (14.58).
  3. In equation (14.58) we replace \(T\) by \(T_{\mathrm{h}}\). Since \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) does not depend on time, \(\partial T_{\mathrm{h}}/\partial t = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \dot T_{\mathrm{j}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\), and by linearity of the integral (lemma 6.10) row \(i\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\big(\int\rho c A\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x\big)\dot T_{\mathrm{j}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\big(\int kA\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\big)T_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\).
  4. The first integral is a sum over elements of the integrals \(\int\rho c A\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), which by equation (14.57) give the entries of the matrix \(\mat C\) (the same is done in the proof of lemma 10.34 with \(\rho\) in place of \(\rho c\)). The second integral is an entry of the matrix \(\mat K\) by theorem 7.13 and lemma 14.53. Row \(i\) is therefore row \(i\) of equation (14.59).
  5. The symmetry is visible in the integrals, since \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\) are symmetric in \(i\) and \(j\). The positive definiteness of \(\mat C\) is lemma 10.34 with \(\rho c\) in place of \(\rho\) (for \(\vek T \ne \vek 0\), \(\vek T^\T\mat C\vek T = \int\rho c A\,T_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x > 0\)).

Source: COOK (12.4-1), PDF p. 478: the same equation \([\mat C]\{\dot{\mat T}\} + [\mat K_{\mathrm{T}}]\{\mat T\} = \{\mat R_{\mathrm{T}}\}\) from the functional (12.2-1), PDF p. 473. Our proof from the strong form with test functions is not from the source.

Equation (14.59) for the bar is a system of ordinary differential equations of first order for \(n - 1\) functions of time: space is already discretized, time is not. We call it semi-discrete (polidiskretna), because it is discrete in space and continuous in time. The form of its solution is given by the same theorem as for vibration, because \(\mat K\) and \(\mat C\) are symmetric and \(\mat C\) is positive definite.

Theorem 14.59 Transient response by modes (prehodni pojav po načinih)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric and \(\mat C\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(m\), and let \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{m}}\) be the eigenvalues and \(\mat C\)-orthonormal eigencolumns of the pair \((\mat K, \mat C)\) of theorem 10.13. For every initial column \(\vek T^0\) the system \(\mat C\dot{\vek T} + \mat K\vek T = \vek 0\) with \(\vek T(0) = \vek T^0\) has exactly one solution

\[\vek T(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{m}\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} t}\,\big(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat C\,\vek T^0\big)\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} . \tag{14.60}\]

If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, then \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) for every \(r\), every mode is a decaying exponential function and \(\vek T(t) \to \vek 0\) as \(t \to \infty\). Higher modes decay faster: mode \(r\) is reduced by the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} t}\) up to time \(t\), and the ratio of this factor to the factor of mode \(1\) is \(\mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_1)t}\).

Proof

We use the decoupling of theorem 10.20, but for an equation of first order.

  1. Let \(\Phi\) be the modal matrix (definition 10.15) and \(\boldsymbol\eta = \Phi^\T\mat C\,\vek T\). By lemma 10.16, \(\Phi^\T\mat C\Phi = \mat I\), \(\Phi^\T\mat K\Phi = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})\) and \(\vek T = \Phi\boldsymbol\eta\). The matrix \(\Phi\) does not depend on time, so \(\dot{\vek T} = \Phi\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}\).
  2. We multiply the equation \(\mat C\dot{\vek T} + \mat K\vek T = \vek 0\) from the left by \(\Phi^\T\): \(\Phi^\T\mat C\Phi\,\dot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \Phi^\T\mat K\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta = \vek 0\), hence \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) for every \(r\).
  3. Conversely, if \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) for all \(r\), then \(\Phi^\T(\mat C\dot{\vek T} + \mat K\vek T) = \vek 0\). The matrix \(\Phi^\T\) is invertible (step 3 of the proof of theorem 10.20), so \(\mat C\dot{\vek T} + \mat K\vek T = \vek 0\). The system and the decoupled equations are equivalent.
  4. By lemma 9.14 (item 1, \(a = -\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(t_0 = 0\)) the equation \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat C\vek T^0\) has exactly one solution \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} t}\). By step 3 the solution of the system is therefore unique, and \(\vek T = \Phi\boldsymbol\eta = \sum_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is equation (14.60).
  5. If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, then by theorem 10.13 \(\lambda_1 = \min\vek v^\T\mat K\vek v > 0\) among the \(\vek v\) with \(\vek v^\T\mat C\vek v = 1\) (the minimum is positive because \(\vek v \ne \vek 0\)), and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_1 > 0\). Hence \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} t} \to 0\) and \(\vek T(t) \to \vek 0\). The ratio is \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} t}/\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_1 t}\).

Source: COOK §12.4 (PDF p. 478 to 479), (12.4-2) to (12.4-5): the modal method, the eigenproblem, normalization with respect to \([\mat C]\) and \(n\) uncoupled equations. The proof with the lemma on the exponential function, the uniqueness and the converse (steps 3 and 4) are not from the source.

The proof showed that a transient problem of the bar behaves like \(m\) independent equations \(\dot\eta + \lambda\eta = 0\), and that the same objects are at work as in vibration, \(\mat C\)-orthogonal eigencolumns, but in time \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\) appears in place of \(\cos\omega t\). In vibration \(\lambda = \omega^2\) and the modes oscillate, here they decay. We saw the same for the bar with the exact series (section 14.5): the modes \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) decay with the factors \(\mathrm{e}^{-n^2\pi^2\kappa t/L^2}\), the higher ones first, unlike the string (chapter 13), where the modes did not decay. Now we have finitely many such modes and can compute them exactly.

The hypothesis of positive definiteness of \(\mat K\) needs a case where it is missing. Let the bar with two elements (\(h_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/2\), \(\rho c A L = 1\), consistent capacity) be insulated at both ends, so all three nodes are free. The matrix \(\mat K = \tfrac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) is not positive definite, because \(\mat K\vek 1 = \vek 0\): a constant temperature causes no flow. Theorem 10.13 still holds for \(\mat K\) without positive definiteness and gives \(\lambda_1 = 0\), \(\lambda_2 = 12\), \(\lambda_3 = 48\) (NumPy, in the unit \(\kappa/L^2\)). The expansion (14.60) remains correct, because the proof did not use the positive definiteness of \(\mat K\) up to step 4. The last part of the theorem does not hold, because the mode with \(\lambda_1 = 0\) does not decay: \(\mathrm{e}^{0} = 1\). For the start \((1, 0, 0)\) K the temperature of the nodes at \(t = 0{,}1\) is \(0{,}403\), \(0{,}248\) and \(0{,}101\) K, and at \(t = 1\) it is \(0{,}25\) K everywhere and stays so. The heat of the bar has been conserved because the insulation does not let it out of the bar, and it has spread evenly. The final temperature is the average weighted by the capacity of the nodes, \(\vek 1^\T\mat C\vek T^0/\vek 1^\T\mat C\vek 1 = 0{,}25\) K. This is the same phenomenon as in the steady problem with only prescribed flows in section 14.3 (lemma 14.18): the matrix is singular and the solution is determined up to a constant.

For a bar with prescribed temperatures at both ends we know the eigenvalues in closed form, as in vibration (theorem 10.36). We compute them for both kinds of capacity, and figure 14.41 after the lemma shows the numbers.

Lemma 14.60 Eigenvalues of a bar with both temperatures prescribed (lastne vrednosti palice s predpisanima temperaturama na koncih)

Let a uniform bar of length \(L\) with \(kA\) and \(\rho c A\) constant have both end sections at temperature \(0\), divided into \(n \ge 2\) equal elements with \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = L/n\), and let \(\kappa = k/(\rho c)\). For \(r = 1, \dots, n - 1\) let \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}} = r\pi/n\) and \(\vek\phi_{\mathrm{r}} = (\sin\theta_{\mathrm{r}}, \sin 2\theta_{\mathrm{r}}, \dots, \sin(n-1)\theta_{\mathrm{r}})^\T\). Then \(\vek\phi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is an eigencolumn of the pair \((\mat K, \mat C)\) and of the pair \((\mat K, \mat C^{\mathrm{z}})\) with the eigenvalues

\[\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{6\kappa}{h_{\mathrm{e}}^2}\,\frac{1 - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{r}}}{2 + \cos\theta_{\mathrm{r}}} , \qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}} = \frac{2\kappa}{h_{\mathrm{e}}^2}\,\big(1 - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{r}}\big) . \tag{14.61}\]

Both sequences increase, \(0 < \lambda_1 < \dots < \lambda_{\mathrm{n}-1}\), and these are all the eigenvalues of each pair. We have \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}} \le r^2\pi^2\kappa/L^2\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}-1}^{\mathrm{k}} < 12\kappa/h_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}-1}^{\mathrm{z}} < 4\kappa/h_{\mathrm{e}}^2\). The consistent matrix does not give eigenvalues below the exact ones, \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{k}} \ge r^2\pi^2\kappa/L^2\).

Proof

We have to show that every row of the equation \(\mat K\vek\phi = \lambda\mat C\vek\phi\) at \(\vek\phi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is satisfied by the same \(\lambda\), and then the inequalities. Let \(\theta = \theta_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\phi_{\mathrm{j}} = \sin j\theta\) for every integer \(j\). At \(j = 0\) and \(j = n\), \(\phi_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\), because \(\sin n\theta = \sin r\pi = 0\).

  1. Row \(j\) (\(1 \le j \le n - 1\)) of \(\mat K\) is \(\tfrac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}(-\phi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + 2\phi_{\mathrm{j}} - \phi_{\mathrm{j}+1})\), where \(\phi_0 = \phi_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) are the removed end sections. By the addition theorem (corollary 8.15, applied to the angles \(j\theta\) and \(\pm\theta\)), \(\sin(j\theta + \theta) + \sin(j\theta - \theta) = 2\sin j\theta\,\cos\theta\), so \(\phi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \phi_{\mathrm{j}+1} = 2\cos\theta\,\phi_{\mathrm{j}}\). The row is \(\tfrac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}(2 - 2\cos\theta)\,\phi_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. Row \(j\) of \(\mat C\) is \(\tfrac{\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}}{6}(\phi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + 4\phi_{\mathrm{j}} + \phi_{\mathrm{j}+1}) = \tfrac{\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}}{6}(4 + 2\cos\theta)\,\phi_{\mathrm{j}}\), and of \(\mat C^{\mathrm{z}}\) it is \(\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}\,\phi_{\mathrm{j}}\) (an interior node has two elements, each with \(\tfrac12\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}\)).
  3. By steps 1 and 2, row \(j\) of the equation \(\mat K\vek\phi = \lambda\mat C\vek\phi\) is \(\tfrac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}(2 - 2\cos\theta)\,\phi_{\mathrm{j}} = \lambda\,\tfrac{\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}}{6}(4 + 2\cos\theta)\,\phi_{\mathrm{j}}\), which \(\lambda^{\mathrm{k}}\) of equation (14.61) satisfies for every \(j\), because \(\tfrac{k}{\rho c} = \kappa\). For \(\mat C^{\mathrm{z}}\) the equation is \(\tfrac{kA}{h_{\mathrm{e}}}(2 - 2\cos\theta)\,\phi_{\mathrm{j}} = \lambda\rho c A h_{\mathrm{e}}\,\phi_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\lambda^{\mathrm{z}}\) satisfies it. The vector \(\vek\phi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is not zero, because \(\phi_1 = \sin\theta_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\).
  4. Increase. The function \(1 - \cos\theta\) has the derivative \(\sin\theta > 0\) on \((0, \pi)\), and the quotient \((1 - \cos\theta)/(2 + \cos\theta)\) has by the quotient rule the derivative \(3\sin\theta/(2 + \cos\theta)^2 > 0\) (as in step 7 of the proof of theorem 10.36). The angles \(\theta_1 < \dots < \theta_{\mathrm{n}-1} = \pi - \pi/n\) lie in \((0, \pi)\), so both sequences increase.
  5. All of them. By theorem 10.13 the pair has \(n - 1\) eigenvalues, and by corollary 10.14 every eigenvalue is one of them. We have \(n - 1\) different ones, so these are all.
  6. Upper bounds. At \(\theta_{\mathrm{n}-1} < \pi\) we have \(\cos\theta > -1\), hence \((1 - \cos\theta)/(2 + \cos\theta) < 2\) (the inequality \(1 - \cos\theta < 4 + 2\cos\theta\) is \(\cos\theta > -1\)) and \(\lambda^{\mathrm{k}} < 12\kappa/h_{\mathrm{e}}^2\). Likewise \(2(1 - \cos\theta) < 4\) and \(\lambda^{\mathrm{z}} < 4\kappa/h_{\mathrm{e}}^2\).
  7. The lumped one is below the exact one. By lemma 10.37, \(1 - \cos\theta \le \theta^2/2\), so \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}} \le \tfrac{2\kappa}{h_{\mathrm{e}}^2}\cdot\tfrac{\theta_{\mathrm{r}}^2}{2} = \kappa\,(\theta_{\mathrm{r}}/h_{\mathrm{e}})^2 = r^2\pi^2\kappa/L^2\), because \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}}/h_{\mathrm{e}} = r\pi/L\).
  8. The consistent one is above the exact one. The consistent pair is a Ritz approximation of the eigenproblem of a bar with both ends clamped (trial space \(\psi_1, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}-1}\), matrix \(\mat K\) from the form \(B\), matrix \(\mat C\) from the form with \(\rho c A\)), so by theorem 13.55 every value lies above the exact one with the same ordinal number. The exact problem \(-(kA\,\phi')' = \lambda\,\rho c A\,\phi\) with \(\phi(0) = \phi(L) = 0\) is the problem of the bar of section 13.3 with \(EA = kA\), \(\rho A = \rho c A\) and \(\lambda = \omega^2\), and its values are \(r^2\pi^2\kappa/L^2\) (theorem 14.26, the expansion in sines).

Source: Not from the source. The computation is the same as in theorem 10.36, there for a bar with one end free, here for prescribed temperatures at both ends. Theorem 13.55 is proved for \(EA\) and \(\rho A\), here with \(kA\) and \(\rho c A\), which is the same computation. COOK PDF p. 478 to 479 does not give the eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) in closed form.

The proof showed that all the eigenvalues are already known. On figure 14.41 the axes are \(r\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). We test them on a bar with eight elements (\(h_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/8\), \(L = \kappa = 1\)). The smallest is \(\lambda_1^{\mathrm{z}} = 9{,}7434\) for lumped and \(\lambda_1^{\mathrm{k}} = 9{,}9971\) for consistent capacity, and the exact value is \(\pi^2 = 9{,}8696\): the lumped one is below, the consistent one above, as steps 7 and 8 claim. The largest is \(\lambda_7^{\mathrm{z}} = 246{,}26\) for lumped and \(\lambda_7^{\mathrm{k}} = 686{,}51\) for consistent, and the bounds are \(4/h_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = 256\) and \(12/h_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = 768\). On the graph these are the grey (exact), orange (consistent) and blue (lumped) values for \(r = 1, \dots, 7\) and the two upper bounds. At low \(r\) the curves are almost together, at high \(r\) they part, because higher modes vary faster along the bar. An arc of mode \(r\) between two consecutive zeros spans \(n/r\) elements, all eight at \(r = 1\), only \(8/7\) elements at \(r = 7\), and a piecewise linear function does not describe such a short arc well (as in vibration, section 10.7.2 of chapter 10).

Everything that follows stands on these numbers (upper bounds): the largest eigenvalue is the phenomenon that the time step must still see. The question is how to compute the solution (14.60) for a body where we do not know the eigenvalues or there are too many to compute. Then we solve equation (14.59) step by step. If the temperature \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\) is known at time \(t_{\mathrm{s}} = s\,\Delta t\), we look for the temperature \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1}\) at time \(t_{\mathrm{s}+1}\). The equation says that the rate of heat storage \(\mat C\dot{\vek T}\) equals the flow \(-\mat K\vek T\). Over a step we compare them by replacing the rate with the difference \((\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1} - \vek T_{\mathrm{s}})/\Delta t\) and computing the flow at a weighted average of the temperatures at the start and the end of the step.

We show the same rule on a single mode \(\dot\eta = -\lambda\eta\), which is the easiest to understand. We draw the axes of time and \(\eta\). Let \(\lambda\,\Delta t = z = 3\) and \(\eta = 1\) at time \(t_{\mathrm{s}}\). The exact solution is the curve \(\mathrm{e}^{-z\tau}\) (\(\tau = (t - t_{\mathrm{s}})/\Delta t\)), at the end of the step \(\mathrm{e}^{-3} = 0{,}0498\). The rule that takes the flow at the start of the step, forward, draws a line with the slope of the curve at the start, \(-\lambda\eta = -3\), and lands at \(1 - 3 = -2\), below zero. The rule that takes the flow at the end of the step, backward, draws a line with the slope that the equation \(\dot\eta = -\lambda\eta\) prescribes at its end point: this slope is \(-\lambda\eta_{\mathrm{s}+1}\), so \(\eta_{\mathrm{s}+1}\) has to be computed at the same time, from \(\eta_{\mathrm{s}+1} = \eta_{\mathrm{s}} - z\,\eta_{\mathrm{s}+1}\). We get \(\eta_{\mathrm{s}+1} = 1/(1 + z) = 0{,}25\), above the exact value. The average of the two, the trapezoidal rule, gives the slope \(-\tfrac{\lambda}{2}(\eta_{\mathrm{s}} + \eta_{\mathrm{s}+1})\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{s}+1} = (1 - z/2)/(1 + z/2) = -0{,}2\).

All three rules are members of one family. We write it for a system.

Definition 14.61 The β-scheme (shema s parametrom β)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric and \(\mat C\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(m\), \(\vek f(t)\) a column of heat loads, \(\Delta t > 0\) a time step, \(t_{\mathrm{s}} = s\,\Delta t\) and \(\vek T_0\) the initial temperature. The scheme with parameter \(\beta \in [0, 1]\) (figure 14.42) for the system \(\mat C\dot{\vek T} + \mat K\vek T = \vek f\) is the sequence of columns \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\) that satisfies

\[\mat C\,\frac{\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1} - \vek T_{\mathrm{s}}}{\Delta t} + \mat K\big((1 - \beta)\,\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} + \beta\,\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1}\big) = (1 - \beta)\,\vek f_{\mathrm{s}} + \beta\,\vek f_{\mathrm{s}+1} , \qquad \vek f_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek f(t_{\mathrm{s}}) . \tag{14.62}\]

At \(\beta = 0\) the scheme is called the forward scheme (shema naprej, forward Euler), at \(\beta = \tfrac12\) the trapezoidal rule or Crank-Nicolson scheme, and at \(\beta = 1\) the backward scheme (shema nazaj, backward Euler).

Source: COOK (12.4-6) to (12.4-8), PDF p. 479: the same scheme with parameter \(\beta\) ("β = 0 forward difference or Euler, β = 1/2 Crank-Nicolson or trapezoidal rule, β = 1 backward difference", PDF p. 480). COOK writes \((\tfrac1{\Delta t}[\mat C] + \beta[\mat K_{\mathrm{T}}])\{\mat T\}_{\mathrm{n}+1} = \dots\), which is equation (14.62) rearranged.

The names have a reason in where we take the flow. At \(\beta = 0\) we take it in the known state and look forward from it, at \(\beta = 1\) in the state we are still looking for, so we look backward from the new time. At \(\beta = \tfrac12\) the flow is the average of the two ends, which is the same average as in the trapezoidal rule of chapter 10 (definition 10.63), here for an equation of first order, and hence the name trapezoidal rule (blackwhite line). At \(\beta = 0\) and a diagonal lumped capacity \(\mat C^{\mathrm{z}}\) the step reduces to a division, \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1} = \vek T_{\mathrm{s}} - \Delta t\,(\mat C^{\mathrm{z}})^{-1}(\mat K\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{s}})\), so lumped capacity is usually combined with the forward scheme (COOK PDF p. 480: little work per step, but \(\Delta t\) is small too). At \(\beta > 0\) every step requires solving a system with the matrix \(\mat C + \beta\Delta t\,\mat K\), which does not depend on \(s\) and which we factor once (COOK PDF p. 479).

What the scheme does with a single mode is told by the following lemma.

Lemma 14.62 Amplification factor of the scheme (ojačitveni faktor sheme)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric and \(\mat C\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(m\) with eigenpairs \((\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})\) of theorem 10.13, \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge 0\), \(\beta \in [0, 1]\) and \(\Delta t > 0\). The matrix \(\mat C + \beta\Delta t\,\mat K\) is positive definite, hence invertible, and the scheme (14.62) with \(\vek f = \vek 0\) gives exactly one sequence \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\) for every \(\vek T_0\). The modal coordinates \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat C\,\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\) satisfy

\[\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}+1} = g_\beta(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t)\,\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}} , \qquad g_\beta(z) = \frac{1 - (1 - \beta)\,z}{1 + \beta\,z} , \tag{14.63}\]

and \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} g_\beta(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t)^s\,\eta_{\mathrm{r},0}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat C\,\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}}^2\).

Proof

We have to show invertibility, the splitting into modes and the sum of squares.

  1. For \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\), \(\vek x^\T(\mat C + \beta\Delta t\,\mat K)\vek x \ge \vek x^\T\mat C\vek x > 0\), because \(\beta\Delta t\,\vek x^\T\mat K\vek x \ge 0\). As in step 5 of the proof of lemma 10.64 this gives invertibility. Equation (14.62) is then \((\mat C + \beta\Delta t\,\mat K)\,\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1} = (\mat C - (1 - \beta)\Delta t\,\mat K)\,\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\) with exactly one solution \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1}\).
  2. We multiply the equation at \(\vek f = \vek 0\) from the left by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\). Since \(\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat C\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\mat K\), \(\mat C\) are symmetric, \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat C\). Hence \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}}\).
  3. From step 2: \((\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}+1} - \eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}})/\Delta t + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\big((1 - \beta)\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}} + \beta\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}+1}\big) = 0\). With \(z = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\) it follows that \((1 + \beta z)\,\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}+1} = (1 - (1 - \beta)z)\,\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}}\), which is equation (14.63).
  4. By corollary 10.14, \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and by induction from step 3, \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}} = g^s\eta_{\mathrm{r},0}\). Since \(\Phi^\T\mat C\Phi = \mat I\) (lemma 10.16), \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat C\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = \boldsymbol\eta_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\boldsymbol\eta_{\mathrm{s}}\).

Source: COOK (12.4-9), PDF p. 479 to 480, states the stability limit without proof ("numerically stable [12.7]"). The proof is not from the source.

The exact solution of a single mode multiplies \(\eta\) by \(\mathrm{e}^{-z}\) over a step (grey curve on the graph of the step). Every scheme multiplies it by a different number. The difference is visible in the expansion (SymPy), \(\mathrm{e}^{-z} - g_\beta(z) = (\tfrac12 - \beta)\,z^2 + O(z^3)\), and at \(\beta = \tfrac12\) it is \(z^3/12 + O(z^4)\). For a small step, forward and backward are therefore accurate to first order (the error per step is of order \(z^2\), over \(1/\Delta t\) steps of order \(\Delta t\)), and the trapezoidal rule to second order (COOK PDF p. 480: "second-order accurate", and only first order for \(\beta \ne \tfrac12\)). A test on the first mode of the lumped bar with eight elements, \(\lambda_1 = 9{,}7434\), at \(\Delta t = 0{,}002\) (\(z = 0{,}0195\)) and time \(t = 0{,}1\) after \(50\) steps: the exact value of the semi-discrete solution is \(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_1 t} = 0{,}37744\). Forward gives \(0{,}37383\) (\(-0{,}96\) %), backward \(0{,}38099\) (\(+0{,}94\) %) and the trapezoidal rule \(0{,}37743\) (\(-0{,}003\) %). All three differ from the true solution of the bar, \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi^2 t} = 0{,}37271\), by another \(1{,}3\) %, but that is an error in space, not in time, and it comes from the elements. The errors of forward and backward have opposite signs and about the same size, because the expansion has the terms \(\pm z^2/2\).

Accuracy is not the only question. At a large step the graph of the step shows that the forward scheme lands below zero, so there must be a condition on the size of the step. Lemma 14.62 gives it exactly: the sequence \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\) is bounded exactly when all \(g^s\) are bounded, that is, when \(|g_\beta(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t)| \le 1\). In chapter 10 we wrote the definition of boundedness for vibration (definition 10.65), here we have it for first order: a scheme is stable (stabilna) at the step \(\Delta t\) if for every start \(\vek T_0\) there is a \(B\) such that \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat C\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} \le B\) for every \(s\).

Theorem 14.63 Stability of the forward scheme (stabilnost sheme naprej)

Let \(\mat K\) be positive definite and \(\mat C\) symmetric positive definite, \(\lambda_{\max}\) the largest eigenvalue of the pair \((\mat K, \mat C)\) and \(\vek f = \vek 0\). The scheme (14.62) at \(\beta = 0\) is stable exactly when

\[\Delta t \le \Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}} . \tag{14.64}\]

At \(\Delta t < \Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) every mode decays in absolute value but changes sign if \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t > 1\). At \(\Delta t > \Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) the sequence is unbounded for every start that has a component \(\eta_{\mathrm{m},0} \ne 0\) in the mode \(m\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = \lambda_{\max}\).

Proof

We use lemma 14.62 with \(\beta = 0\) and \(g_0(z) = 1 - z\).

  1. By the lemma, \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat C\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} g_0(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t)^{2s}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r},0}^2\). If \(|g_0(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t)| \le 1\) for every \(r\), the sum is at most \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r},0}^2 = \vek T_0^\T\mat C\vek T_0\) and the sequence is bounded.
  2. For \(z > 0\), \(|1 - z| \le 1\) exactly when \(0 \le z \le 2\) (for \(z \le 1\), \(1 - z \ge 0\) and less than \(1\), for \(z > 1\), \(|1 - z| = z - 1 \le 1\) at \(z \le 2\)). Since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \le \lambda_{\max}\), the condition for all \(r\) is equivalent to \(\lambda_{\max}\Delta t \le 2\), which is equation (14.64).
  3. If \(\lambda_{\max}\Delta t > 2\), then \(|1 - \lambda_{\max}\Delta t| > 1\), and for a start with \(\eta_{\mathrm{m},0} \ne 0\), \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat C\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} \ge |1 - \lambda_{\max}\Delta t|^{2s}\,\eta_{\mathrm{m},0}^2 \to \infty\) as \(s \to \infty\). The scheme is not stable.
  4. At \(\Delta t < \Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\), \(|g_0| < 1\), so every mode decays. The factor \(1 - \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\) is negative exactly when \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t > 1\), so the mode changes sign at every step.

Source: COOK (12.4-9), PDF p. 479 to 480: "if β < 0,5 the algorithm is conditionally stable", the largest step \(2/\lambda_{\max}\) with the largest eigenvalue (12.4-2) (at \(\beta = 0\)). The proof with lemma 14.62 is not from the source.

The proof showed where the condition comes from: the forward scheme takes \(z\,\eta\) away from the mode \(\eta\) and \((1 - z)\,\eta\) remains. At \(z > 1\) it takes away more than there is of the mode and crosses zero. At \(z > 2\) the overshoot is larger than the original value and the size grows. This is shown by the graph of the step at \(z = 3\) (the orange line ends at \(-2\)) and by the graph of the factor that follows.

On the graph the axes are \(z = \lambda\Delta t\) and \(g\), the exact factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-z}\) is the grey curve that falls from \(1\) towards \(0\) and never becomes negative. The bounds \(\pm 1\) are dashed: inside them the mode is smaller at the end of the step than at the start. The forward scheme is the line \(1 - z\), which crosses the lower bound at \(z = 2\), where \(\Delta t = \Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) for the mode with \(\lambda = \lambda_{\max}\). The number of steps up to a given time is therefore set by the largest eigenvalue, although we are interested in the slow modes.

How much this costs is shown by the numbers for a bar with eight elements (\(L = \kappa = 1\)). Lumped capacity gives \(\lambda_{\max} = 246{,}26\) and \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = 0{,}00812\), consistent \(686{,}51\) and \(0{,}00291\) (lemma 14.60, the upper bounds on the graph of eigenvalues). The lemma also gives an estimate without computing eigenvalues: since \(\lambda_{\max} < 4\kappa/h_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) for lumped and \(< 12\kappa/h_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) for consistent capacity, \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} > h_{\mathrm{e}}^2/(2\kappa)\) and \(> h_{\mathrm{e}}^2/(6\kappa)\) respectively, and every step up to these values is stable. The critical step is therefore proportional to \(h_{\mathrm{e}}^2\). With \(16\) elements \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) of lumped capacity is \(0{,}00197\), which is \(4{,}12\) times less than with eight. A half-size element means a four times smaller step, so four times more steps, and twice as many nodes, so eight times more work in one dimension. The fastest mode contributes nothing meanwhile: in the lumped bar with eight elements it falls to \(1\) % in the time \(\ln 100/\lambda_{\max} = 0{,}0187\), which is \(2{,}3\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\), while the first mode needs \(0{,}473\) to reach \(1\) %. The step of the forward scheme is therefore set by a phenomenon that has long been dead.

The limit is sharp, which we show just before it and just after it on the fastest mode of the lumped bar with eight elements. At \(\Delta t = 0{,}99\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) the factor is \(-0{,}98\): the size after \(100\) steps is \(0{,}133\) of the original and after \(1000\) steps \(1{,}7\cdot 10^{-9}\), the mode decays with sign changes. At \(\Delta t = 1{,}01\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) the factor is \(-1{,}02\): the size after \(100\) steps is \(7{,}2\) times the original and after \(1000\) steps \(4{,}0\cdot 10^{8}\) times. One percent in the step separates a solution from nonsense (the dashed vertical line at \(z = 2\) on the graph of the factor). A start that does not contain the fastest mode hides the limit. Take as the start the values \(\sin(\pi x_{\mathrm{j}})\) at the nodes, which is the first eigencolumn and is \(\mat C\)-orthogonal to the last one up to \(9\cdot 10^{-17}\), and the step \(\Delta t = 10\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\). The first mode is multiplied by \(1 - \lambda_1\Delta t = 0{,}209\) over a step. The largest temperature is \(4{,}0\cdot 10^{-4}\) after five steps, which is the correct value \(0{,}209^5\), so the computation still works then. After ten steps it is \(1{,}0\cdot 10^{-4}\) instead of the correct \(1{,}6\cdot 10^{-7}\), after fifteen \(2{,}6\cdot 10^{2}\) and after twenty \(6{,}6\cdot 10^{8}\), because the rounding error contains the fastest mode, and that grows with the factor \(-19\) per step. That is why the definition of stability demands boundedness for every start: a computation that works with a given start is not yet a stable computation.

Theorem 14.64 Stability of the β-scheme for β ≥ 1/2 (stabilnost sheme s parametrom β pri β ≥ 1/2)

Let \(\mat K\) be positive definite and \(\mat C\) a symmetric positive definite matrix, \(\vek f = \vek 0\) and \(\tfrac12 \le \beta \le 1\). For every \(\Delta t > 0\) and every start \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1}^\T\mat C\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1} < \vek T_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat C\vek T_{\mathrm{s}}\) if \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} \ne \vek 0\), and \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} \to \vek 0\). The scheme is unconditionally stable (brezpogojno stabilna). The factor \(g_\beta(z)\) is positive for every \(z > 0\) exactly at \(\beta = 1\). At \(\tfrac12 \le \beta < 1\), \(g_\beta(z) < 0\) for \(z > 1/(1 - \beta)\), so for the trapezoidal rule at \(z > 2\).

Proof

We use lemma 14.62 and estimate \(g_\beta(z)\) for \(z > 0\).

  1. The denominator \(1 + \beta z\) is positive, so \(g_\beta(z) < 1\) exactly when \(1 - (1 - \beta)z < 1 + \beta z\), that is \(-z < 0\), which holds.
  2. Because of the positive denominator, the inequality \(g_\beta(z) > -1\) is equivalent to \(1 - (1 - \beta)z > -1 - \beta z\), that is \(2 + (2\beta - 1)z > 0\). At \(\beta \ge \tfrac12\), \(2\beta - 1 \ge 0\), so the left side is at least \(2 > 0\) and the inequality holds for every \(z > 0\).
  3. By steps 1 and 2, \(|g_\beta(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t)| < 1\) for every \(r\), and by the lemma \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1}^\T\mat C\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} g^2\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}}^2 < \sum_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}}^2\) if some \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{s}} \ne 0\), that is \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} \ne \vek 0\). Since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) (theorem 14.59), \(g^s \to 0\) as \(s \to \infty\) (a geometric sequence with \(|g| < 1\)), so \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}} \to \vek 0\). The sequence is bounded by \(\vek T_0^\T\mat C\vek T_0\) at every \(\Delta t\).
  4. Sign. At \(\beta = 1\), \(g_1 = 1/(1 + z) > 0\). At \(\beta < 1\) the numerator \(1 - (1 - \beta)z\) is negative exactly when \(z > 1/(1 - \beta)\) and the denominator is positive, so \(g_\beta < 0\). At \(\beta = \tfrac12\) this is \(z > 2\).

Source: COOK PDF p. 480: "If β > 0,5 the algorithm is unconditionally stable in linear problems", "numerical stability (but not accuracy!) is guaranteed as Δt becomes indefinitely large". The same source remarks on the trapezoidal rule "annoying oscillations in response to suddenly imposed temperature changes" (PDF p. 480). The proof and the point about the sign are not from the source.

At \(\beta = \tfrac12\) the theorem holds with the same proof, because \(2\beta - 1 \ge 0\) suffices (COOK states "\(\beta > 0{,}5\)" and lists the trapezoidal rule as unconditionally stable in the table, PDF p. 480). At a large step the backward scheme and the trapezoidal rule have a factor between the bounds, as the blue and blackwhite curve on the graph of the factor show, and the forward scheme only up to the critical point.

A test of theorem 14.64 is the trapezoidal rule at a large step. The theorem says it is stable, and its last point says that this is less than we expect from a computation: the factor is negative at \(z > 2\), and the temperature of a node changes sign, although it should only fall (blackwhite curve below the axis). Let us look at this with numbers at \(z = \lambda_{\max}\Delta t = 20\) (lumped bar with eight elements, \(\Delta t = 0{,}0812\)).

Example 14.65 Crank-Nicolson stable but not sensible (Crank-Nicolson stabilen, a ne smiseln)

A bar with eight elements and lumped capacity (\(L = \kappa = 1\)) has at time \(0\) the temperature \(1\) K at node \(x_4\) and \(0\) elsewhere (start). The step is \(\Delta t = 10\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = 0{,}08122\), \(z_{\max} = 20{,}00\). The factors of the fastest mode are \(g_0 = 1 - 20 = -19{,}00\), \(g_{1/2} = (1 - 10)/(1 + 10) = -0{,}8182\) and \(g_1 = 1/21 = 0{,}0476\). A computation of the three schemes (NumPy, \(\vek T_{\mathrm{s}+1}\) from equation (14.62)) gives for node \(x_4\) and for the lowest temperature on the bar

step \(s\) exact backward trapezoidal forward
1, \(x_4\) \(0{,}1137\) \(0{,}2014\) \(-0{,}4164\) \(-9{,}3957\)
2, \(x_4\) \(0{,}0514\) \(0{,}0841\) \(0{,}4259\) \(142{,}31\)
3, \(x_4\) \(0{,}0233\) \(0{,}0442\) \(-0{,}2607\) \(-2352{,}5\)
1, lowest \(0{,}0430\) \(0{,}0327\) \(-0{,}4164\) \(-9{,}3957\)

The exact solution of the semi-discrete system (theorem 14.59) is positive at all the computed times and decreases at node \(x_4\). The backward scheme is positive and decreases at \(x_4\), but at the first step it is \(0{,}2014\) instead of \(0{,}1137\), because at such a large step it cannot follow the fast modes, which are in reality already dead within one step, and it smooths them out too slowly. The trapezoidal rule has after the first step the temperature \(-0{,}4164\) K at node \(x_4\), below the lowest initial temperature \(0\) K and below the boundary temperature \(0\) K. Heat flows only from a higher temperature to a lower one (lemma 14.4), so no part of the bar can become colder than the coldest thing around it, just as a piece of ice in a freezer does not become colder than the freezer. A scheme that does this is nonsense for a bar, although it is stable. The forward rule is unbounded in this case.

We read the figure by rows. The upper row is the trapezoidal rule, the lower the backward scheme, both with the same start and the same large step. At \(s = 0\) both rows have the hat of the initial field. At \(s = 1\) the upper row has a dip in the middle. The cause is the fast modes. The start has nonzero components only in the odd modes \(r = 1, 3, 5, 7\), because \(\sin(4r\pi/8) = \sin(r\pi/2) = 0\) for even \(r\). At \(z = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t > 2\) the factor \(g_{1/2}\) is negative (theorem 14.64), and this holds for \(r = 3, 5, 7\) with \(z = 6{,}4\), \(14{,}4\) and \(20\) and the factors \(-0{,}52\), \(-0{,}76\) and \(-0{,}82\). The fastest of them, \(\sin(7j\pi/8)\), has an opposite sign from node to node. At node \(x_4\) these three modes give \(-0{,}13\), \(-0{,}19\) and \(-0{,}20\) K after the first step, and the first mode only \(+0{,}11\) K, together \(-0{,}42\) K. At \(s = 2\) and \(s = 3\) the dip and the hill swap places, because the sign of these modes turns at every step and their size falls only with factors between \(0{,}52\) and \(0{,}82\), while the exact solution (grey dashed) has almost nothing of them left, because \(\mathrm{e}^{-z} \le \mathrm{e}^{-6{,}4} = 0{,}0016\). The lower row is smooth and positive. The difference lies in the behaviour of the factors at large \(z\) (figure 14.43): \(g_{1/2} \to -1\) and \(g_1 \to 0\). The backward scheme answers a mode that is already dead within the step with zero, and the trapezoidal rule keeps it at almost the same size. COOK (PDF p. 480) therefore suggests an improved scheme for suddenly imposed temperature changes, which we do not treat here.

The theorem therefore does not say that the computation at a large step is accurate or sensible, only that it is bounded. We choose the scheme by what we demand from the computation (figure 14.43). If we are interested in the slow modes and the temperature must remain sensible, we take the backward scheme, even with a large step, but with an error of first order. If we need second order, we take the trapezoidal rule with a step for which \(\lambda_{\max}\Delta t \le 2\) and \(g_{1/2} \ge 0\). For very short phenomena and lumped capacity the forward scheme is the cheapest per step, but tied to \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\).

What we showed. The transient response of a bar with finite elements is the system \(\mat C\dot{\vek T} + \mat K\vek T = \vek 0\) (lemma 14.58), whose solution is a sum of decaying modes (theorem 14.59) with eigenvalues that we know for a bar with prescribed temperatures (lemma 14.60). Every scheme with parameter \(\beta\) multiplies a mode over a step by \(g_\beta(\lambda\Delta t)\) (lemma 14.62), and stability, sign and accuracy depend on this factor. The forward scheme is stable only at \(\Delta t \le 2/\lambda_{\max}\) (theorem 14.63), the backward scheme and the trapezoidal rule at every step, and the trapezoidal rule changes the sign of modes with \(\lambda\Delta t > 2\) (theorem 14.64). For two- and three-dimensional bodies the matrices are larger, but all three properties remain, because the proofs use only the symmetry of the matrices \(\mat K\) and \(\mat C\) and their positive definiteness, not the shape of the bar (figure 14.43 holds for every mode of every body). The elements for the plane and for space are in chapter 15.

14.12 Connections

The abbreviations of subjects are the same as in section 1.19. In this chapter we computed stresses from the temperature and carried the temperature into finite elements by the weak form. Now we ask what of this is not special to heat. Two things hold for all the following subjects: the equation this chapter solved appears in other fields, and the decay of modes, known from the copper bar, separates heat conduction from vibration.

14.12.1 The same equation in other fields

For a steady field the derivative in time is zero. The equation of theorem 14.8 is then \(\nabla\cdot(k\nabla T) + Q = 0\), and for constant conductivity \(k\) it is \(k\,\nabla^2 T + Q = 0\), where \(\nabla^2\) is the Laplace operator of definition 11.5 and \(Q\) is the power of the source per unit volume. The deflection of a stretched membrane under pressure and the stress function in torsion have the same form, and chapter 16 will treat them (MK, VD). The source (COOK, §12.5, PDF p. 483, read) writes the equation for a variable \(\varphi\) and lists, among others, ground water (hydraulic head), the stretched membrane (lateral deflection), elastic torsion (warping function or Prandtl stress function), electrostatics and potential flow. For the membrane \(k\) is the surface tension and \(Q\) the lateral pressure, for the warping function \(k\) is one and \(Q\) is zero. The letter \(k\) here has another meaning than the shear correction factor of chapter 5, and the letter \(c\) means the specific heat for heat and the wave speed for the string. Fields described by the same equation are called analogous, because the solution of one tells the shape of the solutions of the others. The word says that the equations agree, not the physical quantities.

Let us see what carries over. Take a square region \(\Omega\) of side \(1\) and an edge where \(\varphi = 0\). For heat this condition is a prescribed temperature, for the membrane a clamped edge. Let the source have \(Q/k = 1\). On a rectangle we solved by a series of sines only the equation without a source, with a nonzero temperature on one edge (theorem 14.35, section 14.6). With a source and a zero edge we take a double series of sines. Each term \(\sin m\pi x \sin n\pi y\) is zero on the whole edge, and \(\nabla^2\) multiplies it by \(-\pi^2(m^2 + n^2)\). We expand the constant \(1\) in a series of the same terms. The coefficients are the products of the sine coefficients of the function \(1\) in \(x\) and in \(y\) (formula (13.8)), that is \(\frac{4}{m\pi}\cdot\frac{4}{n\pi} = \frac{16}{\pi^2 m n}\) for odd \(m\) and \(n\) and zero for even ones. We divide these coefficients by \(\pi^2(m^2 + n^2)\), so that \(-\nabla^2\varphi\) equals this series. The series \(\varphi(x, y) = \sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}\ \mathrm{odd}} \frac{16}{\pi^4 m n (m^2 + n^2)} \sin m\pi x \sin n\pi y\) gives \(\varphi = 0{,}0737\) at the centre with \(20\) and with \(30\) odd terms in each direction (NumPy, num-12.out). We do not prove the convergence of the series here. Its contours are closed curves that crowd towards the edge, because \(\varphi\) is steepest at the edge. They are drawn at \(0{,}2\), \(0{,}4\), \(0{,}6\) and \(0{,}8\) of the central value. The cut through the middle \(y = 1/2\) is drawn on the right over the axis \(x\) with the height \(\varphi\). This profile is a dome. We compare it with the parabola \(4x(1-x)\), the shape of the solution on a long strip between \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\). On the strip \(\varphi\) does not depend on \(y\), so the equation is \(\varphi'' = -Q/k\) and the solution is \(\varphi = \frac{Q}{2k}\,x(1-x)\) with the central value \(0{,}1250\). At \(x = 1/4\) the ratio to the centre is \(0{,}7500\) for the strip and \(0{,}778\) for the square. The difference is small, but the centre of the square is much lower (\(0{,}0737\) against \(0{,}1250\)), because part of the source flows out towards the edges \(y = 0\) and \(y = 1\), while in the strip all of it flows out in the direction \(x\).

The theorems carry over with the equation. By theorem 14.17 (point 2), with \(Q = 0\) and \(\varphi = 0\) on the whole edge the solution is zero. A membrane without pressure stays flat, and a stress function without a source is zero. The equation alone therefore does not fix the shape, the solution is awakened only by a source or a nonzero edge. The same theorem with the same proof (the energy \(\int k|\nabla w|^2\), step 8 of the proof) holds for all the fields of this family, so a solution with the boundary conditions of section 14.3 is unique everywhere under the conditions of point 2. The weak form (theorem 14.49) and the functional (lemma 14.51) have the same form for all these fields. The Ritz and Galerkin methods are therefore equal for all of them by theorem 6.44, and the element matrix of lemma 14.53 is for them what the stiffness matrix is for the bar (AK, chapter 15). The source warns here that there may be subtle but important differences in how the equations are used in different fields, so great care is needed when another field is solved by software for heat (COOK, PDF p. 483).

14.12.2 Modes that decay

For the string in chapter 13 and for the bar in section 14.5 the spatial shapes are the same sines \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\). Only the time part differs. For the string mode \(n\) varies in time as \(A\cos(n\omega_1 t) + B\sin(n\omega_1 t)\) with frequency \(n\omega_1\), that is \(n\) times the first (theorem 13.7, point 2, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi c/L\)). For heat it varies as \(e^{-n^2\lambda_1 t}\) with the decay rate \(n^2\lambda_1\), where \(\lambda_1 = \kappa\pi^2/L^2\) (theorem 14.26, equation (14.27)).
