The ratio \(n^2\) instead of \(n\) is no accident. For the string the equation has a second derivative in time, so \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = c^2 (n\pi/L)^2\) and the frequency is a square root. For heat the derivative is of first order, so \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} = \kappa (n\pi/L)^2\) and the root disappears.

Take the copper bar of example 14.27 (length \(L = 80\) cm, \(\kappa = 1{,}1576\) cm²/s, KREYSZIG, §12.6, PDF pp. 587-588), where \(\lambda_1 = 1{,}7852\cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/s. The time in which the amplitude of a mode falls to half is \(\ln 2/(n^2\lambda_1)\) and equals \(388{,}3\) s for \(n = 1\), \(97{,}1\) s for \(n = 2\) and \(43{,}1\) s for \(n = 3\). Both halves of the figure have the same scale, \(2{,}2\) cm per unit of time, but different units. On the left are the amplitudes of heat in units of the halving time of the first mode, on the right the amplitudes of the string in units of the period of the first mode. On the left the blue curve \(n = 1\) falls to one half at time \(1\), the orange one \(n = 2\) already at a quarter of that time and the grey one \(n = 3\) at a ninth. On the right all three curves oscillate about zero, and \(n = 3\) has three times as many oscillations as \(n = 1\). Let all modes start with the same amplitude. The ratio of mode \(n\) to the first is then \(e^{-(n^2 - 1)\lambda_1 t}\), and at time \(388{,}3\) s we have \(\lambda_1 t = \ln 2\). The second mode is then at \(2^{-3} = 0{,}125\) of the amplitude of the first, the third at \(2^{-8} = 0{,}0039\) and the fourth at \(2^{-15} = 0{,}00003\). When the first mode is at one half, the second is therefore only an eighth of the first, and the third and higher ones are below \(0{,}4\) percent of the first. For heat a shortened model with a few first modes (DSK, chapter 21) therefore loses nothing that would last, and the higher modes vanish on their own. For an undamped string every mode still oscillates with full amplitude after that time, so a dropped mode changes the solution for good.

The decoupling into modes also works for finite elements, where theorem 10.13 gives it. For heat this is theorem 14.59, in which each mode decays with \(e^{-\lambda t}\). A consequence is a difference in time stepping. An explicit step for heat must satisfy \(\Delta t \le 2/\lambda_{\max}\) (theorem 14.63). For a bar of equal elements of length \(h\) with lumped capacity, \(\lambda_{\max} < 4\kappa/h^2\), and on a fine mesh it is close to this bound (lemma 14.60, for eight elements and \(L = \kappa = 1\) we have \(\lambda_{\max} = 246{,}26\) against the bound \(256\)). The critical step is therefore slightly above \(h^2/(2\kappa)\) and roughly proportional to \(h^2\). For waves the critical step of central differences with lumped mass is just above \(h/c\) (section 10.12, figure 10.39), roughly proportional to \(h\). When the mesh is refined, the thermal step therefore shrinks faster: for an element of half the length it is about four times shorter, the wave step about two times.

14.12.3 Other connections

  • Thermal stresses: first the temperature by sections 14.2 to 14.6, then the stresses by theorem 14.39 (VT, MK, chapter 11). This is the uncoupled problem (definition 14.38). For bodies of complicated shape we solve it by finite elements: the temperature as a scalar field on a triangle (COOK, §1.3, PDF p. 21, read), the stresses from the initial strain \(\alpha\,\Delta T\) by definition 7.48 and lemma 7.49 (AK, chapter 15). An example in the source (COOK, §12.6, PDF pp. 483-485) computes the steady temperature field of a flanged pipe joint before going on to the stress analysis. The source also notes that the assumption of an insulated contact surface is pessimistic for the stresses, because it increases the nearby temperature gradients, and large gradients are often accompanied by large stresses.
  • Thermal bending: theorem 5.37 of chapter 5 holds only for a temperature linear in height, and lemma 14.41 extends it to an arbitrary temperature (VT, MK). Plates and shells (chapters 18 and 22) are not treated in this section.
  • Weak form and the Ritz method: the Galerkin method does not need a functional, the Ritz method does. Steady conduction has one (lemma 14.51 in section 14.9), so by theorem 6.44 the two agree (AK, VT, chapter 6).
  • Limits of the model: the chapter worked with a rigid conductor at rest, isotropic, with constant \(k\) and \(c\) (section 14.2). Radiation has a heat flux proportional to the fourth power of the absolute temperature and gives a highly nonlinear problem (COOK, §12.3, PDF pp. 476-478, read), and a temperature-dependent conductivity does too (COOK, PDF p. 469). The coupling term that connects temperature and deformation is small for most materials under static or quasi-static loading (SADD, PDF p. 379, read), but the chapter has no quantitative estimate. Fluid flow in contact with a hot body, for example in internal combustion engines and solar collectors, is regarded by the source (CM, §8.3.5, PDF p. 410, read) as a coupled problem outside its scope. When a model is still enough is a question of modelling (AK, chapter 17).
  • The infinite bar: the Fourier integral replaces the series when the bar has no ends and only the initial temperature is given (KREYSZIG, §12.7, PDF pp. 594-599, read). Chapter 9 only named the Fourier integral, its proof is not in the book.
  • Limits of the chapter: proved are uniqueness, the series solutions for the bar and the rectangle, the thermal stresses from the temperature, the weak form and the elements. Cited but not proved are radiation, the dependence of \(k\) on temperature, the size of the coupling term, the Fourier integral, inelastic residual stresses after unequal cooling the convergence of the plane series up to an edge where the temperature jumps (only in the mean), and the convergence of the double sine series for the square with a source. The book has no values of \(k\) and \(c\) for steel, so the steel examples are in dimensionless numbers.

From history

William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, took Fourier's book out of the library on 1 May 1840, at the age of sixteen, and in a fortnight had gone right through it. Maxwell called it a great mathematical poem (CAJORI, PDF p. 287). Kelvin wrote of Fourier's work on heat that it is difficult to say whether its original quality, its transcendent interest or its perennially important instructiveness for physical science is most to be praised (CAJORI, PDF p. 287).

Kelvin thus judged Fourier's work on heat to be instructive for all the physical sciences. Above we saw a small part of this: the same equation, the same theorems and the same methods, different physics.
